# few bottles: the cocktail menu

> Classic drinks from one small home bar, decoded from the house
> shorthand on the printed card.

185 drinks, 89 stirred, 72 shaken, 24 built, 50 ingredients. The interactive app is https://fewbottles.com/. This file is the same menu spelled out, so nothing has to run JavaScript.

Barline reads left to right in build order, base spirit first, and
ends with one token for glass plus garnish. A bare number is ounces
beside a spirit and dashes beside bitters. `h` `q` `Q` are 1/2, 1/4,
3/4 oz, and `t` is a top: fill the glass with the mixer over the ice
already in it. The last token is matched longest-first, so `ccin` is
a coupe with grated cinnamon. Garnish is optional; it never gates a
drink. Egg white takes no measure.

## Stirred

Spirit only. Stir on ice until cold, strain, no dilution past that.

### Aged Rum

#### Pedro Martinez

`2,1,q,3,10,2b,R` · stirred · Aged Rum · Martini family

- 2 oz Aged rum
- 1 oz Sweet vermouth
- 1/4 oz Maraschino liqueur
- 3 dashes Orange bitters
- 10 dashes Angostura bitters
- 2 barspoons Absinthe
- Rocks, iced

Aged rum and sweet vermouth sit two to one, the Martinez ratio, with a quarter ounce of maraschino as the cherry glue. Ten dashes of Angostura is a bark flood, and three orange bitters keep peel in the mix. Two barspoons of absinthe is a pour you can taste, anise laid over the rum. Ice in the rocks glass is the point: this one is meant to sit and dilute.

The Pedro Martinez is a rum Martinez from Michael Shea at Rum Club in Portland, Oregon, published by Imbibe in August 2020. Shea builds it on Demerara rum with Cocchi Vermouth di Torino, maraschino, aromatic bitters, orange bitters, and a few drops of absinthe, stirred and strained over a large cube. It is a modern sugarcane version of the gin Martinez, not a recipe from the nineteenth-century manuals. This menu keeps the two-to-one rum and vermouth, the quarter of maraschino, and the rocks glass with ice, yet it pours ten dashes of Angostura and two barspoons of absinthe, heavier than Shea's drops.

- [Imbibe, Pedro Martinez Cocktail](https://imbibemagazine.com/recipe/pedro-martinez-cocktail/)

#### Rum Old Fashioned

`2,1b,2,1,Ro` · stirred · Aged Rum · Old-Fashioned family

- 2 oz Aged rum
- 1 barspoon Demerara syrup
- 2 dashes Angostura bitters
- 1 dash Orange bitters
- Rocks, iced, Orange twist

Two ounces of aged rum, one barspoon of demerara, nothing more for sugar. The molasses of the syrup and the barrel of the rum are the same family, so the drink reads as rum first, then spice. Two dashes of Angostura and one of orange bitters keep clove and peel in the glass. Rocks, ice, and an orange twist: it sits.

The Old-Fashioned takes its name from drinkers in the 1870s who asked for an old-fashioned whiskey cocktail after bartenders began dressing the Whiskey Cocktail with absinthe, curacao, and other liqueurs. The formula itself is older: spirit, sugar, water, and bitters, the definition printed in The Balance and Columbian Repository in 1806. A rum Old-Fashioned is that template with the whiskey swapped out, a substitution that became common in craft bars in the 2000s as aged rum was treated as a sipping spirit. This menu pours two ounces of aged rum, one barspoon of demerara syrup, two dashes of Angostura, and one of orange bitters, over ice with an orange twist.

- [Difford's Guide, Old Fashioned cocktail history](https://www.diffordsguide.com/g/1198/old-fashioned-cocktail/history)

#### Kingston Negroni

`1,1,1,Ro` · stirred · Aged Rum · Negroni family

- 1 oz Aged rum
- 1 oz Campari
- 1 oz Sweet vermouth
- Rocks, iced, Orange twist

Equal ounces of aged rum, Campari, and sweet vermouth, over ice. Rum in the gin slot puts molasses and overripe fruit where juniper was, and the Campari has to push through that instead of sitting beside it. The cube gives up water slowly, so it rounds off as it stands. Rocks with ice, orange twist.

Joaquín Simó built the Kingston Negroni at Death & Co in New York's East Village in late 2009, the day the importer Eric Seed walked in with a bottle of Smith & Cross, a navy-strength pot-still Jamaican rum. He reached for Carpano Antica for the vermouth, on the grounds that Smith & Cross is no shrinking violet and needed a vermouth that could stand in front of it. The drink went on the Death & Co menu in spring 2010, was on the list at Rickhouse in San Francisco by that autumn, and was printed in the bar's 2014 book. This menu pours an ounce each of aged rum, Campari, and sweet vermouth, stirred, rocks with ice, orange twist.

- [Punch, How the Kingston Negroni Became a Modern Classic](https://punchdrink.com/articles/kingston-negroni-became-modern-classic-jamaican-rum-cocktail-recipe/)

### Apple Brandy

#### So So Cocktail

`1,1,h,h,cc` · stirred · Apple Brandy · Martini family

- 1 oz Gin
- 1 oz Dry vermouth
- 1/2 oz Apple brandy
- 1/2 oz Grenadine
- Coupe, Cherry

Equal gin and dry vermouth, a half ounce of apple brandy riding underneath, and a half ounce of grenadine that tastes of pomegranate. The gin is the drink; the apple is a peel of orchard. Dry vermouth keeps it lean, so the grenadine is the only roundness. Coupe, cherry.

The So So Cocktail appears in Harry MacElhone's 1923 Harry of Ciro's ABC of Mixing Cocktails, credited to Mr. P. Soso, manager of Ciro's Club in London (MacElhone also names the Kit-Kat Club). The printed formula is one-sixth grenadine, one-sixth Calvados, one-third Cinzano vermouth, one-third gin. Harry Craddock repeats it in the 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book with Italian vermouth in place of the brand. This menu files under apple brandy and is mostly gin. It also swaps the Italian vermouth for dry, and it pours a half ounce of grenadine rather than a sixth.

- [Difford's Guide, So So Cocktail](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/1794/so-so-cocktail)
- [The Savoy Cocktail Book (1930), p. 151](https://euvs-vintage-cocktail-books.cld.bz/1930-The-Savoy-Cocktail-Book/151/)

#### Dempsey

`1h,1h,h,q,c` · stirred · Apple Brandy · Fancy family

- 1 1/2 oz Apple brandy
- 1 1/2 oz Gin
- 1/2 oz Grenadine
- 1/4 oz Absinthe
- Coupe

Equal ounces and a half of apple brandy and gin, so neither wins. Half an ounce of grenadine is a real pour, pomegranate against the orchard, and a quarter ounce of absinthe is enough anise to coat the glass. Stirred, no juice, coupe. Pink, wormwood-edged brandy and gin.

Robert Vermeire prints the Dempsey in Cocktails How to Mix Them (1922) and says it was introduced at Deauville in 1921 after Jack Dempsey knocked out Georges Carpentier on 2 July 1921 at Boyle's Thirty Acres in Jersey City, the first million-dollar gate. Vermeire's formula is two-thirds Calvados to one-third gin, with dashes of absinthe and a teaspoon of grenadine. Harry MacElhone, the same year, credits Fred Martin at the Casino de Deauville in 1922, and uses a dash of Anis del Osa. Both claims stay in print. This menu splits apple brandy and gin equally, then pours half an ounce of grenadine and a quarter ounce of absinthe, heavier than the dashes.

- [Difford's Guide, Dempsey](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/629/dempsey)

#### Corpse Reviver No. 1

`1h,Q,Q,cc` · stirred · Apple Brandy · Martini family

- 1 1/2 oz Cognac
- 3/4 oz Apple brandy
- 3/4 oz Sweet vermouth
- Coupe, Cherry

Cognac first, an ounce and a half, then three-quarters each of apple brandy and sweet vermouth. The apple is a second brandy. No juice, no bitters, stirred. Two brandies and vermouth, orchard under grape. Coupe, cherry.

Harry Craddock prints Corpse Reviver No. 1 in The Savoy Cocktail Book in 1930: half brandy, a quarter apple brandy or Calvados, a quarter Italian vermouth, "to be taken before 11 a.m., or whenever steam and energy are needed." Difford's Guide notes that the drink is sometimes credited to Frank Meier at the Ritz Bar in Paris, although Meier makes no claim in his 1936 The Artistry of Mixing Drinks. The No. 2, gin, Lillet, orange liqueur, lemon, and absinthe, is a different cocktail and is not on this menu. This one leads with cognac. The menu pours an ounce and a half of cognac and three-quarters each of apple brandy and sweet vermouth.

- [Difford's Guide, Corpse Reviver No.1 (Savoy recipe)](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/471/corpse-reviver-no1-savoy-recipe)

#### Newark

`1,1,h,h,c` · stirred · Apple Brandy · Martini family

- 1 oz Apple brandy
- 1 oz Sweet vermouth
- 1/2 oz Fernet
- 1/2 oz Maraschino liqueur
- Coupe

Equal ounces of apple brandy and sweet vermouth, a fifty-fifty Manhattan on orchard. Half an ounce of Fernet, half an ounce of maraschino, so mint and cherry sit against the apple. Stirred, coupe, no twist.

Jim Meehan prints the Newark in The PDT Cocktail Book (2011), credited to bartender Jim Kearns: equal Laird's apple brandy and sweet vermouth, a quarter ounce each of Fernet-Branca and maraschino, orange twist. It is a Red Hook with apple brandy in place of rye and Fernet in place of some of the maraschino. This menu keeps the equal apple and vermouth, yet it pours a half ounce each of Fernet and maraschino, and it skips the twist.

- [Punch, Newark](https://punchdrink.com/recipes/newark/)
- [Difford's Guide, Newark](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/3175/newark)

### Cognac

#### Burnt Fuselage

`1,1,1,c` · stirred · Cognac · Martini family

- 1 oz Cognac
- 1 oz Dry vermouth
- 1 oz Orange liqueur
- Coupe

Equal ounces of cognac, dry vermouth, and orange liqueur, so the orange is a third of the drink. Candied peel sits against the cognac; dry vermouth cuts the sugar. Stirred, no bitters, coupe, no twist. A stiff orange Manhattan, grape and peel.

The Burnt Fuselage first appears in Harry MacElhone's 1927 Barflies and Cocktails, in the Cocktails Around Town section listing drinks of regulars at Harry's New York Bar in Paris. MacElhone credits Colonel C.W. Chuck Kerwood of Philadelphia, President of the International League of Aviators, who wanted a stiff steadier when he came down to earth: one-third Grand Marnier, one-third cognac, and one-third French vermouth. Kerwood was known as the wild man of aviation. This menu keeps the equal parts and the coupe, with no bitters and no twist.

- [Difford's Guide, Burnt Fuselage](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/4912/burnt-fuselage)

#### Palace Hotel

`1h,1h,1b,cl` · stirred · Cognac · Martini family

- 1 1/2 oz Cognac
- 1 1/2 oz Sweet vermouth
- 1 barspoon Orange liqueur
- Coupe, Lemon twist

Equal ounces and a half of cognac and sweet vermouth, grape on grape, a Manhattan ratio. One barspoon of orange liqueur is peel. No bitters. Stirred, coupe, lemon twist. A brandy Manhattan with a thin orange film.

A drink called Palace Hotel does not appear in the pre-1970 manuals under that name, nor in Difford's, Punch, or Imbibe. The nearest parent is the Harvard, which George J. Kappeler prints in 1895 Modern American Drinks: equal brandy and Italian vermouth, gum, Angostura, and a seltzer top. Albert Stevens Crockett, in Old Waldorf Bar Days (1931), ties the name to the college on the Charles. This menu keeps the equal cognac and sweet vermouth and the lemon twist, yet it drops the bitters and the soda, and puts a barspoon of orange liqueur in their place.

- [Difford's Guide, Harvard](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/934/harvard)

#### Metropole

`1h,1h,2,1,cc` · stirred · Cognac · Martini family

- 1 1/2 oz Cognac
- 1 1/2 oz Dry vermouth
- 2 dashes Peychaud's bitters
- 1 dash Orange bitters
- Coupe, Cherry

Equal ounces and a half of cognac and dry vermouth, so neither wins. Two dashes of Peychaud's pull it toward cherry and anise. One dash of orange bitters is peel on the dry vermouth. Stirred, coupe, cherry. It reads pink and lean.

George J. Kappeler prints the Metropole in 1895 Modern American Drinks as the house cocktail of the Hotel Metropole at Broadway and 42nd Street: equal brandy and French vermouth, gum, Peychaud's, orange bitters, and a cherry. It is a dry, Peychaud's turn on O.H. Byron's 1884 Metropolitan. Albert Stevens Crockett, in The Old Waldorf Bar Days (1931), calls the hotel somewhat lively. The street-level Cafe Metropole held an all-night license; Herman Rosenthal was shot outside it in 1912, and the hotel went bankrupt that July. This menu keeps Kappeler's equal parts, two dashes of Peychaud's, one of orange bitters, and the cherry. No gum.

- [Difford's Guide, Metropole](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/2496/metropole)
- [Esquire, Metropole (David Wondrich)](https://www.esquire.com/food-drink/drinks/recipes/a3711/metropole-drink-recipe/)

#### Brandy Crusta

`2,q,q,q,2,Rl` · stirred · Cognac · Daisy family

- 2 oz Cognac
- 1/4 oz Maraschino liqueur
- 1/4 oz Demerara syrup
- 1/4 oz Lemon juice
- 2 dashes Angostura bitters
- Rocks, iced, Lemon twist

Two ounces of cognac, then a quarter each of maraschino, demerara, and lemon. The lemon is an accent; the drink is still a cocktail. Two dashes of Angostura sit under cherry and brown sugar. Stirred. Rocks with ice and a lemon twist. It sits.

Joseph Santini, an Italian bartender in New Orleans, built the Crusta in the 1850s, either at the City Exchange in the French Quarter or at Jewel of the South on Gravier Street, which he opened in 1855. Jerry Thomas prints it in the 1862 Bar-Tender's Guide, misspelling Santini as Santina and calling him Spanish. The name is the sugar crust on the rim; the lemon is a dash, not a pour. David Wondrich, in The Oxford Companion, treats that citrus as an accent, and traces the Sidecar through the Daisy instead. This menu pours two ounces of cognac, a quarter each of maraschino, demerara, and lemon, two dashes of Angostura, over ice, no crust.

- [The Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails, The Brandy Crusta](https://www.spiritsanddistilling.com/dictionary/acref-9780199311132-e-266)
- [Difford's Guide, Brandy Crusta](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/310/brandy-crusta)

#### Ritz

`Q,h,q,q,3,cfo` · stirred · Cognac · Daisy family

- 3/4 oz Cognac
- 1/2 oz Maraschino liqueur
- 1/4 oz Demerara syrup
- 1/4 oz Lemon juice
- 3 dashes Angostura bitters
- Coupe, Flamed orange twist

Three-quarters of an ounce of cognac, so this is a small drink. Half an ounce of maraschino is the sweet and the cherry; a quarter each of demerara and lemon. Three dashes of Angostura is a lot of bark for so little spirit. Stirred, coupe, flamed orange twist.

Dale DeGroff built a Ritz Cocktail at Aurora in New York in 1985, later printed in The Craft of the Cocktail (2002) as a tribute to the Ritz drinks of Paris and Madrid: three-quarters cognac, half orange liqueur, a quarter each of maraschino and lemon, topped with Champagne, and a flamed orange twist. This menu keeps the small cognac, the maraschino, the lemon, and the flamed twist. It drops the Champagne and the orange liqueur, adds a quarter of demerara and three dashes of Angostura, and stirs it.

- [Imbibe, Ritz Cocktail](https://imbibemagazine.com/recipe/ritz-cocktail/)
- [Difford's Guide, Ritz Cocktail](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/1677/ritz-cocktail)

### Bourbon

#### Old-Fashioned

`2,1b,2,R` · stirred · Bourbon · Old-Fashioned family

- 2 oz Bourbon
- 1 barspoon Demerara syrup
- 2 dashes Angostura bitters
- Rocks, iced

Two ounces of bourbon, one barspoon of demerara, two dashes of Angostura. The sugar is a film; the bitters are bark and clove against the corn. Rocks with ice. It sits.

The cocktail itself is spirit, sugar, water, and bitters, defined in The Balance and Columbian Repository on 13 May 1806. By the 1870s bartenders were dressing the Whiskey Cocktail with curacao, maraschino, and absinthe; drinkers who wanted the older formula asked for an old-fashioned whiskey cocktail. Robert Hess and David Wondrich, in The Oxford Companion, reject the Pendennis Club origin: Chicago papers were already talking about old-fashioned cocktails in 1880, a year before the Louisville club was founded. This menu pours two ounces of bourbon, one barspoon of demerara, and two dashes of Angostura, over ice. No fruit.

- [The Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails, The Old-Fashioned Cocktail](https://www.spiritsanddistilling.com/dictionary/acref-9780199311132-e-377)
- [Difford's Guide, Old Fashioned cocktail history](https://www.diffordsguide.com/g/1198/old-fashioned-cocktail/history)

#### Boulevardier

`1h,1,1,R` · stirred · Bourbon · Negroni family

- 1 1/2 oz Bourbon
- 1 oz Campari
- 1 oz Sweet vermouth
- Rocks, iced

An ounce and a half of bourbon against a full ounce each of Campari and sweet vermouth. The whiskey leads a little; Campari is nearly a third of the drink. Stirred, rocks with ice. Bitter orange, grape, and corn whiskey, and the cube.

The Boulevardier first appears in print in Harry MacElhone's 1927 Barflies and Cocktails, not in the main recipe list but in Arthur Moss's Cocktails Round Town essay, credited to Erskine Gwynne. Gwynne was an American in Paris who edited a monthly magazine of the same name from 1927 to 1932; Moss prints it as equal parts Campari, Italian vermouth, and bourbon. Ted Haigh notes that Americans had barely heard of Campari in 1927, and that the Negroni would not see print for another twenty years. This menu keeps the bourbon and the rocks glass, yet it pours an ounce and a half of whiskey against an ounce each of Campari and sweet vermouth.

- [Imbibe, History Lesson: The Boulevardier](https://imbibemagazine.com/the-history-of-the-boulevardier-cocktail/)
- [Punch, In Search of the Ultimate Boulevardier](https://punchdrink.com/articles/ultimate-best-boulevardier-cocktail-recipe/)

#### Fancy Cocktail

`1h,q,1b,2,cl` · stirred · Bourbon · Fancy family

- 1 1/2 oz Bourbon
- 1/4 oz Orange liqueur
- 1 barspoon Demerara syrup
- 2 dashes Angostura bitters
- Coupe, Lemon twist

An ounce and a half of bourbon, a quarter ounce of orange liqueur, one barspoon of demerara, two dashes of Angostura. The orange liqueur is peel and a little sugar. Stirred, coupe, lemon twist. An Old-Fashioned with curacao in the sugar slot, served up.

Jerry Thomas prints the Fancy Brandy Cocktail and Fancy Gin Cocktail in the 1862 Bar-Tender's Guide as the plain Cocktail strained into a fancy wine-glass, lemon on the rim and a piece of peel thrown on top. Wayne Curtis, in Imbibe, notes that the difference is mostly the glass. Thomas's later Improved Cocktail is the one that adds maraschino and absinthe; the version here is the older fancy, whiskey with a splash of orange liqueur rather than those. This menu pours an ounce and a half of bourbon, a quarter of orange liqueur, a barspoon of demerara, two dashes of Angostura, coupe, lemon.

- [Imbibe, Mixopedia: Fancy Drinks](https://imbibemagazine.com/mixopedia-fancy-drinks/)

#### Manhattan

`2,1,2,cc` · stirred · Bourbon · Martini family

- 2 oz Bourbon
- 1 oz Sweet vermouth
- 2 dashes Angostura bitters
- Coupe, Cherry

Two ounces of bourbon to one of sweet vermouth, so the whiskey leads. Two dashes of Angostura sit under the vermouth's grape and spice. Stirred, coupe, cherry. Corn, bark, and the cherry at the bottom.

The Manhattan is American whiskey, Italian vermouth, and bitters, first named in print in an 1882 Gotham Gossip column syndicated out of New York, and first given a full recipe in O.H. Byron's 1884 The Modern Bartenders' Guide. The Manhattan Club dinner for Samuel Tilden in 1874, later tied to Jennie Jerome, is a late story: she was in England with a month-old Winston Churchill. William F. Mulhall, writing in 1923, credited a man named Black who kept a place on Broadway; David Wondrich found George Black's Manhattan Inn near Houston Street in the 1870s. Early books call for rye or bourbon, often at equal parts. This menu files under bourbon, pours two to one, two dashes of Angostura, coupe, cherry.

- [The Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails, The Manhattan Cocktail](https://www.spiritsanddistilling.com/dictionary/acref-9780199311132-e-359)
- [Difford's Guide, Manhattan cocktail history](https://www.diffordsguide.com/g/1221/manhattan-cocktail/history)

#### Fancy Free

`2,h,1,1,Ro` · stirred · Bourbon · Fancy family

- 2 oz Bourbon
- 1/2 oz Maraschino liqueur
- 1 dash Angostura bitters
- 1 dash Orange bitters
- Rocks, iced, Orange twist

Two ounces of bourbon, half an ounce of maraschino. One dash of Angostura, one of orange bitters. The cherry liqueur is almond and pit as much as fruit, and it does the sweetening. Stirred, rocks with ice, orange twist.

The Fancy Free first appears in Crosby Gaige's Cocktail Guide and Ladies' Companion, printed in 1941: a jigger of Fine Arts whiskey, two dashes of maraschino, a dash each of Angostura and orange bitters, shaken, strained into a sugar-rimmed cocktail glass. Gaige was a New York publisher and theatrical producer; Punch treats the naming as his. Revival bartenders, working from Milk & Honey spec sheets, dropped the sugar rim, stirred it, and poured it over ice with an orange twist. This menu keeps the two ounces of bourbon, the half ounce of maraschino, one dash of each bitters, rocks, orange.

- [Punch, Bring Back the Fancy Free](https://punchdrink.com/articles/bring-back-the-fancy-free/)
- [Difford's Guide, Fancy Free](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/738/fancy-free)

#### Frisco

`2,h,R` · stirred · Bourbon · Fancy family

- 2 oz Bourbon
- 1/2 oz Bénédictine
- Rocks, iced

Two ounces of bourbon, half an ounce of Bénédictine, nothing else. Honey, baking spice, and herbs against the whiskey. Stirred, rocks with ice. Short, sweet, herbal whiskey.

The Frisco first prints in William "Cocktail Bill" Boothby's 1934 The World's Drinks and How to Mix Them as three-quarters of a jigger of whisky and a quarter of Bénédictine, stirred on a lump of ice with a lemon twist and a water chaser. Lucius Beebe repeats it in 1946 as two ounces of bourbon and three-quarters of Bénédictine, up. David Embury, in 1948, allows lemon juice; later books split the drink into a Frisco and a Frisco Sour. This menu keeps Boothby's two-ingredient whiskey and Bénédictine, on bourbon, over ice, no juice and no twist.

- [Difford's Guide, Frisco Sour](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/2417/frisco-sour)

#### Derby

`2,Q,h,h,cm` · stirred · Bourbon · Daisy family

- 2 oz Bourbon
- 3/4 oz Lime juice
- 1/2 oz Sweet vermouth
- 1/2 oz Orange liqueur
- Coupe, Mint

Two ounces of bourbon against three-quarters of an ounce of lime, so the lime is loud. Half an ounce each of sweet vermouth and orange liqueur dress it: grape and peel under the citrus. Stirred, despite the juice. Coupe, mint. Bourbon and lime sit in the same glass, cold.

At least three drinks share the name Derby. The gin-and-peach-bitters version is Harry MacElhone, 1926, later in the Savoy. The version here is the bourbon one: lime, sweet vermouth, and orange curacao, which Ted Haigh reprints from Trader Vic's 1947 Bartender's Guide, one of three Derbies Vic listed. Vic's formula is a short pour of bourbon against a heavy lime, and it is shaken. This menu keeps the lime, the vermouth, the orange liqueur, and the mint, yet it pours two ounces of bourbon and stirs the drink.

- [Serious Eats, The Derby](https://www.seriouseats.com/derby-cocktail-bourbon-vermouth-grand-marnier-lime-recipe)

#### Cock 'n' Bull Special

`Q,Q,h,q,1,R` · stirred · Bourbon · Fancy family

- 3/4 oz Bourbon
- 3/4 oz Bénédictine
- 1/2 oz Cognac
- 1/4 oz Orange liqueur
- 1 dash Angostura bitters
- Rocks, iced

Three-quarters of an ounce of bourbon, three-quarters of Bénédictine, so the herbal liqueur is a full partner. Half an ounce of cognac, a quarter of orange liqueur, one dash of Angostura. Stirred, rocks with ice. Honey, orange peel, grape, corn, and bark, a small drink that sits.

The Cock 'n' Bull Special is named for Jack Morgan's British-style pub on Hollywood's Sunset Strip, opened in 1937 and later the house of the Moscow Mule. Ted Saucier prints it in Bottom's Up (1951) as a courtesy of the Cock 'n Bull: half an ounce of brandy, three-quarters each of Bénédictine and bourbon, a quarter of Cointreau, stirred, poured over a cube in a large chilled champagne glass, orange twist. The drink therefore dates between the bar's opening and 1951. This menu keeps those measures and adds a dash of Angostura, over ice in a rocks glass, no twist.

- [Difford's Guide, Cock N' Bull](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/30469/cock-n-bull)

#### Fanciulli

`2,Q,q,cl` · stirred · Bourbon · Martini family

- 2 oz Bourbon
- 3/4 oz Sweet vermouth
- 1/4 oz Fernet
- Coupe, Lemon twist

Two ounces of bourbon, three-quarters of sweet vermouth, and a quarter ounce of Fernet standing where the bitters would be. That quarter is enough to run mint and bitter bark the whole length of the drink. Stirred, coupe, lemon twist. A Manhattan with menthol in it.

Albert Stevens Crockett prints the Fanciulli in Old Waldorf Bar Days in 1931, recording what the Waldorf bar poured before Prohibition. The name is usually read as Francesco Fanciulli, the Italian-born composer who took the United States Marine Band over from John Philip Sousa in 1892; Crockett weighed and rejected a link to Puccini's La fanciulla del West, noting that the drink's origin considerably antedates the premiere of that opera at the Metropolitan on 10 December 1910. The old formula is two parts whiskey to one each of sweet vermouth and Fernet-Branca; most bars now pour a quarter ounce. This menu pours two ounces of bourbon, three-quarters of sweet vermouth, and a quarter of Fernet, coupe, lemon twist.

- [Difford's Guide, Fanciulli](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/25114/fanciulli)

### Rye

#### Old Pal

`1,1,1,1b,R` · stirred · Rye · Negroni family

- 1 oz Rye
- 1 oz Campari
- 1 oz Dry vermouth
- 1 barspoon Demerara syrup
- Rocks, iced

Equal ounces of rye, Campari, and dry vermouth, so Campari is a third of the drink. Bitter orange and rye heat sit against a dry wine cut, and one barspoon of demerara is brown sugar in a lean formula, rounding the Campari. Rocks with ice. It sits.

The Old Pal first prints in Harry MacElhone's 1927 Barflies and Cocktails, not in the A-Z list but in Arthur Moss's Cocktails Round Town essay, the same appendix that carries the Boulevardier. Moss credits William "Sparrow" Robinson, sports editor of the New York Herald in Paris, with equal parts Canadian Club, Italian vermouth, and Campari, dedicated to Moss as My Old Pal. However, by the 1929 edition of Harry's ABC of Mixing Cocktails the vermouth is French, dry, and that is the formula that stuck. This menu keeps equal rye, Campari, and dry vermouth, adds a barspoon of demerara, and pours it over ice.

- [Difford's Guide, Old Pal](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/1430/old-pal)
- [Serious Eats, The Old Pal and a New Friend](https://www.seriouseats.com/classic-cocktail-old-pal-cocktail-history-harry-macelhone)

#### Saratoga

`1,1,1,2,cl` · stirred · Rye · Martini family

- 1 oz Rye
- 1 oz Cognac
- 1 oz Sweet vermouth
- 2 dashes Angostura bitters
- Coupe, Lemon twist

Equal ounces of rye, cognac, and sweet vermouth, so neither spirit leads. The cognac rounds the rye; two dashes of Angostura sit under grape and barrel. Stirred, coupe, lemon. A Manhattan that split the whiskey with brandy.

David Wondrich, in The Oxford Companion, treats the Saratoga as two competing drinks that shared the name of the New York spa town. Jerry Thomas's posthumous 1887 Bar-Tenders Guide prints equal ponies of brandy, whiskey, and vermouth with two dashes of Angostura, shaken, in a claret glass with a quarter slice of lemon. Harry Johnson, the following year, printed a fancy brandy cocktail with a squirt of champagne. For thirty years the books took sides; by the 1930s both were a memory. This menu is Thomas's split-base Manhattan: one ounce each of rye, cognac, and sweet vermouth, two dashes of Angostura, coupe, lemon.

- [Difford's Guide, Saratoga Cocktail](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/2196/saratoga-cocktail)
- [The Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails, The Saratoga](https://www.spiritsanddistilling.com/dictionary/acref-9780199311132-e-409)

#### Monte Carlo

`1Q,h,1,R` · stirred · Rye · Fancy family

- 1 3/4 oz Rye
- 1/2 oz Bénédictine
- 1 dash Angostura bitters
- Rocks, iced

An ounce and three-quarters of rye against a half ounce of Benedictine. Honey, baking spice, and herbs ride on the whiskey, and one dash of Angostura is bark at the end. Rocks with ice. It sits.

The Monte Carlo first prints in David Embury's 1948 The Fine Art of Mixing Drinks: one part Benedictine, two parts rye, one or two dashes of Angostura, shaken with cracked ice. Embury, a New York tax lawyer, called it a bit on the sweet side and suggested lemon juice and more rye. No bartender or bar is named. The drink is a Manhattan with Benedictine in place of vermouth, served here over ice. This menu pours an ounce and three-quarters of rye, a half ounce of Benedictine, and one dash of Angostura.

- [Difford's Guide, Monte Carlo](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/2506/monte-carlo)

#### Improved Coctail

`2,1b,1b,1b,2,Rl` · stirred · Rye · Old-Fashioned family

- 2 oz Rye
- 1 barspoon Maraschino liqueur
- 1 barspoon Absinthe
- 1 barspoon Simple syrup
- 2 dashes Angostura bitters
- Rocks, iced, Lemon twist

Two ounces of rye, then a barspoon each of maraschino, absinthe, and simple. The absinthe is in the drink, anise against cherry pit and sugar. Two dashes of Angostura. Rocks with ice, lemon. Rye first, then wormwood.

Jerry Thomas prints the Improved Whiskey Cocktail in the 1876 Bar-Tender's Guide as the Improved Brandy Cocktail with whiskey in place of brandy: Boker's or Angostura, gum, maraschino, a dash of absinthe, lemon oil, shaken. The improvement is European liqueur on the old cocktail of spirit, sugar, and bitters, the same dressing drinkers later asked to skip when they called for an old-fashioned whiskey cocktail. The name here spells it Coctail, as the paper menu does. This menu pours two ounces of rye, a barspoon each of maraschino, absinthe, and simple, two dashes of Angostura, over ice with a lemon twist.

- [Difford's Guide, Improved Whiskey Cocktail](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/5083/improved-whiskey-cocktail)
- [Eater, Building on a Classic: the Evolution of the Improved Cocktail](https://www.eater.com/drinks/2016/4/1/11322654/cocktail-recipe-maraschino-absinthe-cheers)

#### Sazerac

`2,1b,4,r,r` · stirred · Rye · Old-Fashioned family

- 2 oz Rye
- 1 barspoon Simple syrup
- 4 dashes Peychaud's bitters
- rinse Absinthe
- Rocks

Two ounces of rye, one barspoon of simple, four dashes of Peychaud's. The absinthe is a rinse, a thin anise film on the glass. Four dashes of Peychaud's is a lot: cherry and spice, enough to pink the drink. Rocks with no ice. The barspoon of sugar is the softness in it.

The Sazerac takes its name from Sazerac de Forge et Fils cognac, imported into New Orleans by Sewell Taylor around 1850 and poured at the Sazerac Coffee House with Antoine Peychaud's bitters. Thomas Handy took the bar around 1870; phylloxera wrecked French stocks, and rye replaced the cognac. Stanley Clisby Arthur's 1937 Famous New Orleans Drinks credits Leon Lamothe with the absinthe around 1870. However, David Wondrich treats the named drink as later, a bottled whiskey cocktail first printed by William T. Boothby in 1908. New Orleans named it the official cocktail of the city in 2008. This menu pours two ounces of rye, one barspoon of simple, four dashes of Peychaud's, an absinthe rinse, rocks with no ice.

- [Difford's Guide, Sazerac (New Orleans style)](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/3390/sazerac-new-orleans-style)

#### Red Hook

`2,h,h,cc` · stirred · Rye · Martini family

- 2 oz Rye
- 1/2 oz Sweet vermouth
- 1/2 oz Maraschino liqueur
- Coupe, Cherry

Two ounces of rye, then a half ounce each of sweet vermouth and maraschino. The vermouth is grape and sugar; the cherry liqueur is almond and pit. Stirred, coupe, cherry. Rye first, then a thin cherry film.

Vincenzo Errico built the Red Hook at Sasha Petraske's Milk & Honey in New York in 2003, a Manhattan crossed with a Brooklyn and named for the south Brooklyn neighborhood. Errico, an Italian bartender Petraske brought over after opening Milk & Honey London, used Punt e Mes, the bittersweet Turin vermouth, with rye and maraschino. He told Imbibe a fellow Italian neighbor in Brooklyn suggested the name. This menu keeps the two ounces of rye and the half ounce of maraschino, yet it pours sweet vermouth in place of Punt e Mes.

- [Imbibe, Red Hook Cocktail](https://imbibemagazine.com/recipe/red-hook-recipe/)

#### Waldorf

`2,Q,q,2,cc` · stirred · Rye · Martini family

- 2 oz Rye
- 3/4 oz Sweet vermouth
- 1/4 oz Absinthe
- 2 dashes Angostura bitters
- Coupe, Cherry

Two ounces of rye, three-quarters sweet vermouth, a quarter ounce of absinthe. The absinthe is in the drink, anise over grape, and two dashes of Angostura sit under both. Stirred, coupe, cherry. A Manhattan with wormwood in it.

Jacques Straub prints the Waldorf in 1913 Manual of Mixed Drinks as equal rye, Italian vermouth, and absinthe, with two dashes of orange bitters, shaken. Albert Stevens Crockett repeats it in Old Waldorf Bar Days (1931) as a third each of whiskey, absinthe, and Italian vermouth, a dash of Manhattan bitters, frappe, from the old Waldorf Hotel on Fifth Avenue, demolished in 1929 for the Empire State Building. Dale DeGroff later cut the absinthe to a rinse. This menu pours two ounces of rye, three-quarters sweet vermouth, a quarter ounce of absinthe, and two dashes of Angostura, coupe, cherry.

- [Difford's Guide, Waldorf No. 1](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/2600/waldorf-cocktail-no1)

#### The Slope

`2h,Q,q,1,cc` · stirred · Rye · Martini family

- 2 1/2 oz Rye
- 3/4 oz Sweet vermouth
- 1/4 oz Apricot liqueur
- 1 dash Angostura bitters
- Coupe, Cherry

Two and a half ounces of rye, three-quarters sweet vermouth, a quarter of apricot liqueur. Stone fruit against a large rye pour. One dash of Angostura. Stirred, coupe, cherry. The apricot is orchard on a Manhattan.

Julie Reiner built The Slope in 2006 and named it for Park Slope, first served at Flatiron Lounge, then as the house Manhattan at Clover Club, which she opened in Brooklyn in 2008. Jim Meehan printed the rye, Punt e Mes, apricot, and Angostura formula in GQ in 2010. This menu keeps the two and a half ounces of rye, three-quarters vermouth, and a quarter of apricot, yet it pours sweet vermouth in place of Punt e Mes.

- [Difford's Guide, The Slope](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/2853/the-slope)
- [GQ, The Platinum Age of the Cocktail](https://www.gq.com/story/the-platinum-age-of-the-cocktail-2)

#### Vieux Carré

`Q,Q,Q,1b,1,1,Rl` · stirred · Rye · Martini family

- 3/4 oz Rye
- 3/4 oz Cognac
- 3/4 oz Sweet vermouth
- 1 barspoon Bénédictine
- 1 dash Angostura bitters
- 1 dash Peychaud's bitters
- Rocks, iced, Lemon twist

Three-quarters of an ounce each of rye, cognac, and sweet vermouth, equal and small. One barspoon of Benedictine is honey and herbs. One dash of Angostura, one of Peychaud's. Rocks with ice, lemon. Split-base Manhattan with an herbal film.

Walter Bergeron, head bartender at the Hotel Monteleone in New Orleans, built the Vieux Carré in the 1930s and named it for the French Quarter, the old square. Stanley Clisby Arthur prints it in 1937: equal rye, cognac, and Italian vermouth, a half teaspoon of Benedictine, a dash each of Peychaud's and Angostura. The Carousel Bar, where the drink now lives, opened in 1949; Bergeron was mixing it in the hotel's earlier lounge. Chuck Taggart, in The Oxford Companion, notes Bergeron had worked the bar before Prohibition and returned at Repeal. This menu keeps the equal three-quarters and both bitters, with a barspoon of Benedictine, over ice with a lemon twist.

- [Difford's Guide, Vieux Carré Cocktail](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/2048/vieux-carre-cocktail)
- [The Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails, The Vieux Carré](https://www.spiritsanddistilling.com/dictionary/acref-9780199311132-e-442)

#### Cocktail de la Louisiane

`Q,Q,Q,2b,3,clc` · stirred · Rye · Martini family

- 3/4 oz Rye
- 3/4 oz Sweet vermouth
- 3/4 oz Bénédictine
- 2 barspoons Absinthe
- 3 dashes Peychaud's bitters
- Coupe, Lemon twist, Cherry

Equal three-quarters of rye, sweet vermouth, and Benedictine, so the herbal liqueur is a third of the drink. Two barspoons of absinthe is anise you can taste. Three dashes of Peychaud's. Stirred, coupe, lemon and cherry. Honey, wormwood, and rye.

Stanley Clisby Arthur prints Cocktail à la Louisiane in Famous New Orleans Drinks and How to Mix 'Em (1937) as the special cocktail of Restaurant de la Louisiane, a French Quarter Creole house opened in 1881: equal rye, Italian vermouth, and Benedictine, three or four dashes each of absinthe substitute and Peychaud's, strained onto a cherry. Whether it predates Walter Bergeron's Vieux Carré is disputed; both first see print in Arthur's book. This menu keeps Arthur's equal three-quarters, pours two barspoons of absinthe and three dashes of Peychaud's, coupe, lemon and cherry.

- [Difford's Guide, La Louisiane](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/2985/la-louisiane)
- [Saveur, Drink the Secret Cocktail of New Orleans](https://www.saveur.com/la-louisiane-new-orleans-cocktail-history/)

#### Toronto

`2,q,1b,2,Ro` · stirred · Rye · Old-Fashioned family

- 2 oz Rye
- 1/4 oz Fernet
- 1 barspoon Demerara syrup
- 2 dashes Angostura bitters
- Rocks, iced, Orange twist

Two ounces of rye, a quarter ounce of Fernet, one barspoon of demerara, two dashes of Angostura. The Fernet is mint and bitter against the whiskey; the sugar is a film. Stirred, rocks with ice, orange twist. An Old-Fashioned with Fernet in the glass.

Robert Vermeire prints a Fernet Cocktail in Cocktails: How to Mix Them (1922), equal Fernet and cognac or rye, and notes that Canadians of Toronto appreciated it. David Embury, in The Fine Art of Mixing Drinks (1948), names it the Toronto: Canadian whisky, a quarter ounce of Fernet, sugar, Angostura. Modern specs keep two ounces of rye and a quarter of Fernet. This menu pours that, with a barspoon of demerara and two dashes of Angostura, over ice with an orange twist.

- [Punch, Toronto](https://punchdrink.com/recipes/toronto/)
- [Difford's Guide, Toronto](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/2040/toronto)

#### Little Italy

`2,Q,h,cc` · stirred · Rye · Negroni family

- 2 oz Rye
- 3/4 oz Sweet vermouth
- 1/2 oz Cynar
- Coupe, Cherry

Two ounces of rye to three-quarters of sweet vermouth, so the whiskey leads. Half an ounce of Cynar is artichoke bitter in the Campari slot. Stirred, coupe, cherry. A rye Negroni, leaner, no gin.

Audrey Saunders built the Little Italy at Pegu Club in New York in 2005: two ounces of rye, three-quarters sweet vermouth, half an ounce of Cynar, cherry. It is a Manhattan with Cynar in place of bitters, or a rye Negroni with the gin dropped. Robert Simonson treats it as a modern classic. This menu keeps Saunders's pour and the cherry.

- [Punch, Little Italy](https://punchdrink.com/recipes/little-italy/)
- [Difford's Guide, Little Italy](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/3083/little-italy)

#### Bensonhurst

`2,1,h,b,c` · stirred · Rye · Martini family

- 2 oz Rye
- 1 oz Dry vermouth
- 1/2 oz Maraschino liqueur
- 1 barspoon Cynar
- Coupe

Two ounces of rye, a full ounce of dry vermouth, half an ounce of maraschino, a barspoon of Cynar. The dry vermouth keeps the whiskey lean, and the maraschino carries the sugar as cherry pit and almond. The barspoon of Cynar is the artichoke bitterness that arrives last and stays. Stirred, coupe, no ice.

Chad Solomon made the Bensonhurst in 2006 while working at Milk & Honey in Manhattan, and named it for the Brooklyn neighbourhood near where he lived. It is a riff on the Brooklyn, which is itself a Manhattan built on dry vermouth and maraschino, with Cynar taking the fourth slot. Dozens of Brooklyn variations came out of New York in the years after, and this is one of the few still ordered by name. This menu pours two ounces of rye, an ounce of dry vermouth, half an ounce of maraschino, and a barspoon of Cynar, stirred, coupe.

- [Difford's Guide, Bensonhurst](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/541/bensonhurst)

#### Greenpoint

`2,h,h,1,1,cl` · stirred · Rye · Martini family

- 2 oz Rye
- 1/2 oz Chartreuse
- 1/2 oz Sweet vermouth
- 1 dash Angostura bitters
- 1 dash Orange bitters
- Coupe, Lemon twist

Two ounces of rye with a half ounce each of yellow Chartreuse and sweet vermouth, the two of them splitting the sweet slot evenly under the whiskey. A dash each of Angostura and orange bitters. Stirred, coupe, lemon twist. Rye spice, then honey and herbs, then grape, with the bitters holding the seam.

Michael McIlroy made the Greenpoint at Milk & Honey in New York in 2006, one of the Brooklyn neighborhood riffs on the 1909 Brooklyn cocktail that came out of that bar. Saveur prints a version that appears to come from McIlroy himself, with a full ounce of Punt e Mes and a teaspoon of yellow Chartreuse; the one in Sam Ross's Bartender's Choice, the closest thing to a Milk & Honey book, uses plain sweet vermouth and two dashes of Angostura. The half-and-half spec is the one that spread. This menu pours two ounces of rye, a half ounce each of yellow Chartreuse and sweet vermouth, and a dash each of Angostura and orange bitters, coupe, lemon twist.

- [Punch, The Greenpoint](https://punchdrink.com/recipes/greenpoint/)
- [Difford's Guide, Greenpoint](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/3635/greenpoint)

### Scotch

#### Bobby Burns

`1h,1,h,cl` · stirred · Scotch · Martini family

- 1 1/2 oz Scotch
- 1 oz Sweet vermouth
- 1/2 oz Bénédictine
- Coupe, Lemon twist

An ounce and a half of scotch against a full ounce of sweet vermouth, so the grape sits nearly even with the malt. Half an ounce of Bénédictine is honey and herbs, a pour not a dash, enough to coat the drink. Stirred, coupe, lemon twist. Scotch first, then the liqueur's spice.

The Bobby Burns is a Scotch Manhattan with Bénédictine. Harry Craddock prints it in The Savoy Cocktail Book in 1930 as equal Italian vermouth and Scotch whisky with three dashes of Bénédictine. Albert Stevens Crockett, a year later in Old Waldorf-Astoria Bar Days, lists a Robert Burns with absinthe and orange bitters, and says it may have been named for the poet or for a cigar salesman who bought at the old Waldorf bar. Earlier printings use Baby Burns (Bishop and Babcock, 1900) and Robert Burns (Grohusko, 1910). This menu keeps Craddock's scotch, sweet vermouth, and Bénédictine, yet it pours an ounce and a half of whiskey, a full ounce of vermouth, and a half ounce of the liqueur.

- [Difford's Guide, Bobby Burns cocktail history](https://www.diffordsguide.com/encyclopedia/1075/cocktails/bobby-burns)
- [The Savoy Cocktail Book (1930), Bobby Burns](https://savoycocktaildatabase.com/cocktails/bobby-burns-cocktail/)

#### Affinity

`1h,Q,Q,2,clc` · stirred · Scotch · Martini family

- 1 1/2 oz Scotch
- 3/4 oz Sweet vermouth
- 3/4 oz Dry vermouth
- 2 dashes Angostura bitters
- Coupe, Lemon twist, Cherry

An ounce and a half of scotch, then three-quarters each of sweet and dry vermouth, so the whiskey leads and the vermouths split. Two dashes of Angostura sit under both. Stirred, coupe, lemon and cherry. A Perfect Manhattan on scotch: malt, grape, and bark.

The Affinity first appears in The New York Sun on 28 October 1907 as a Broadway cocktail of Scotch whisky, Italian vermouth, powdered sugar, and orange bitters. The version that stuck, equal French vermouth, Italian vermouth, and Scotch with aromatic bitters, prints in Jacob A. Didier's The Reminder in 1909, is repeated by Hugo Ensslin in 1917, and is the formula Harry Craddock puts in The Savoy Cocktail Book in 1930. This menu keeps both vermouths and two dashes of Angostura, yet it pours an ounce and a half of scotch against three-quarters of each vermouth, so the whiskey leads.

- [Difford's Guide, Affinity](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/19/affinity)
- [The Savoy Cocktail Book (1930), Affinity Cocktail](https://savoycocktaildatabase.com/cocktails/affinity-cocktail/)

#### Rob Roy

`2,1,2,c` · stirred · Scotch · Martini family

- 2 oz Scotch
- 1 oz Sweet vermouth
- 2 dashes Orange bitters
- Coupe

Two ounces of scotch to one of sweet vermouth, the Manhattan ratio. Two dashes of orange bitters, not Angostura, so peel rather than bark sits under the malt. Stirred, coupe, no garnish on the menu. Leaner than a bourbon Manhattan, orange oil in the grape.

The Rob Roy is a Scotch Manhattan, named for Reginald De Koven and Harry B. Smith's 1894 Broadway operetta about the Highland outlaw Robert Roy MacGregor. The Waldorf-Astoria, then on Fifth Avenue near Herald Square Theatre, is the usual credit; other writers point to the Fifth Avenue Hotel. David Wondrich found Henry A. Orphal at Duke's House in Hoboken, around 1895, swapping Scotch into a Manhattan for a whisky salesman who would not drink anything else. Early books often use orange bitters; later ones shift to Angostura. This menu keeps two ounces of scotch, one of sweet vermouth, and two dashes of orange bitters, coupe.

- [Difford's Guide, Rob Roy](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/1681/rob-roy)
- [Punch, Rob Roy](https://punchdrink.com/recipes/rob-roy/)

#### Scotch Old-Fashioned

`2,1b,1,1,R` · stirred · Scotch · Old-Fashioned family

- 2 oz Scotch
- 1 barspoon Simple syrup
- 1 dash Angostura bitters
- 1 dash Orange bitters
- Rocks, iced

Two ounces of scotch, one barspoon of simple, one dash of Angostura and one of orange bitters. The sugar is a film; peel and bark sit under the malt. Stirred, rocks with ice. Scotch first, then the two bitters against the whiskey.

The cocktail is spirit, sugar, water, and bitters, defined in The Balance and Columbian Repository on 13 May 1806. By the 1870s bartenders were dressing the Whiskey Cocktail with curacao and absinthe; drinkers who wanted the older formula asked for an old-fashioned whiskey cocktail. Scotch is one of the spirits that definition already allowed. This menu pours two ounces of scotch, one barspoon of simple, one dash of Angostura and one of orange bitters, over ice. No fruit.

- [The Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails, The Old-Fashioned Cocktail](https://www.spiritsanddistilling.com/dictionary/acref-9780199311132-e-377)
- [Difford's Guide, Old Fashioned cocktail history](https://www.diffordsguide.com/g/1198/old-fashioned-cocktail/history)

#### Automobile

`Q,Q,Q,2,cc` · stirred · Scotch · Martini family

- 3/4 oz Scotch
- 3/4 oz Gin
- 3/4 oz Sweet vermouth
- 2 dashes Orange bitters
- Coupe, Cherry

Three-quarters of an ounce each of scotch, gin, and sweet vermouth, so none of the three wins. Two dashes of orange bitters keep peel in the mix. Stirred, coupe, cherry. Juniper against malt, grape in the middle. A short equal-parts drink: two and a quarter ounces before the ice.

Jacques Straub prints an Auto Cocktail in 1914 Drinks as equal French vermouth, Tom gin, and Scotch whiskey, shaken. Frank Meier, at the Ritz Bar in Paris, prints the Automobile in The Artistry of Mixing Drinks in 1934: a dash of orange bitters and one-third each of Italian vermouth, gin, and Scotch whisky, stirred. This menu follows Meier. It pours three-quarters of an ounce each of scotch, gin, and sweet vermouth, two dashes of orange bitters, coupe, cherry.

- [Difford's Guide, Automobile](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/15692/automobile)
- [1914 Drinks by Jacques Straub, p. 18](https://euvs-vintage-cocktail-books.cld.bz/1914-Drinks/18/)

#### Telling Phoebe

`1h,Q,h,h,cc` · stirred · Scotch · Martini family

- 1 1/2 oz Scotch
- 3/4 oz Sweet vermouth
- 1/2 oz Fernet
- 1/2 oz Bénédictine
- Coupe, Cherry

An ounce and a half of scotch, three-quarters of sweet vermouth, half an ounce each of Fernet and Bénédictine. The whiskey leads a Rob Roy; Fernet is mint against peat, Bénédictine honey and spice. Stirred, coupe, cherry.

Chantal Tseng built Telling Phoebe as a homage to R.O. Kwon's novel The Incendiaries, for one of her literary cocktail nights. Brett Adams and Jacob Grier print it in Raising the Bar (2022): an ounce and a half of scotch, three-quarters sweet vermouth, half an ounce each of Fernet and Bénédictine, cherry. It drinks as a Rob Roy with Fernet and Bénédictine splitting the bitter-sweet slot. This menu keeps that pour.

- [Cocktail Virgin Slut, Telling Phoebe](https://cocktailvirgin.blogspot.com/2023/09/telling-phoebe.html)

### Light Rum

#### Country Club

`1h,1,h,1,cl` · stirred · Light Rum · Martini family

- 1 1/2 oz Light rum
- 1 oz Dry vermouth
- 1/2 oz Orange liqueur
- 1 dash Orange bitters
- Coupe, Lemon twist

An ounce and a half of light rum against a full ounce of dry vermouth, nearly even. Half an ounce of orange liqueur is peel and sugar, and one dash of orange bitters sits under both. Stirred, coupe, lemon twist. Lean rum, dry grape, candied orange.

Albert Stevens Crockett prints the Country Club in the 1935 Old Waldorf-Astoria Bar Book as half Bacardi, half French vermouth, and a dash of orange curaçao, among the amendments to the old Waldorf list. William T. Boothby's 1934 World Drinks has a different Country Club, whiskey with orange bitters in a bar glass. The Savoy Country Club Cooler is French vermouth, grenadine, and soda, a different drink. This menu keeps Crockett's light rum, dry vermouth, and orange liqueur, yet it pours an ounce and a half of rum, a full ounce of vermouth, a half ounce of orange liqueur, and a dash of orange bitters, coupe, lemon.

- [1935 Old Waldorf-Astoria Bar Book, p. 128](https://euvs-vintage-cocktail-books.cld.bz/1935-Old-Waldorf-Astoria-Bar-Book/128/)

#### Yacht Club

`2,1,q,c` · stirred · Light Rum · Martini family

- 2 oz Light rum
- 1 oz Sweet vermouth
- 1/4 oz Apricot liqueur
- Coupe

Two ounces of light rum to one of sweet vermouth, a Manhattan ratio on cane. A quarter ounce of apricot liqueur is stone fruit, not a dash. Stirred, coupe, no twist on the menu. Rum first, then grape, then a thin apricot film.

A Yacht Club Cocktail of rum, Italian vermouth, and apricot prints in the 1948 Ron Daiquiri Coctelera booklet from Havana: two-thirds Daiquiri rum, one-third Italian vermouth, a dash of apricot brandy, stirred. David Embury includes a Yacht Club of the same bones in The Fine Art of Mixing Drinks the same year; Difford's adapts that printing. This menu keeps the two-to-one rum and sweet vermouth and puts a quarter ounce of apricot liqueur in place of the dash.

- [1948 Ron Daiquiri Coctelera, Yacht Club Cocktail](https://euvs-vintage-cocktail-books.cld.bz/1948-Ron-Daiquiri-Coctelera-Cocktail-Book-Habana-Cuba/16/)
- [Difford's Guide, Yacht Club](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/2111/yacht-club)

#### El Presidente

`1h,Q,h,b,co` · stirred · Light Rum · Martini family

- 1 1/2 oz Light rum
- 3/4 oz Dry vermouth
- 1/2 oz Orange liqueur
- 1 barspoon Grenadine
- Coupe, Orange twist

An ounce and a half of light rum, three-quarters of dry vermouth, half an ounce of orange liqueur, a barspoon of grenadine. Stirred, so it comes out clear and heavy in the glass. The barspoon of grenadine is pomegranate on the finish and a shade of colour; the orange liqueur is where the sugar actually is. Coupe, orange twist.

Havana, mid-1910s. The earliest known recipe is in John B. Escalante's Manual del Cantinero of 1915, which the French historian Fernando Castellon found in Cuba's Biblioteca Nacional, and Basil Woon's 1928 When It's Cocktail Time in Cuba called the drink the aristocrat of cocktails. David Wondrich credits Constantino Ribalaigua on the strength of a 1937 interview by Jack Cuddy, in which Ribalaigua claimed it. David Embury drew the line plainly in his 1948 The Fine Art of Mixing Drinks: if vermouth instead of citrus is used with the grenadine, the name is El Presidente. This menu pours an ounce and a half of light rum, three-quarters of dry vermouth, half an ounce of orange liqueur, and a barspoon of grenadine, stirred, coupe, orange twist.

- [Difford's Guide, El Presidente](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/701/el-presidente)

### Cachaça

#### Brazilian Negroni

`1q,Q,Q,Ro` · stirred · Cachaça · Negroni family

- 1 1/4 oz Cachaça
- 3/4 oz Campari
- 3/4 oz Sweet vermouth
- Rocks, iced, Orange twist

An ounce and a quarter of cachaça against three-quarters each of Campari and sweet vermouth. The cane spirit leads a little; Campari is still a third of the drink. Stirred, rocks with ice, orange twist. A Negroni in sugarcane, grassy and bitter orange.

Swap gin for cachaça in a Negroni and the drink is a Brazilian Negroni, a substitution that spread with cachaça's craft revival in the 2000s. Difford's and later books print it as a Negroni ratio on cachaça. This menu pours an ounce and a quarter of cachaça against three-quarters each of Campari and sweet vermouth, over ice with an orange twist, so the cane leads the way the Boulevardier lets bourbon lead.

- [Difford's Guide, Negroni](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/1328/negroni)

#### Cornerstone

`1h,h,q,2,co` · stirred · Cachaça · Old-Fashioned family

- 1 1/2 oz Cachaça
- 1/2 oz Grenadine
- 1/4 oz Fernet
- 2 dashes Orange bitters
- Coupe, Orange twist

An ounce and a half of cachaça, half an ounce of grenadine, a quarter of Fernet. The pomegranate is the sugar; the Fernet is mint and bitter against the cane. Two dashes of orange bitters are peel. Stirred, coupe, orange twist.

Brett Adams and Jacob Grier print the Cornerstone in Raising the Bar (2022), in the Fernet chapter: an ounce and a half of cachaça, half an ounce of grenadine, a quarter of Fernet, two dashes of orange bitters, orange twist. A drink of this name does not appear in the pre-1970 manuals. It drinks as an Old-Fashioned on cane spirit, grenadine in the sugar slot, Fernet as the bitter. This menu keeps that pour.

- [Willamette Week, Raising the Bar](https://www.wweek.com/drink/2023/03/29/a-new-book-by-two-local-mixologists-tells-you-how-to-stock-your-bar-cart-one-bottle-at-a-time/)

#### Rabo de Galo

`2,h,h,Ro` · stirred · Cachaça · Negroni family

- 2 oz Cachaça
- 1/2 oz Sweet vermouth
- 1/2 oz Cynar
- Rocks, iced, Orange twist

Two ounces of cachaça with a half ounce each of sweet vermouth and Cynar. The cachaça is grassy and raw sugar, the vermouth rounds it, and the Cynar puts artichoke bitterness on the end. Stirred, rocks with ice, orange twist. It gets colder and wider as the cube goes.

The Rabo de Galo, rooster's tail, took hold in São Paulo in the mid-1950s after Cinzano opened a vermouth factory there and set about persuading Brazilians to mix the imported wine with their own cachaça. It was a shot in the pés-sujos, the dirty-feet bars, before it was a cocktail, poured about two parts cachaça to one of vermouth and thrown back. Cynar came later, and São Paulo bartenders now pour it beside the vermouth or in place of it; Derivan Ferreira de Souza started a national competition for the drink in 2017. This menu pours two ounces of cachaça and a half ounce each of sweet vermouth and Cynar, over ice with an orange twist.

- [Punch, Brazil's Favorite Cachaça Cocktail Is the Rabo de Galo](https://punchdrink.com/articles/rabo-de-gala-cachaca-cocktail-recipe-brazil/)
- [Difford's Guide, Rabo de Galo](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/3889/rabo-de-galo)

### Tequila

#### Rosita

`1h,1,h,h,1,Ro` · stirred · Tequila · Negroni family

- 1 1/2 oz Tequila
- 1 oz Campari
- 1/2 oz Sweet vermouth
- 1/2 oz Dry vermouth
- 1 dash Angostura bitters
- Rocks, iced, Orange twist

An ounce and a half of tequila against a full ounce of Campari, so the bitter leads. Half an ounce each of sweet and dry vermouth split the wine, a Perfect Negroni with agave. One dash of Angostura is spice. Stirred, rocks, ice, orange twist.

The Rosita first appears, creator unknown, in the 1974 Mr. Boston Official Bartender's Guide: one ounce tequila, one ounce Campari, half an ounce each of dry and sweet vermouth, stirred on cracked ice, lemon twist. Gary Regan reprinted it in The Bartender's Bible (1991) with more tequila and a dash of Angostura, then forgot he had. Terry Sullivan and Regan traced it back in 2007 in the San Francisco Chronicle. Mexico City is sometimes named; no period citation supports that. This menu keeps Regan's ounce and a half of tequila and the dash of Angostura, yet it pours a full ounce of Campari and garnishes with orange.

- [Imbibe, The Rosita Cocktail](https://imbibemagazine.com/recipe/the-rosita-cocktail-recipe/)
- [Difford's Guide, Rosita](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/1696/rosita)

#### One Chance Fancy

`2,q,q,2,Ro` · stirred · Tequila · Fancy family

- 2 oz Tequila
- 1/4 oz Orange liqueur
- 1/4 oz Sweet vermouth
- 2 dashes Angostura bitters
- Rocks, iced, Orange twist

Two ounces of tequila, a quarter of orange liqueur, a quarter of sweet vermouth. The vermouth is the sugar; the orange liqueur is peel. Two dashes of Angostura. Stirred, rocks, ice, orange twist. It drinks as a tequila Fancy Cocktail, spirit first, liqueur as dressing.

Jerry Thomas prints the Fancy Brandy Cocktail in 1862 as the plain Cocktail strained into a wine glass with lemon on the rim: spirit, gum, bitters, and curacao. Brett Adams and Jacob Grier, in Raising the Bar (2022), still treat The Fancy as whiskey, orange liqueur, and bitters, an Old-Fashioned with a liqueur in the sugar slot. A drink called One Chance Fancy does not appear in the pre-1970 manuals, nor under that name in Difford's, Punch, or Imbibe. This menu puts the Fancy template on tequila, with a quarter ounce of sweet vermouth in the sugar slot, two dashes of Angostura, over ice with an orange twist.

- [Willamette Week, Raising the Bar (The Fancy)](https://www.wweek.com/drink/2023/03/29/a-new-book-by-two-local-mixologists-tells-you-how-to-stock-your-bar-cart-one-bottle-at-a-time/)

### Mezcal

#### El Camino

`1,1,h,4,Ro` · stirred · Mezcal · Fancy family

- 1 oz Mezcal
- 1 oz Rye
- 1/2 oz Bénédictine
- 4 dashes Peychaud's bitters
- Rocks, iced, Orange twist

Equal ounces of mezcal and rye, so smoke and pepper share the glass. Half an ounce of Bénédictine is honey and baking spice. Four dashes of Peychaud's pull anise and cherry through both spirits. Stirred, rocks with ice, orange twist.

The El Camino is the house cocktail of the Chestnut Club in Santa Monica, on the list since the bar opened in 2014. Imbibe printed the spec: equal mezcal and rye, half an ounce of Bénédictine, four dashes of Peychaud's, over a large cube with an orange twist. It drinks as a split-base Fancy, smoke against rye heat, the liqueur in the sugar slot. This menu keeps that pour.

- [Kindred Cocktails, The El Camino](https://kindredcocktails.com/cocktail/el-camino-0)
- [Difford's Guide, El Camino](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/13511/el-camino)

#### 1910

`Q,Q,1,h,2,co` · stirred · Mezcal · Martini family

- 3/4 oz Mezcal
- 3/4 oz Cognac
- 1 oz Sweet vermouth
- 1/2 oz Maraschino liqueur
- 2 dashes Peychaud's bitters
- Coupe, Orange twist

Three-quarters each of mezcal and cognac, a full ounce of sweet vermouth, so the wine leads. Half an ounce of maraschino is cherry and almond. Two dashes of Peychaud's. Stirred, coupe, orange twist. A smoky Martinez, grape and pit.

Ezra Star built the 1910 at Drink in Boston around 2014, named for the year the Mexican Revolution began and as a nod to the bar's 1919, a rum Manhattan named for the Molasses Flood. Punch prints three-quarters each mezcal and cognac, a half ounce of maraschino, an ounce of Punt e Mes, two dashes of Peychaud's, orange twist. It is a Martinez with smoke and grape brandy in place of gin. This menu keeps those measures on sweet vermouth.

- [Punch, 1910](https://punchdrink.com/recipes/1910/)
- [Difford's Guide, 1910](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/4834/1910)

#### Mezcal Negroni

`1,1,1,Ro` · stirred · Mezcal · Negroni family

- 1 oz Mezcal
- 1 oz Campari
- 1 oz Sweet vermouth
- Rocks, iced, Orange twist

Equal ounces of mezcal, Campari, and sweet vermouth, over ice. Smoke and roasted agave stand where juniper does in the original, and the smoke is the loudest thing in the glass until the ice opens it up. Campari and mezcal are bitter in different directions, and holding those two apart is most of what the vermouth is for. Rocks with ice, orange twist.

There is no single author. Phil Ward, who opened the agave bar Mayahuel in New York in 2009, is the name most often attached to it and takes no credit himself, saying only that pouring one was obvious in the bar's early days. Joaquín Simó remembers first drinking one in the early days of Death & Co, after Ward had taken to mezcal, and later built his own variations at Pouring Ribbons. Lynnette Marrero puts the arrival around 2009 and calls it entirely organic, something that happened while a lot of bartenders were working through amari and mezcal at the same time. This menu pours an ounce each of mezcal, Campari, and sweet vermouth, stirred, rocks with ice, orange twist.

- [Punch, How the Mezcal Negroni Became a Menu Mainstay](https://punchdrink.com/articles/mezcal-negronis-world-cocktail-recipe/)

### Vodka

#### Tipsy Coachman

`1h,Q,1,Rl` · stirred · Vodka · Fancy family

- 1 1/2 oz Vodka
- 3/4 oz Bénédictine
- 1 dash Angostura bitters
- Rocks, iced, Lemon twist

An ounce and a half of vodka, three-quarters of Bénédictine, one dash of Angostura. Honey and herbs, vodka as the thinner so the liqueur is a third of the drink. Stirred, rocks with ice, lemon twist. It sits, herbal and sweet, with bark at the end.

The formula is the Gypsy Queen: vodka, Bénédictine, and bitters. David Wondrich found the earliest printing in a 1938 booklet from New York's Russian Tea Room, one of the first American vodka cocktails. David Embury reprints it in 1948 as Gypsy or Gypsy Queen and prefers a drier ratio than the original one-to-two. A drink called Tipsy Coachman does not appear under that name in those books; the phrase is older, from Oliver Goldsmith, and later a legal doctrine. This menu keeps the ounce and a half of vodka, three-quarters of Bénédictine, and a dash of Angostura, over ice with a lemon twist.

- [Difford's Guide, Gypsy Queen](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/2804/gypsy-queen)

#### Vodka Martini

`2,h,cl` · stirred · Vodka · Martini family

- 2 oz Vodka
- 1/2 oz Dry vermouth
- Coupe, Lemon twist

Two ounces of vodka, half an ounce of dry vermouth. Four to one; the wine is in the drink. Stirred, coupe, lemon twist. Cold, grape.

A vodka Martini prints in a 1935 Smirnoff pamphlet at three parts vodka to one of French vermouth, with lemon peel in the mixing glass. Lucius Beebe puts two versions in The Stork Club Bar Book in 1946. Ted Saucier, in 1952 Bottoms Up, credits photographer Jerome Zerbe with a four-to-one Vodkatini and a lemon twist. John G. Martin at Heublein spent the 1940s and 1950s selling Smirnoff as a mixer. This menu is two ounces of vodka to half an ounce of dry vermouth, stirred, coupe, lemon.

- [Difford's Guide, Vodkatini / Vodka Martini](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/2054/vodkatini-vodka-martini)

### Gin

#### Quill

`1,1,1,q,co` · stirred · Gin · Negroni family

- 1 oz Gin
- 1 oz Campari
- 1 oz Sweet vermouth
- 1/4 oz Absinthe
- Coupe, Orange twist

Equal ounces of gin, Campari, and sweet vermouth, so Campari is a third of the drink, then a quarter ounce of absinthe in the mix, not a rinse. That is a real pour of anise, enough to sit on the Campari rather than perfume the glass. Stirred, coupe, orange twist. Bitter orange, grape, and wormwood, served up.

The Quill first prints in the 1996 edition of Harry's ABC of Mixing Cocktails, where Andrew and Duncan MacElhone added forty-odd recipes to Harry MacElhone's original books and credited this one to Frank C. Payne of New York. It is not in the earlier editions, nor in MacElhone's 1927 Barflies and Cocktails. Payne was a theatrical press agent in the Theatrical Press Representatives of America, which published a magazine called The Quill. The drink is a Negroni with absinthe. This menu keeps the equal ounces and puts a quarter ounce of absinthe in the build, coupe, orange twist.

- [Difford's Guide, Quill](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/5064/quill)
- [Serious Eats, If You Like Negronis, Try the Quill](https://www.seriouseats.com/classic-cocktail-quill-negroni-variation-with-absinthe-history-story)

#### Negroni

`1,1,1,R` · stirred · Gin · Negroni family

- 1 oz Gin
- 1 oz Campari
- 1 oz Sweet vermouth
- Rocks, iced

Equal ounces of gin, Campari, and sweet vermouth. Campari is a third of the drink: bitter orange against grape and juniper. Stirred, rocks with ice, no twist on the menu. The cube is the dilution, so the Campari stays loud as it sits.

The usual story puts Count Camillo Negroni at Caffe Casoni on Via de' Tornabuoni in Florence around 1919, asking Fosco Scarselli to stiffen his Americano with gin in place of soda. Luca Picchi reconstructed that account in 2002; it is the better-supported one. However, Colonel Hector Andres Negroni later said there was no Camillo in the family tree and pointed instead to General Pascal Olivier Comte de Negroni. The equal-parts formula does not see print until Amedeo Gandiglio's 1947 Cocktails Portfolio. This menu pours one ounce each of gin, Campari, and sweet vermouth, over ice, no garnish letter.

- [Difford's Guide, History of the Negroni](https://www.diffordsguide.com/g/1078/negroni-cocktail/history)
- [Punch, The Negroni Has a Secret](https://punchdrink.com/articles/negroni-cocktail-recipe-has-a-secret-history/)

#### Claridge

`1,1,h,h,c` · stirred · Gin · Martini family

- 1 oz Gin
- 1 oz Dry vermouth
- 1/2 oz Apricot liqueur
- 1/2 oz Orange liqueur
- Coupe

Equal ounces of gin and dry vermouth, then a half ounce each of apricot liqueur and orange liqueur, so the two liqueurs together match the gin. Stone fruit and candied peel sit against a dry wine cut. Stirred, coupe, no twist on the menu. Apricot and orange on a wet Martini.

Harry MacElhone prints the Claridge in 1922 Harry's ABC of Mixing Cocktails, credited to Leon, bartender at Claridge's Hotel on the Champs-Elysees in Paris: one-third gin, one-third French vermouth, one-sixth apricot brandy, one-sixth Cointreau. Harry Craddock repeats the formula in The Savoy Cocktail Book in 1930, and prints the same measures again as the Frankenjack. The London hotel of the same name is a later guess; Leon's Paris house is the one in the book. This menu keeps equal gin and dry vermouth and a half ounce of each liqueur, stirred, coupe.

- [Difford's Guide, Claridge Cocktail](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/440/claridge-cocktail)
- [The 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book, Claridge Cocktail](https://savoycocktaildatabase.com/cocktails/claridge-cocktail/)

#### Lucien Gaudin

`1,h,h,h,co` · stirred · Gin · Negroni family

- 1 oz Gin
- 1/2 oz Campari
- 1/2 oz Dry vermouth
- 1/2 oz Orange liqueur
- Coupe, Orange twist

An ounce of gin against half ounces of Campari, dry vermouth, and orange liqueur, so gin leads and the three modifiers split. Bitter orange and candied peel sit against a dry wine cut, leaner than a Negroni and more orange. Stirred, coupe, orange twist.

Named for Lucien Gaudin, a French fencer who won gold in foil and epee at the 1924 Paris Olympics and again in 1928 at Amsterdam. The drink first prints in RIP's 1929 Cocktails de Paris, credited to Charlie of Le Cheval Pie, a Paris restaurant that ran from 1925 to 1930, and it took the Coupe d'honneur at the Professional Bartenders Championship in Paris on 2 February 1929. RIP is Georges Gabriel Thenon. This menu pours an ounce of gin and a half ounce each of Campari, dry vermouth, and orange liqueur, coupe, orange.

- [Difford's Guide, Lucien Gaudin](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/2709/lucien-gaudin)
- [Cold Glass, The Lucien Gaudin Cocktail](https://cold-glass.com/2014/12/05/the-lucien-gaudin-cocktail/)

#### Martinez

`1h,1,h,q,1,1,co` · stirred · Gin · Martini family

- 1 1/2 oz Gin
- 1 oz Sweet vermouth
- 1/2 oz Dry vermouth
- 1/4 oz Maraschino liqueur
- 1 dash Orange bitters
- 1 dash Angostura bitters
- Coupe, Orange twist

An ounce and a half of gin against a full ounce of sweet vermouth and a half of dry, so the wine is wet and split. A quarter ounce of maraschino is cherry pit and almond, and one dash each of orange bitters and Angostura keep peel and bark in the mix. Stirred, coupe, orange. It drinks as a gin Manhattan with both vermouths and a cherry film.

O.H. Byron prints the Martinez in 1884 The Modern Bartender's Guide as "Same as Manhattan, only you substitute gin for whisky," on a page with two Manhattan formulas. Jerry Thomas's posthumous 1887 Bar-Tender's Guide gives the first full spec: a pony of Old Tom gin, a wine-glass of vermouth, two dashes of maraschino, a dash of Boker's bitters. The California stories, Jerry Thomas at the Occidental and Julio Richelieu in Martinez, stay unproven. This menu pours an ounce and a half of gin, both vermouths, a quarter of maraschino, and one dash each of orange bitters and Angostura, coupe, orange.

- [Difford's Guide, Martinez](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/1264/martinez-diffords-recipe)
- [Punch, Martinez](https://punchdrink.com/recipes/martinez/)

#### Ford Cocktail

`1h,1h,q,2,co` · stirred · Gin · Martini family

- 1 1/2 oz Gin
- 1 1/2 oz Dry vermouth
- 1/4 oz Bénédictine
- 2 dashes Orange bitters
- Coupe, Orange twist

Equal ounces and a half of gin and dry vermouth, then a quarter ounce of Bénédictine, honey and herbs as a pour rather than a dash. Two dashes of orange bitters keep peel in the mix. Stirred, coupe, orange twist. A wet Martini with an herbal film.

George J. Kappeler prints the Ford Cocktail in 1895 Modern American Drinks: three dashes of Bénédictine, three dashes of orange bitters, half a jigger of Tom gin, half a jigger of French vermouth, orange peel. He does not name a Ford. Ted Haigh, in Vintage Spirits and Forgotten Cocktails, points to Malcolm Webster Ford, the 1880s all-around athlete and journalist, rather than Henry, whose company postdates the recipe. This menu keeps the equal gin and dry vermouth and the orange bitters, yet it pours a quarter ounce of Bénédictine, coupe, orange.

- [Difford's Guide, Ford Cocktail](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/3379/ford-cocktail)
- [Cold Glass, The Ford Cocktail](https://cold-glass.com/2020/01/10/a-martini-with-something-in-it-the-ford-cocktail/)

#### Journalist

`1h,h,h,q,q,1,cl` · stirred · Gin · Martini family

- 1 1/2 oz Gin
- 1/2 oz Sweet vermouth
- 1/2 oz Dry vermouth
- 1/4 oz Orange liqueur
- 1/4 oz Lemon juice
- 1 dash Angostura bitters
- Coupe, Lemon twist

An ounce and a half of gin, then a half ounce each of sweet and dry vermouth, a Perfect Martini ratio. A quarter ounce of orange liqueur and a quarter ounce of lemon sit in the same glass: peel and pith, enough lemon that the drink is tart even stirred. One dash of Angostura. Coupe, lemon twist. Citrus in a stirred gin drink.

Harry Craddock prints the Journalist in The Savoy Cocktail Book in 1930: two-thirds Gordon's dry gin, one-sixth each of French and Italian vermouth, two dashes of lemon juice, two dashes of curaçao, one dash of Angostura, shaken. No bartender is named. Paul Clarke, in Serious Eats, treats it as a Perfect Martini with dashes of lemon and orange liqueur. This menu keeps both vermouths and the Angostura, yet it pours a quarter ounce each of orange liqueur and lemon, stirred, coupe, lemon.

- [Difford's Guide, Journalist](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/1072/journalist)
- [The 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book, Journalist Cocktail](https://savoycocktaildatabase.com/cocktails/journalist-cocktail/)
- [Serious Eats, Journalist Cocktail](https://www.seriouseats.com/journalist-cocktail-recipe)

#### Vancouver

`1h,Q,h,1,cO` · stirred · Gin · Martini family

- 1 1/2 oz Gin
- 3/4 oz Dry vermouth
- 1/2 oz Bénédictine
- 1 dash Orange bitters
- Coupe, Olive

An ounce and a half of gin against three-quarters of dry vermouth, so the wine is a real pour, then a half ounce of Bénédictine, honey and herbs nearly even with the vermouth. One dash of orange bitters. Stirred, coupe, orange twist. Gin first, then the liqueur's spice on a dry wine.

The Vancouver prints in the About Town Cocktail Book, issued in Vancouver around 1925 by Mitchell Publishing: fifty percent gin, thirty percent French vermouth, twenty percent Bénédictine, a dash of orange bitters, olive. Joseph A. Fitchett, head bar steward of the Vancouver Club, checked the recipes. A later story, told to Steve da Cruz in 2006, put a sweet-vermouth version at the Sylvia Hotel after 1954. Alex Black, in Scout Magazine in 2020, showed that the 1925 Vancouver used dry vermouth; the sweet one in the same book is the Fitchett. This menu keeps dry vermouth: an ounce and a half of gin, three-quarters vermouth, a half ounce of Bénédictine, and one dash of orange bitters, coupe, orange.

- [Difford's Guide, Vancouver](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/2759/vancouver)
- [Scout Magazine, We've Been Making the Vancouver Cocktail Wrong](https://scoutmagazine.ca/weve-been-making-the-vancouver-cocktail-wrong-for-15-years/)

#### Wiffin

`1h,Q,h,1d,cl` · stirred · Gin · Martini family

- 1 1/2 oz Gin
- 3/4 oz Sweet vermouth
- 1/2 oz Cognac
- 1 dash Absinthe
- Coupe, Lemon twist

An ounce and a half of gin against three-quarters of sweet vermouth, then a half ounce of cognac, grape spirit under gin. One dash of absinthe is a thin anise wash, not a pour. Stirred, coupe, lemon twist. Two spirits and vermouth, wormwood at the edge.

The Wiffin is not a pre-1970 bar-book drink. P. G. Wodehouse, in the 1928 story "The Passing of Ambrose," has Ambrose Wiffin sketch a cocktail of gin, Italian vermouth, a spot of old brandy, and a dash of absinthe. David Wondrich reconstructed the formula in Australian Bartender in 2011: English gin, Italian vermouth, cognac, and a dash or two of absinthe. This menu pours an ounce and a half of gin, three-quarters sweet vermouth, a half ounce of cognac, and one dash of absinthe, coupe, lemon.

- [Difford's Guide, Wiffin](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/23463/wiffin)
- [David Wondrich, The Wiffin, Australian Bartender](https://australianbartender.com.au/2011/08/24/david-wondrich-the-wiffin/)

#### Fitchett

`1h,Q,q,1,cc` · stirred · Gin · Martini family

- 1 1/2 oz Gin
- 3/4 oz Sweet vermouth
- 1/4 oz Bénédictine
- 1 dash Orange bitters
- Coupe, Cherry

An ounce and a half of gin against three-quarters of sweet vermouth, then a quarter ounce of Bénédictine, honey and herbs as a film rather than a half-ounce pour. One dash of orange bitters. Stirred, coupe, cherry. Gin first, grape, then a thin herbal coat. Wetter and less herbal than the Vancouver on this menu.

The Fitchett prints in the same About Town Cocktail Book as the Vancouver, around 1925. The unnamed writer credits Joseph A. Fitchett, head bar steward of the Vancouver Club: of the thousand and one drinks he can mix, it is the best. The formula is fifty percent gin, thirty percent Italian vermouth, twenty percent Bénédictine, a dash of orange bitters, olive or cherry. It is the sweet-vermouth sibling of the Vancouver in that book. This menu keeps the gin and sweet vermouth, yet it pours only a quarter ounce of Bénédictine, coupe, cherry.

- [Difford's Guide, Vancouver (Fitchett recipe)](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/2759/vancouver)
- [Scout Magazine, We've Been Making the Vancouver Cocktail Wrong](https://scoutmagazine.ca/weve-been-making-the-vancouver-cocktail-wrong-for-15-years/)

#### Martini

`2,1,1,cl` · stirred · Gin · Martini family

- 2 oz Gin
- 1 oz Dry vermouth
- 1 dash Orange bitters
- Coupe, Lemon twist

Two ounces of gin to one of dry vermouth, so the wine is a third of the drink, not a rinse. One dash of orange bitters is peel in the glass. Stirred, coupe, lemon twist. It drinks wet and cold: juniper, then the vermouth's wormwood and grape, then a thin orange film.

The first gin-and-vermouth drinks print in 1883 newspaper copy from Cleveland and Chicago, still called Manhattans, then as Martinez in O.H. Byron's 1884 The Modern Bartender's Guide and as Martini in Harry Johnson's 1888 Bartenders' Manual: Old Tom, sweet vermouth, curaçao, gum, and bitters. The Dry Martini, French vermouth and a drier gin, is named in New York by 1896 and is the dominant version by 1900. Two-to-one gin to vermouth appears in the late 1890s and is standard by the 1910s; orange bitters stay until the 1940s, then drop as the ratio marches past five-to-one. This menu keeps the wet 2:1, one dash of orange bitters, coupe, lemon.

- [The Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails, The Martini](https://www.spiritsanddistilling.com/dictionary/acref-9780199311132-e-361)
- [Difford's Guide, Martini cocktail history](https://www.diffordsguide.com/g/1121/martini/martini-history)

#### Villa Straylight

`2,1,h,1b,c` · stirred · Gin · Martini family

- 2 oz Gin
- 1 oz Dry vermouth
- 1/2 oz Orange liqueur
- 1 barspoon Absinthe
- Coupe

Two ounces of gin to one of dry vermouth, the wet Martini on this menu, then a half ounce of orange liqueur as candied peel, and a barspoon of absinthe in the mix, not a rinse. The anise is a pour you can taste, laid over the orange. Stirred, coupe, no garnish. Wet gin, peel, and wormwood.

Villa Straylight does not appear in the pre-1970 manuals, nor under that name in Difford's, Punch, or Imbibe. It is a house drink on this menu, named for the Tessier-Ashpool villa at the end of Freeside in William Gibson's 1984 Neuromancer. The build is this menu's wet Martini, two ounces of gin to one of dry vermouth, plus a half ounce of orange liqueur and a barspoon of absinthe in the mix. Harry Johnson's 1888 Martini already carried orange curaçao; the absinthe is the Tuxedo's anise, poured rather than rinsed. Coupe, no garnish.

- [Difford's Guide, Martini cocktail history](https://www.diffordsguide.com/g/1121/martini/martini-history)
- [Difford's Guide, Tuxedo cocktail and its many variations](https://www.diffordsguide.com/encyclopedia/1511/cocktails/tuxedo-cocktail-and-its-many-variations)

#### Casino

`2,h,2,Rc` · stirred · Gin · Fancy family

- 2 oz Gin
- 1/2 oz Maraschino liqueur
- 2 dashes Orange bitters
- Rocks, iced, Cherry

Two ounces of gin, a half ounce of maraschino, two dashes of orange bitters. The cherry liqueur is almond and pit as much as fruit, and it does the sweetening; there is no lemon. Stirred. Rocks with ice and a cherry. It sits: gin first, then a cherry film, and the cube.

Jacob A. Didier prints the Casino in 1909 The Reminder: two dashes each of maraschino, orange bitters, and lemon juice, a drink of Tom gin, stirred, cherry. Hugo R. Ensslin copies it almost verbatim in 1916 Recipes for Mixed Drinks, and Harry Craddock repeats it in the 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book. David Embury, in 1948, swaps orange juice for the bitters and tells you to mix it like an Aviation. This menu drops the lemon, pours a half ounce of maraschino rather than dashes, keeps two dashes of orange bitters, and serves it over ice in a rocks glass with a cherry.

- [Difford's Guide, Casino](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/2332/casino)
- [The Savoy Cocktail Book (1930), Casino Cocktail](https://savoycocktaildatabase.com/cocktails/casino-cocktail)

#### Dry Orange Martini

`2,Q,q,2,c` · stirred · Gin · Martini family

- 2 oz Gin
- 3/4 oz Dry vermouth
- 1/4 oz Orange liqueur
- 2 dashes Orange bitters
- Coupe
