Two ounces of gin, three-quarters of dry vermouth, a quarter ounce of orange liqueur, two dashes of orange bitters. The vermouth still leads the dressing; the liqueur is peel and a little sugar, not a third of the drink. Stirred, coupe. Drier than this menu's Martini, with candied orange instead of a twist.

Wayne Collins built the Dry Orange Martini in 2003 for Maxxium UK: two ounces of gin, three-quarters of dry vermouth, a quarter of orange liqueur, two dashes of orange bitters. Collins was a London bartender who ran Mixxit, Maxxium's training programme, and later put the White Negroni into wider print. The parent is the Dry Martini; Harry Johnson's 1888 Martini already carried orange curaçao, which later books dropped as the drink dried out. This menu keeps Collins's measures and the coupe.

- [Difford's Guide, Dry Orange Martini](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/678/dry-orange-martini)

#### Tuxedo #2

`2,Q,q,3,r,co` · stirred · Gin · Martini family

- 2 oz Gin
- 3/4 oz Dry vermouth
- 1/4 oz Maraschino liqueur
- 3 dashes Orange bitters
- rinse Absinthe
- Coupe, Orange twist

Two ounces of gin against three-quarters of dry vermouth, so the gin leads. A quarter ounce of maraschino is cherry pit and almond, and three dashes of orange bitters is a lot of peel. The absinthe is a rinse, a thin anise film on the glass rather than a pour. Stirred, coupe, orange twist. A dressed Martini, gin first, then cherry, peel, and wormwood.

Harry Johnson prints the Tuxedo in his 1900 Bartenders' Manual: equal Old Tom and French vermouth, dashes of maraschino, absinthe, and orange bitters. The name is the Tuxedo Club in Tuxedo Park, New York, opened in 1886. Harry Craddock, in the 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book, splits the family: his No. 1 is gin, dry vermouth, lemon peel, and absinthe; his No. 2 is Johnson's original with dry gin in place of Old Tom. This menu's Tuxedo #2 keeps the maraschino, the orange bitters, and the absinthe, yet it pours two ounces of gin to three-quarters of vermouth, a quarter of maraschino, three dashes of bitters, and an absinthe rinse, coupe, orange.

- [Difford's Guide, Tuxedo cocktail and its many variations](https://www.diffordsguide.com/encyclopedia/1511/cocktails/tuxedo-cocktail-and-its-many-variations)
- [The Savoy Cocktail Book (1930), Tuxedo Cocktail (No. 2)](https://savoycocktaildatabase.com/cocktails/tuxedo-cocktail-no-2/)

#### Hanky Panky

`1h,1h,1b,co` · stirred · Gin · Martini family

- 1 1/2 oz Gin
- 1 1/2 oz Sweet vermouth
- 1 barspoon Fernet
- Coupe, Orange twist

Equal ounces and a half of gin and sweet vermouth, a fifty-fifty Martinez ratio. One barspoon of Fernet is mint and bitter, enough to taste, not enough to own the drink. Stirred, coupe, orange twist.

Ada Coleman created the Hanky Panky at the Savoy's American Bar in London, where she was head bartender from 1903 to 1926. Harry Craddock prints it in the 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book, credited to her: equal Italian vermouth and gin, two dashes of Fernet-Branca, orange peel. The story attached is actor Charles Hawtrey asking her for something with a punch, and naming the result. This menu keeps the equal gin and sweet vermouth, pours a barspoon of Fernet, coupe, orange.

- [Difford's Guide, Hanky Panky](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/930/hanky-panky-cocktail)
- [The Savoy Cocktail Book (1930), Hanky Panky Cocktail](https://euvs-vintage-cocktail-books.cld.bz/1930-The-Savoy-Cocktail-Book/80/)

#### Racquet Club

`2,1,1b,2,cl` · stirred · Gin · Martini family

- 2 oz Gin
- 1 oz Dry vermouth
- 1 barspoon Crème de cacao
- 2 dashes Orange bitters
- Coupe, Lemon twist

Two ounces of gin to one of dry vermouth, a dry Martini ratio. One barspoon of crème de cacao is chocolate as a film. Two dashes of orange bitters are peel. Stirred, coupe, lemon twist. Gin, dry wine, and a thin cocoa finish.

Hugo R. Ensslin prints a Racquet Club Cocktail in Recipes for Mixed Drinks (1916/1917): gin, French vermouth, orange bitters. Harry Craddock's Savoy keeps gin and French vermouth with orange bitters and a lemon. Later specs put a barspoon of crème de cacao in the dressing, chocolate against the dry gin. This menu pours two ounces of gin, one of dry vermouth, a barspoon of cacao, two dashes of orange bitters, lemon twist.

- [Difford's Guide, Racquet Club](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/1618/racquet-club-cocktail)

#### Bijou

`1,1,1,1,Rl` · stirred · Gin · Martini family

- 1 oz Gin
- 1 oz Chartreuse
- 1 oz Sweet vermouth
- 1 dash Orange bitters
- Rocks, iced, Lemon twist

Equal ounces of gin, green Chartreuse, and sweet vermouth, so the herbal liqueur is a third of the drink. One dash of orange bitters is peel. Stirred, rocks with ice, lemon twist. Gin, Chartreuse, and grape, and the cube.

Harry Johnson prints the Bijou in his 1900 Bartender's Manual as equal Plymouth gin, green Chartreuse, and sweet vermouth, a dash of orange bitters, a cherry, and a lemon twist, the name from the French for jewel, the three liquids standing for diamond, emerald, and ruby. Johnson claimed it; David Wondrich notes it may be older. Most later books serve it up. This menu keeps the equal parts and the orange bitters, and pours it over ice with a lemon twist.

- [Difford's Guide, Bijou](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/224/bijou-cocktail)
- [Imbibe, Bijou Cocktail](https://imbibemagazine.com/recipe/bijou-cocktail/)

#### Cin-Cyn

`1,1,1,Ro` · stirred · Gin · Negroni family

- 1 oz Gin
- 1 oz Cynar
- 1 oz Sweet vermouth
- Rocks, iced, Orange twist

Equal ounces of gin, Cynar, and sweet vermouth, so the artichoke amaro is a third of the drink. Stirred, rocks with ice, orange twist. A Negroni with Cynar in the Campari slot, softer bitter, still orange.

Cin-Cyn is a play on cin-cin, the Italian toast, and on Cynar. It is a Negroni with Cynar in place of Campari, equal parts, over ice with an orange twist. Difford's treats it as a sweeter, less bitter Negroni riff. A drink of this name does not appear in the pre-1970 manuals; it belongs to the amaro revival of the 2000s. This menu keeps the equal parts and the rocks glass.

- [Difford's Guide, Cin-Cyn](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/5458/cin-cyn)

#### Physically Forgotten

`1h,Q,h,2,cl` · stirred · Gin · Fancy family

- 1 1/2 oz Gin
- 3/4 oz Cynar
- 1/2 oz Maraschino liqueur
- 2 dashes Orange bitters
- Coupe, Lemon twist

An ounce and a half of gin, three-quarters of Cynar, half an ounce of maraschino. The gin leads; artichoke bitter and cherry liqueur split the rest. Two dashes of orange bitters. Stirred, coupe, lemon twist.

Alise Moffatt built Physically Forgotten at Shift Drinks in Portland, Oregon. Brett Adams and Jacob Grier print it in Raising the Bar (2022): an ounce and a half of gin, three-quarters Cynar, half an ounce of maraschino, two dashes of orange bitters, lemon twist. It drinks as a Martinez with Cynar in the vermouth slot. This menu keeps that pour.

- [Cocktail Virgin Slut, Physically Forgotten](https://cocktailvirgin.blogspot.com/2023/09/physically-forgotten.html)

#### Cardinale

`1h,Q,Q,cl` · stirred · Gin · Negroni family

- 1 1/2 oz Gin
- 3/4 oz Campari
- 3/4 oz Dry vermouth
- Coupe, Lemon twist

An ounce and a half of gin, three-quarters of Campari, three-quarters of dry vermouth. More gin than either modifier, and dry vermouth in the sweet slot, so the juniper stays in front and the Campari reads as bitter orange peel over a lean drink. Stirred, coupe, lemon twist.

Giovanni Raimondo made the Cardinale at the Excelsior Hotel in Rome in 1950, for a cardinal in the city at the summons of Pope Pius XII for the Jubilee. That build was roughly an ounce of gin, half an ounce of dry Moselle, and a third of an ounce of Campari, with a clove-studded orange peel; dry vermouth replaced the wine later, likely for availability and for keeping. David Wondrich points out that the name is older: Piero Grandi's 1926 Campari book Cocktails lists a Campari Cardinal made with sweet vermouth, and Paolo Ponzo found a dry-vermouth Cardinale in Amedeo Gandiglio's 1947 Cocktails Portfolio, the same book that first prints the equal-parts Negroni. This menu pours an ounce and a half of gin, three-quarters of Campari, and three-quarters of dry vermouth, stirred, coupe, lemon twist.

- [Punch, What Is the Cardinale Cocktail?](https://punchdrink.com/articles/next-best-negroni-cardinale-cocktail-recipe/)

#### Alaska

`2,h,1,cl` · stirred · Gin · Fancy family

- 2 oz Gin
- 1/2 oz Chartreuse
- 1 dash Orange bitters
- Coupe, Lemon twist

Two ounces of gin to a half ounce of yellow Chartreuse, so the liqueur is a fifth of the pour: honey, dried herbs, and a faint saffron cast in the glass. One dash of orange bitters. Stirred, coupe, lemon twist. Juniper first, sweetness second, and an herbal finish that outlasts both.

The Alaska first appears in Jacques Straub's Manual of Mixed Drinks in 1913, made with Old Tom gin, yellow Chartreuse, and orange bitters. Harry Craddock prints it in The Savoy Cocktail Book in 1930 with more gin and less Chartreuse, and adds a note: so far as can be ascertained this delectable potion is NOT the staple diet of the Esquimaux, and it was probably first thought of in South Carolina, hence its name. David Embury, in 1948, records it as sometimes called the Oriental and prefers it drier still. This menu pours two ounces of gin, a half ounce of yellow Chartreuse, and one dash of orange bitters, coupe, lemon twist.

- [Imbibe, Rediscovering the Alaska Cocktail](https://imbibemagazine.com/rediscovering-the-alaska-cocktail/)
- [Difford's Guide, Alaska (Savoy Recipe)](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/33/alaska-savoy-recipe)

#### Angel Face

`1,1,1,c` · stirred · Gin · Fancy family

- 1 oz Gin
- 1 oz Apple brandy
- 1 oz Apricot liqueur
- Coupe

Equal ounces of gin, apple brandy, and apricot, three bottles at the same weight. Stirred, coupe. Juniper and orchard apple with apricot over the top, and since the apricot is a liqueur it is the sugar in the drink as well as the fruit. Three ounces of spirit and nothing to lengthen it, so it drinks warm and slow.

Harry Craddock prints the Angel Face in The Savoy Cocktail Book in 1930 as a third each of dry gin, apricot brandy, and Calvados, shaken and strained into a cocktail glass. His apricot brandy meant the drier eau-de-vie rather than the sweetened liqueur most bars reach for now, which is why the modern version reads sweeter than his did. The name gets attached to Abe Angel Face Kaminsky, who robbed Detroit speakeasies, though nothing ties him to the glass. This menu keeps the equal ounces and stirs it, since there is no juice, egg, or syrup carrying it, coupe.

- [Difford's Guide, Angel Face](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/521/angel-face)

#### Fifty-Fifty

`1h,1h,d,cO` · stirred · Gin · Martini family

- 1 1/2 oz Gin
- 1 1/2 oz Dry vermouth
- 1 dash Orange bitters
- Coupe, Olive

An ounce and a half each of gin and dry vermouth, one dash of orange bitters. Half the drink is wine, so it is softer and lower proof than the Martini and the vermouth's grape and wormwood share the front with the juniper. Stirred, coupe, an olive. Salt from the olive against the wine.

Equal parts was the Martini ratio before Prohibition. Hugo Ensslin prints the Fifty-Fifty in 1917 in Recipes for Mixed Drinks, and Harry Craddock repeats it in the 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book: half gin, half French vermouth. The dry decades pushed the vermouth down to a rinse, and the ratio came back in New York in the late 1990s, at Sasha Petraske's Milk & Honey and then as Audrey Saunders' Fitty-Fitty at the Pegu Club in 2005, with orange bitters. This menu pours an ounce and a half each of gin and dry vermouth and one dash of orange bitters, stirred, coupe, olive.

- [Difford's Guide, Dry Martini (1:1 ratio) Fifty-Fifty](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/2162/dry-martini-11-ratio-fifty-fifty)
- [Punch, The Fifty-Fifty Martini Is Back](https://punchdrink.com/articles/fifty-fifty-martini-cocktail-recipe-is-back/)

#### Dirty Martini

`2,h,q,cO` · stirred · Gin · Martini family

- 2 oz Gin
- 1/2 oz Dry vermouth
- 1/4 oz Olive brine
- Coupe, Olive

Two ounces of gin, half an ounce of dry vermouth, a quarter ounce of brine from the olive jar. The brine is salt and a little vinegar, and it turns the drink savoury and slightly cloudy. Juniper first, then salt, then the vermouth. Stirred, coupe, an olive.

John O'Connor at the Waldorf-Astoria is credited with the first one in 1901, a Martini with olives muddled into it. Brine as a measured ingredient prints by 1930 in G. H. Steele's My New Cocktail Book. Franklin Roosevelt mixed his own at two parts gin to one of vermouth with a spoon of brine and an olive, and poured them for Churchill and Stalin. This menu pours two ounces of gin, half an ounce of dry vermouth, and a quarter ounce of brine, stirred, coupe, olive.

- [Punch, The Dirty Martini Cleans Up Its Act](https://punchdrink.com/articles/dirty-martini-recipe-cleans-up-olive-brine-cocktails-dante-nyc/)
- [VinePair, The History of Martini Olives](https://vinepair.com/articles/history-martini-olives-superstition/)

### Vermouth

#### Duplex

`1h,1h,2,co` · stirred · Vermouth · Vermouth family

- 1 1/2 oz Sweet vermouth
- 1 1/2 oz Dry vermouth
- 2 dashes Orange bitters
- Coupe, Orange twist

Equal ounces and a half of sweet and dry vermouth, so neither wins. Two dashes of orange bitters are peel on the split wine. Stirred, no spirit, coupe, orange twist. Grape and spice, cold, with a thin orange film on the wine.

Albert Stevens Crockett, in Old Waldorf Bar Days (1931), lists the Duplex as equal Italian and French vermouth with two dashes of orange bitters or two squeezes of orange peel, and calls it parent of the original Bronx. Johnnie Solon of the Waldorf said he was making a Duplex when Traverson, head waiter of the Empire Room, challenged him to invent a new cocktail, and he added gin and orange juice. This menu is the Waldorf Duplex: an ounce and a half of each vermouth, two dashes of orange bitters, stirred, coupe, orange twist.

- [Albert Stevens Crockett, Old Waldorf Bar Days (1931), Duplex](https://euvs-vintage-cocktail-books.cld.bz/1931-Ol-Waldorf-Astoria-Bar-Days-by-Albert-Stevens-Crockett/132/)
- [Crockett, Old Waldorf Bar Days, Solon on the Bronx](https://euvs-vintage-cocktail-books.cld.bz/1931-Ol-Waldorf-Astoria-Bar-Days-by-Albert-Stevens-Crockett/80/)

#### Vermouth Panaché

`2,1,1,cl` · stirred · Vermouth · Vermouth family

- 2 oz Sweet vermouth
- 1 oz Dry vermouth
- 1 dash Orange bitters
- Coupe, Lemon twist

Two ounces of sweet vermouth to one of dry, so the sweet leads. One dash of orange bitters is peel on the grape. Stirred, coupe, lemon twist. Grape and spice, the sweet vermouth leading, with a thin lemon oil on top.

Panache is French for mixed. Philip Greene, in To Have and Have Another (2012), gives the name Vermouth Panache to a drink Ernest Hemingway described in a 1934 Esquire piece: on a fishing trip off Havana, French and Italian vermouth over ice with a dash of bitters and a lemon peel. Hemingway did not name it. Greene's reconstruction, as printed in Saveur, is three ounces dry to one sweet, Angostura, on the rocks. This menu inverts the ratio, two sweet to one dry, uses orange bitters, and pours it up with a lemon twist.

- [Saveur, Vermouth Panache](https://www.saveur.com/article/recipes/vermouth-panache-cocktail/)
- [Saveur, Vermouth on the Rise](https://www.saveur.com/article/wine-and-drink/vermouth-on-the-rise/)

#### Diplomat

`2,1,q,clc` · stirred · Vermouth · Vermouth family

- 2 oz Dry vermouth
- 1 oz Sweet vermouth
- 1/4 oz Maraschino liqueur
- Coupe, Lemon twist, Cherry

Two ounces of dry vermouth to one of sweet, so the dry wine is two thirds of the drink, then a quarter ounce of maraschino. No bitters, no base spirit. Cherry glue on two vermouths, dry leading. Stirred, coupe, lemon and cherry.

Robert Vermeire prints it as Diplomate in Cocktails: How to Mix Them (1922), "very well known in the French Diplomatic Service." Harry Craddock's 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book anglicizes the name: two-thirds French vermouth, one-third Italian, a dash of maraschino, shaken, cherry and lemon peel. Patrick Gavin Duffy's 1934 Official Mixer's Manual stirs the same formula. This menu keeps the two-to-one dry to sweet, pours a quarter ounce of maraschino rather than a dash, and skips the bitters later writers add. Coupe, lemon, cherry.

- [Difford's Guide, Diplomat](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/648/diplomat)
- [The Kitchn, The Diplomat Cocktail](https://www.thekitchn.com/the-9bottle-bar-recipe-the-diplomat-cocktail-drink-recipes-from-the-kitchn-207294)

#### Chrysanthemum

`2,h,2b,co` · stirred · Vermouth · Vermouth family

- 2 oz Dry vermouth
- 1/2 oz Bénédictine
- 2 barspoons Absinthe
- Coupe, Orange twist

Two ounces of dry vermouth, half an ounce of Benedictine, two barspoons of absinthe. The vermouth is the drink; the liqueur is honeyed spice; two barspoons of absinthe is a pour, anise laid over the wine. Stirred, coupe, orange twist.

Hugo R. Ensslin prints the Chrysanthemum in Recipes for Mixed Drinks (1917, and likely the 1916 first edition): equal French vermouth and Benedictine, three dashes of absinthe, orange peel. Harry Craddock's 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book dries it to two-thirds vermouth and one-third Benedictine, still three dashes of absinthe, and notes it was "well-known and very popular in the American Bar of the S.S. Europa." Difford's suggests the name may track Scott Joplin's 1904 ragtime piece The Chrysanthemum, issued on record in 1916. This menu is two ounces of dry vermouth, half an ounce of Benedictine, and two barspoons of absinthe, stirred, orange twist.

- [Difford's Guide, Chrysanthemum](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/2338/chrysanthemum)
- [Imbibe, Chrysanthemum Cocktail](https://imbibemagazine.com/recipe/chrysanthemum-cocktail/)

#### Tip Top

`2,Q,2,cl` · stirred · Vermouth · Vermouth family

- 2 oz Dry vermouth
- 3/4 oz Bénédictine
- 2 dashes Orange bitters
- Coupe, Lemon twist

Two ounces of dry vermouth, three-quarters Benedictine, two dashes of orange bitters. The liqueur is a real pour of honey and spice, not a few dashes. Orange bitters pull peel through the wine. Stirred, coupe, lemon twist.

Albert Stevens Crockett prints Tiptop in Old Waldorf Bar Days (1931): four dashes of Benedictine, two dashes of Angostura, one jigger of French vermouth, stirred, lemon peel. No bartender is named. Difford's later scales the Benedictine to three-quarters of an ounce. This menu keeps that pour and the lemon twist, and uses two dashes of orange bitters in place of Angostura.

- [Difford's Guide, Tip Top Cocktail](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/2889/tip-top-cocktail)
- [Old Waldorf Bar Days (1931), p. 167](https://euvs-vintage-cocktail-books.cld.bz/1931-Ol-Waldorf-Astoria-Bar-Days-by-Albert-Stevens-Crockett/167/)

#### Bamboo

`1h,1h,d,2,cOl` · stirred · Vermouth · Vermouth family

- 1 1/2 oz Sherry
- 1 1/2 oz Dry vermouth
- 1 dash Angostura bitters
- 2 dashes Orange bitters
- Coupe, Olive, Lemon twist

Equal ounces and a half of dry sherry and dry vermouth, so there is no base spirit. One dash of Angostura, two of orange bitters. Stirred, coupe, olive and lemon twist. Nutty, dry wine, a little bark.

Louis Eppinger is credited with the Bamboo at the Grand Hotel in Yokohama, sometime in the 1890s: equal sherry and dry vermouth, bitters, a twist. It appears in American books by 1908. David Wondrich, in Imbibe, treats it as the low-proof cousin of the Martini, sherry in the gin slot. This menu pours equal ounces and a half, one dash of Angostura and two of orange bitters, coupe, olive and lemon.

- [Difford's Guide, Bamboo](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/196/bamboo-cocktail)
- [Imbibe, Bamboo Cocktail](https://imbibemagazine.com/recipe/bamboo-cocktail/)

#### Bitter Giuseppe

`2,1,q,6,Rl` · stirred · Vermouth · Negroni family

- 2 oz Cynar
- 1 oz Sweet vermouth
- 1/4 oz Lemon juice
- 6 dashes Orange bitters
- Rocks, iced, Lemon twist

Two ounces of Cynar, an ounce of sweet vermouth, a quarter of lemon, six dashes of orange bitters. No base spirit, so it is low proof, and artichoke bitterness runs the whole length of it with the vermouth holding what sugar there is. The quarter ounce of lemon is the odd part, and it is what keeps the Cynar from going flat. Rocks with ice, lemon twist.

Stephen Cole made the Bitter Giuseppe at The Violet Hour in Chicago in 2007, when an Italian chef came into the bar and Cole guessed he would want a Cynar Manhattan, built with Carpano Antica. It came out sweet, so he added lemon juice, which a stirred spirit drink was not supposed to take, and kept adjusting until he had a quarter ounce of lemon and six dashes of orange bitters. He credits the Ti' Punch of Martinique for the idea that citrus belongs in a stirred glass, and tells the story in The Bartender's Manifesto in 2022. This menu pours two ounces of Cynar, an ounce of sweet vermouth, a quarter of lemon, and six dashes of orange bitters, stirred, rocks with ice, lemon twist.

- [Punch, Bitter Giuseppe](https://punchdrink.com/recipes/bitter-giuseppe/)
- [Difford's Guide, Bitter Giuseppe](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/4856/bitter-giuseppe)

#### Adonis

`1h,Q,2,co` · stirred · Vermouth · Vermouth family

- 1 1/2 oz Sherry
- 3/4 oz Sweet vermouth
- 2 dashes Orange bitters
- Coupe, Orange twist

An ounce and a half of sherry to three-quarters of sweet vermouth, two fortified wines and nothing stronger, so it pours low. Two dashes of orange bitters. Stirred, coupe, orange twist. Nutty dry wine under the vermouth's grape and sugar, light enough to drink before dinner.

The Adonis is named for William Gill's Adonis, a musical burlesque that opened in Chicago in the summer of 1884 and moved to the Bijou Theatre in New York that September with Henry E. Dixey in the title role. The Waldorf is usually credited with the drink. The first print record is a Pearls from Billy, the Bartender column in the New York Sun on 27 March 1887, which puts the making of it around 1885 or 1886. It is the sweet half of the pair of nineteenth-century sherry aperitifs, the Bamboo being the dry one. This menu pours an ounce and a half of sherry, three-quarters of sweet vermouth, and two dashes of orange bitters, coupe, orange twist.

- [Punch, Adonis](https://punchdrink.com/recipes/adonis/)
- [Difford's Guide, Adonis](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/18/adonis)

#### Coronation No. 1

`1h,1h,d,2,c` · stirred · Vermouth · Vermouth family

- 1 1/2 oz Sherry
- 1 1/2 oz Dry vermouth
- 1 dash Maraschino liqueur
- 2 dashes Orange bitters
- Coupe

The Bamboo with maraschino in it: an ounce and a half each of amontillado and dry vermouth, a dash of maraschino, two dashes of orange bitters. Nutty, dry wine, with the maraschino's cherry and almond just showing and the orange bitters on the finish. Stirred, coupe, nothing on top. Low proof, dry, and fragrant.

Named for the coronation of Edward VII, set for June 1902 and put back to August by the King's appendix. It first prints in Charles Mahoney's 1905 Hoffman House Bartender's Guide, credited to Joseph Rose of Murry Bros. Cafe in Newark, New Jersey, where it had taken second prize in the Police Gazette bartenders' contest of 1903. Harry Craddock's 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book has it as half sherry, half French vermouth, a dash of maraschino, two dashes of orange bitters, shaken. This menu stirs it, since there is no juice in it: an ounce and a half each of sherry and dry vermouth, a dash of maraschino, two of orange bitters, coupe.

- [Difford's Guide, Coronation Cocktail No. 1](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/470/coronation-cocktail-no1)

### Fernet

#### Fernet and Ginger

`1,4,RLw` · stirred · Fernet · Highball family

- 1 oz Fernet
- 4 oz Ginger beer
- Rocks, iced, Lime wheel

One ounce of Fernet, four ounces of ginger beer, over ice. The ginger beer is the drink; the Fernet is mint and bitter through the spice. Lime squeezed in and dropped. A highball. It sits.

Fernet and ginger beer is a bartender's highball, Fernet-Branca lengthened with ginger, a squeeze of lime. It does not appear under a fixed name in the pre-1970 manuals; it belongs to the Fernet-Branca cult that took hold in San Francisco bars in the 2000s and then everywhere else. Brett Adams and Jacob Grier print it in Raising the Bar (2022) as an ounce of Fernet and four of ginger beer, lime wedge in. This menu keeps that pour, rocks with ice.

- [Punch, The Magic of Fernet-Branca Cocktails](https://punchdrink.com/articles/dark-magic-fernet-branca-hanky-panky-cocktail-recipe/)

## Shaken

Anything with juice, egg, or syrup carrying the drink. Hard shake, double strain.

### Aged Rum

#### Winter Daiquiri

`2,1,h,2,c` · shaken · Aged Rum · Sour family

- 2 oz Aged rum
- 1 oz Lime juice
- 1/2 oz Demerara syrup
- 2 dashes Angostura bitters
- Coupe

Two ounces of aged rum against a full ounce of lime and only a half ounce of demerara: tart, brown sugar, barrel. Two dashes of Angostura pull clove and bark through the lime. Coupe.

The Daiquiri is credited to Jennings Stockton Cox, an American mining engineer at Daiquiri, Cuba, around the turn of the twentieth century, mixing Bacardi, lime, and sugar. Francesco Domenico Pagliuchi wrote in 1948 that he was there and suggested the name; Basil Woon's 1928 When It's Cocktail Time in Cuba records Cox naming it at Santiago's Venus bar. The first recipe-book appearance is Jacques Straub's 1914 Drinks, misspelt Daiguiri. A winter version keeps the sour and changes the rum and the sugar. This menu uses aged rum, demerara syrup, a full ounce of lime against a half ounce of sweetener, and two dashes of Angostura.

- [Difford's Guide, Daiquiri history](https://www.diffordsguide.com/g/1083/daiquiri-cocktail/story)

#### Air Mail

`1h,Q,Q,2,R` · shaken · Aged Rum · Sparkling family

- 1 1/2 oz Aged rum
- 3/4 oz Lime juice
- 3/4 oz Honey syrup
- 2 oz Champagne
- Rocks, iced

A rum sour of an ounce and a half of aged rum, three-quarters lime, three-quarters honey, then two ounces of Champagne over ice in a rocks glass. Honey is thicker and waxier than sugar, so the rum tastes darker than a Daiquiri. The bubbles and the melt are the lift.

The Air Mail first saw print in Bacardi and Its Many Uses, a 1930 pamphlet from the still-Cuban company. Jeff Berry, writing in The Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails, notes that Cuba began air-mail service that year, yet the pamphlet names no bartender. W.C. Whitfield's 1941 Here's How prints it as rum, lime, honey, and Champagne in a highball, with the line "It ought to make you fly high." Some later writers treat it as a rum French 75. The early printings, however, are a honey Daiquiri topped with sparkling wine and served long, over ice. This menu keeps the honey and the Champagne, uses aged rum, and pours it in a rocks glass with ice.

- [The Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails, Air Mail](https://www.spiritsanddistilling.com/dictionary/acref-9780199311132-e-232)
- [Difford's Guide, Air Mail](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/27/air-mail)

#### Brass Rail

`1h,h,1,h,2,c3` · shaken · Aged Rum · Daisy family

- 1 1/2 oz Aged rum
- 1/2 oz Bénédictine
- 1 oz Lemon juice
- 1/2 oz Simple syrup
- 2 dashes Orange bitters
- one Egg white
- 3 dashes Angostura bitters (on top)
- Coupe, 3 dashes of bitters

An ounce and a half of aged rum, a half of Benedictine, a full ounce of lemon, a half of simple: a rum sour with a herbal liqueur in the sugar slot. Egg white gives it a foam cap. Two dashes of orange bitters sit in the shake; three dashes of Angostura are dropped on the foam, clove and bark on the white. Coupe.

Tony Abou-Ganim built the Brass Rail as a nightcap for his cousin Helen David, who favored Benedictine, and named it for her bar in Port Huron, Michigan, which she opened in 1937. Difford's Guide adapts the recipe from Abou-Ganim: aged rum, Benedictine, lemon, sugar, egg white, and orange bitters, with a flamed orange twist and cinnamon on the foam. This menu uses aged rum, Benedictine, a full ounce of lemon, half an ounce of simple, two dashes of orange bitters, egg white, and three dashes of Angostura dropped on the foam.

- [Difford's Guide, Brass Rail](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/564/brass-rail)

#### Old Cuban

`1h,Q,1,2,2,cm` · shaken · Aged Rum · Sparkling family

- 1 1/2 oz Aged rum
- 3/4 oz Lime juice
- 1 oz Simple syrup
- 2 dashes Angostura bitters
- one Mint
- 2 oz Champagne
- Coupe, Mint

An ounce and a half of aged rum, three-quarters of lime, a full ounce of simple, two dashes of Angostura, mint shaken in, then two ounces of Champagne. An ounce of syrup is a heavy pour of sugar, and the bitters and the bubbles are what hold it up. Shaking the mint takes the oil and leaves the leaf whole. Coupe, mint on top.

Audrey Saunders built the Old Cuban in 2001 and put it on at Bemelmans Bar in the Carlyle, in Manhattan, where by her account it took off almost immediately. She carried it to the Ritz in London for a pop-up in 2002, then onto the opening menu at Pegu Club in 2005, filed under Champagne Opportunities, and it stayed a bestseller for the fifteen years that bar ran. Saunders describes the aim as a lively yet elegant Champagne cocktail with a neotropical edge; the two parents are the Mojito and the French 75. This menu pours an ounce and a half of aged rum, three-quarters of lime, an ounce of simple, two dashes of Angostura, mint, and two ounces of Champagne, shaken, coupe, mint.

- [Punch, How the Old Cuban Became a Modern Classic](https://punchdrink.com/articles/old-cuban-modern-classic-champagne-mojito-cocktail-recipe/)

#### Ace of Clubs

`2,1,Q,c` · shaken · Aged Rum · Daisy family

- 2 oz Aged rum
- 1 oz Crème de cacao
- 3/4 oz Lime juice
- Coupe

Two ounces of aged rum, a full ounce of crème de cacao, three-quarters of lime. The chocolate is a real pour against the rum; the lime cuts it. Shaken, coupe. A Daiquiri with cacao in the sugar slot.

Esquire printed the Ace of Clubs in April 1939, as the house cocktail of a midtown Manhattan restaurant of that name, where Egidio Archimede Dellamazzacane, Eddie, took over the bar in 1938. David Wondrich reprints two ounces of golden rum, crème de cacao, and lime. The original used a full ounce of cacao; Wondrich cuts it. This menu keeps two ounces of aged rum and three-quarters of lime, and it pours the full ounce of cacao.

- [Esquire, Ace of Clubs (David Wondrich)](https://www.esquire.com/food-drink/drinks/recipes/a3694/ace-of-clubs-drink-recipe/)
- [Difford's Guide, Ace Of Clubs Daiquiri](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/14/ace-of-clubs-daiquiri)

### Apple Brandy

#### Jack Rose

`1h,Q,Q,c` · shaken · Apple Brandy · Sour family

- 1 1/2 oz Apple brandy
- 3/4 oz Lime juice
- 3/4 oz Grenadine
- Coupe

An ounce and a half of apple brandy, three-quarters lime, three-quarters grenadine. Lime, so the sour is sharp and green. Equal grenadine means the drink is as pink as it is tart; the apple sits under pomegranate. Shaken. Coupe.

David Wondrich traces the Jack Rose to Frank Haas at Fred Eberlin's downtown New York bar, named in the New York Press in 1899. Jacob Grohusko's 1908 Jack's Manual is the first printed formula. By Jacques Straub's 1914 Drinks it had become applejack, lime, and grenadine. The name is disputed: Wondrich favors the General Jacqueminot, or Jack, rose, a pink hybrid the drink resembles; Frank J. May claimed it in the 1905 Police Gazette; Bald Jack Rose, the 1912 Rosenthal-case informant, is a later story, and the drink predates him. This menu is Straub's three-ingredient drink: an ounce and a half of apple brandy, three-quarters lime, three-quarters grenadine.

- [The Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails, The Jack Rose](https://www.spiritsanddistilling.com/dictionary/acref-9780199311132-e-345)
- [Difford's Guide, Jack Rose Cocktail](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/1039/jack-rose-cocktail)

#### Pink Lady

`1h,Q,Q,h,cc` · shaken · Apple Brandy · Sour family

- 1 1/2 oz Gin
- 3/4 oz Apple brandy
- 3/4 oz Lime juice
- 1/2 oz Grenadine
- one Egg white
- Coupe, Cherry

Gin at an ounce and a half, then three-quarters of apple brandy and three-quarters of lime, a half ounce of grenadine, and egg white. The foam is the texture; the apple is a real pour. Lime and gin keep it sharp. Grenadine is color and a little pomegranate. Coupe, cherry.

The Pink Lady takes its name from Ivan Caryll's 1911 Broadway musical, starring Hazel Dawn. Wondrich records that the drink mixed for her at Murray's Roman Gardens was ojen with Peychaud's and Angostura, not this one. Jacques Straub's 1913 Manual of Mixed Drinks prints the version that entered the books: equal gin, applejack, and lime, with dashes of grenadine, and no egg. Later recipes drop the apple brandy, add egg white or cream, or both. Craddock's Savoy omits the applejack and adds the white. This menu keeps Straub's gin, apple brandy, lime, and grenadine, and it shakes egg white with them.

- [The Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails, Pink Lady Cocktail](https://www.spiritsanddistilling.com/dictionary/acref-9780199311132-e-384)
- [Difford's Guide, Pink Lady](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/1548/pink-lady)

#### Honeymoon

`1q,1,1b,h,1,Ro` · shaken · Apple Brandy · Daisy family

- 1 1/4 oz Apple brandy
- 1 oz Bénédictine
- 1 barspoon Orange liqueur
- 1/2 oz Lemon juice
- 1 dash Orange bitters
- Rocks, iced, Orange twist

An ounce and a quarter of apple brandy against a full ounce of Benedictine: herb almost even with orchard. A barspoon of orange liqueur and a dash of orange bitters are peel. Half an ounce of lemon lifts it. Rocks, ice, orange twist: it sits and the Benedictine warms.

Hugo R. Ensslin first prints the Honey Moon Cocktail in Recipes for Mixed Drinks (1916): equal Benedictine and apple brandy, juice of half a lemon, three dashes of curacao. Ensslin was at the Hotel Wallick in Times Square. Craddock copies it into the Savoy in 1930. It later turns up at the Brown Derby in Los Angeles, and David Embury (1948) also calls it the Farmer's Daughter, with a much drier applejack-forward ratio. This menu pours an ounce and a quarter of apple brandy, a full ounce of Benedictine, a barspoon of orange liqueur, half an ounce of lemon, and a dash of orange bitters, over ice with an orange twist.

- [Difford's Guide, Honeymoon](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/969/honeymoon)
- [Vintage American Cocktails, Honeymoon](https://vintageamericancocktails.com/honeymoon-cocktail-recipe/)

#### Southern Point

`Q,Q,Q,Q,ca` · shaken · Apple Brandy · Daisy family

- 3/4 oz Apple brandy
- 3/4 oz Elderflower liqueur
- 3/4 oz Orange liqueur
- 3/4 oz Lemon juice
- Coupe, Apple fan

Four equal three-quarter-ounce pours: apple brandy, elderflower liqueur, orange liqueur, lemon. Nothing leads. The elderflower is floral honey against the orchard, and the orange liqueur is peel; the lemon is the whole sour. Coupe, apple garnish. It drinks as a Sidecar that split the cognac and the orange liqueur and put apple and elderflower in their place.

A drink called Southern Point does not appear in the pre-1970 manuals, nor under that name in Difford's, Punch, or Imbibe. Equal-parts sours of this shape are modern, and the elderflower half of it cannot predate Robert Cooper's St-Germain, launched in 2007. The nearest parent is the Sidecar: brandy, orange liqueur, and lemon. This menu swaps cognac for apple brandy, splits the sweet between elderflower and orange liqueur, and pours all four at three-quarters of an ounce, shaken, in a coupe with an apple garnish.

- [VinePair, 8 Things You Should Know About St-Germain Elderflower Liqueur](https://vinepair.com/articles/ntk-st-germain/)

### Cognac

#### Sidecar

`1h,1,Q,cs` · shaken · Cognac · Daisy family

- 1 1/2 oz Cognac
- 1 oz Orange liqueur
- 3/4 oz Lemon juice
- Coupe, Sugar rim

An ounce and a half of cognac, a full ounce of orange liqueur, three-quarters lemon. The orange liqueur is heavier than the lemon, so the drink is peel and candy. Shaken, coupe, sugar rim.

Robert Vermeire prints the Sidecar in May 1922 in Cocktails How to Mix Them: equal cognac, Cointreau, and lemon, very popular in France, and first introduced in London by Pat MacGarry of Buck's Club. Harry MacElhone, who had worked with MacGarry, prints the same formula later that year and later takes the credit himself. Frank Meier at the Ritz Bar in Paris listed it among cocktails new since the war. David Embury, in 1948, credits an unnamed American captain in a Paris sidecar. The origin stays disputed. This menu pours an ounce and a half of cognac, a full ounce of orange liqueur, and three-quarters lemon, shaken, with a sugar rim.

- [The Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails, The Sidecar](https://www.spiritsanddistilling.com/dictionary/acref-9780199311132-e-417)
- [Difford's Guide, Sidecar](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/4791/sidecar)

#### Between the Sheets

`1,1,1,Q,cl` · shaken · Cognac · Daisy family

- 1 oz Cognac
- 1 oz Light rum
- 1 oz Orange liqueur
- 3/4 oz Lemon juice
- Coupe, Lemon twist

An ounce each of cognac, light rum, and orange liqueur, with three-quarters of lemon behind them. Three ounces of alcohol in a coupe, so it drinks hot, and a full third of that is the orange liqueur, carrying the sugar and most of the aroma. The rum sharpens the grape in the cognac; the lemon is what keeps it moving. Coupe, lemon twist.

The earliest documented printing is Frank Shay's 1929 Drawn From The Wood, where the drink is equal parts gin, Bacardi, and Cointreau. Harry Craddock's 1930 The Savoy Cocktail Book prints it in thirds as brandy, Cointreau, and Bacardi rum, which is the version that stuck, and Charles H. Baker's 1939 The Gentleman's Companion carries a Jerusalem version of cognac, Cointreau, dry gin, and lemon in equal parts. Credit is disputed: Harry MacElhone of Harry's New York Bar in Paris is the usual claim, and Johnny Brooks put his own name to it in My 35 Years Behind Bars in 1954. This menu pours an ounce each of cognac, light rum, and orange liqueur with three-quarters of lemon, shaken, coupe, lemon twist.

- [Difford's Guide, Between The Sheets](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/209/between-the-sheets)

#### Champs-Élysées

`1h,h,Q,q,1,cl` · shaken · Cognac · Daisy family

- 1 1/2 oz Cognac
- 1/2 oz Chartreuse
- 3/4 oz Lemon juice
- 1/4 oz Simple syrup
- 1 dash Angostura bitters
- Coupe, Lemon twist

An ounce and a half of cognac, half an ounce of Chartreuse, three-quarters of lemon, a quarter of simple, one dash of Angostura. Green is the Chartreuse this wants; the bar keeps green and yellow as brands of the one bottle, and green has the proof to hold up against brandy. A quarter ounce of sugar leaves the herbs and the lemon to do the talking. Coupe, lemon twist.

The earliest known recipe is in Drinks Long and Short, published in London in 1925 by Nina Toye and A. H. Adair, written out for a party of six: three glasses of brandy, one of the herbal liqueur, and one and a half of sweetened lemon juice, shaken with Angostura. Harry Craddock printed the same proportions in the 1930 The Savoy Cocktail Book with cognac named in place of brandy. No creator is documented; historians place the drink in the first half of the 1920s and treat it as French, named for the avenue between the Arc de Triomphe and the Place de la Concorde. This menu pours an ounce and a half of cognac, half an ounce of Chartreuse, three-quarters of lemon, a quarter of simple, and a dash of Angostura, shaken, coupe, lemon twist.

- [Coqtail, Champs-Elysees cocktail recipe and story](https://www.coqtail.com/en/champs-elysees-cocktail-recipe-story/)

#### Brandy Alexander

`1,1,1,c` · shaken · Cognac · Fancy family

- 1 oz Cognac
- 1 oz Crème de cacao
- 1 oz Cream
- Coupe

Equal ounces of cognac, crème de cacao, and cream, so chocolate and dairy are two thirds of the drink. Shaken, coupe. Grape brandy, cocoa, and a short cream sour with no citrus.

The Alexander starts as a gin drink in Hugo Ensslin's 1916 Recipes for Mixed Drinks: equal gin, crème de cacao, and cream. The brandy version took over in the 1920s and 1930s; Harry Craddock prints a Brandy Alexander in the 1930 Savoy. It became the default Alexander. This menu keeps the equal ounces of cognac, cacao, and cream, shaken, coupe, no dusting of nutmeg.

- [Difford's Guide, Brandy Alexander](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/306/brandy-alexander)
- [Punch, How to Use Crème de Cacao](https://punchdrink.com/articles/creme-de-cacao-liqueur-cocktail-recipes/)

#### Brandy Milk Punch

`2,2,h,Rcin` · shaken · Cognac · Fancy family

- 2 oz Cognac
- 2 oz Cream
- 1/2 oz Simple syrup
- Rocks, iced, Grated cinnamon

Two ounces of cognac, two of cream, half an ounce of simple, shaken hard and poured over ice in a rocks glass. Cold, rich, and only a little sweet; the cream rounds the brandy and the grape and oak come through it. Grated cinnamon on top is the first thing you taste. The classic grate is nutmeg, and this shelf keeps cinnamon.

Milk punch is colonial: spirit, milk, sugar, and spice, drunk in Britain and America through the eighteenth century. New Orleans kept it as a morning drink, and Brennan's made the brandy version a fixture of the city's brunch, shaken with half-and-half, sugar, and vanilla and dusted with nutmeg. Difford's pours it with cognac and whole milk. This menu pours two ounces of cognac, two of cream, and half an ounce of simple, shaken, over ice, grated cinnamon.

- [Difford's Guide, Brandy Milk Punch](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/314/brandy-milk-punch)
- [Imbibe, Brandy Milk Punch](https://imbibemagazine.com/recipe/brandy-milk-punch-recipe/)

### Bourbon

#### Buster Brown

`2,Q,h,3,co` · shaken · Bourbon · Sour family

- 2 oz Bourbon
- 3/4 oz Lemon juice
- 1/2 oz Demerara syrup
- 3 dashes Orange bitters
- Coupe, Orange twist

Two ounces of bourbon, three-quarters lemon, half an ounce of demerara, three dashes of orange bitters. The lemon is a full sour; orange bitters are peel over the brown sugar. Shaken, coupe, orange twist.

The Buster Brown prints in the 1933 Mixer's Guide as a whiskey cocktail: a teaspoon of gum, two dashes of lemon, two dashes of orange bitters, and a jigger of whisky, stirred and strained. The comic-strip boy of the same name had been running in American newspapers since 1902. This menu turns those lemon dashes into three-quarters of an ounce, sweetens with half an ounce of demerara, shakes it, and keeps three dashes of orange bitters. Coupe, orange twist.

- [1933 Mixer's Guide, Cocktail, Buster Brown](https://euvs-vintage-cocktail-books.cld.bz/1933-Mixer-s-Guide/17/)

#### Gold Rush

`2,Q,Q,R` · shaken · Bourbon · Sour family

- 2 oz Bourbon
- 3/4 oz Lemon juice
- 3/4 oz Honey syrup
- Rocks, iced

Two ounces of bourbon, three-quarters lemon, three-quarters honey syrup. Honey is thick and floral against the lemon. Shaken, rocks with ice. Bourbon, citrus, and a brown pour that sits.

T.J. Siegal, a childhood friend of Sasha Petraske, asked for honey syrup in his bourbon sour at Milk & Honey in New York around 2000, shortly after Petraske opened the bar on New Year's Eve 1999. Siegal named it while drinking the first one. Robert Simonson traces the story in Punch; Sam Ross later built the Penicillin from the same honey-sour idea. This menu keeps the two ounces of bourbon and three-quarters each of lemon and honey syrup, over ice. No twist.

- [Punch, How the Gold Rush Became a Modern Classic](https://punchdrink.com/articles/gold-rush-bourbon-cocktail-recipe-became-modern-classic/)
- [Punch, Gold Rush](https://punchdrink.com/recipes/gold-rush/)

#### Whiskey Sour

`2,Q,h,Rcl` · shaken · Bourbon · Sour family

- 2 oz Bourbon
- 3/4 oz Lemon juice
- 1/2 oz Demerara syrup
- one Egg white
- Rocks, iced, Cherry, Lemon twist

Two ounces of bourbon, three-quarters lemon, half an ounce of demerara, egg white. The foam is the texture; demerara is brown sugar under the lemon. Shaken, rocks with ice, cherry and lemon. A short sour with a dry cap.

A whisky sour is named as early as 1826, and Jerry Thomas prints sours in 1862. The Waukesha Plain Dealer uses the name in 1870 without explaining it. Paul Clarke, in The Oxford Companion, tracks egg white as a European addition from the 1920s that was common in America by the 1940s. The Atlanta Daily Constitution put it in 1879: when American meets American, then comes the whisky sour. This menu pours two ounces of bourbon, three-quarters lemon, half an ounce of demerara, egg white, over ice with cherry and lemon. No wine float.

- [The Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails, The Whisky Sour](https://www.spiritsanddistilling.com/dictionary/acref-9780199311132-e-445)

#### Expat

`2,1,h,2,cm` · shaken · Bourbon · Sour family

- 2 oz Bourbon
- 1 oz Lime juice
- 1/2 oz Simple syrup
- 2 dashes Angostura bitters
- Coupe, Mint

Two ounces of bourbon, a full ounce of lime, half an ounce of simple, two dashes of Angostura. Lime, so the sour is sharp and green; the sugar is thin against that ounce of juice. Shaken, coupe, mint. Clove on the lime.

Lauren Schell built the Expat at Little Branch in Manhattan in 2009. She did not name it until she moved overseas and the bar kept sending the bourbon shake out; Expat seemed the obvious word. Erick Castro printed the spec in Eater in 2015: two ounces of bourbon, an ounce of lime, three-quarters simple, Angostura, mint. This menu keeps the bourbon, the full ounce of lime, the mint, and the dashes, yet it pours only half an ounce of simple.

- [Eater, Nine Awesome Cocktails That Should Be Considered Modern Classics](https://www.eater.com/drinks/2015/5/26/8628313/nine-awesome-cocktails-that-should-be-considered-modern-classics)

#### Whiskey Daisy

`2,Q,q,1b,R` · shaken · Bourbon · Daisy family

- 2 oz Bourbon
- 3/4 oz Lemon juice
- 1/4 oz Orange liqueur
- 1 barspoon Simple syrup
- Rocks, iced

Two ounces of bourbon, three-quarters lemon, a quarter of orange liqueur, one barspoon of simple. The orange liqueur is peel in the sugar slot. Shaken, rocks with ice. A short sour that sits.

Jerry Thomas prints the Daisy in the 1876 Bar-Tender's Guide as a sour sweetened with orange liqueur and topped with seltzer, in brandy, whiskey, gin, and rum versions. David Wondrich, in The Oxford Companion, notes an 1883 claim that Billy Taylor gave the idea to Frank Haas at Fred Eberlin's bar near the New York Stock Exchange about 1873. Later daisies swapped grenadine for curaçao and went long. This menu keeps the whiskey, lemon, and orange liqueur, adds a barspoon of simple, and pours it over ice with no soda.

- [The Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails, The Daisy](https://www.spiritsanddistilling.com/dictionary/acref-9780199311132-e-296)

#### Man o' War

`2,Q,h,h,cl` · shaken · Bourbon · Daisy family

- 2 oz Bourbon
- 3/4 oz Orange liqueur
- 1/2 oz Sweet vermouth
- 1/2 oz Lemon juice
- Coupe, Lemon twist

Two ounces of bourbon, three-quarters orange liqueur, half an ounce each of sweet vermouth and lemon. The orange liqueur is heavier than the lemon, so peel leads. Shaken, coupe, lemon twist. A Manhattan sour: grape, whiskey, and candy citrus.

The drink is named for the thoroughbred who won 20 of 21 races in 1919 and 1920, including the Preakness and Belmont. Simon Difford finds no mid-century book recipe and treats the cocktail as modern; a 1915 newspaper Man-o'-war cocktail is condensed milk, alcohol, and eggs. The Indianapolis Star printed the bourbon, Cointreau, sweet vermouth, and lemon formula in 2015 as a Derby drink. This menu pours two ounces of bourbon, three-quarters orange liqueur, half each of sweet vermouth and lemon, coupe, lemon twist.

- [Difford's Guide, Man O' War](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/4819/man-o-war)

#### Little Honey

`1h,Q,h,h,q,Ro` · shaken · Bourbon · Daisy family

- 1 1/2 oz Bourbon
- 3/4 oz Elderflower liqueur
- 1/2 oz Dry vermouth
- 1/2 oz Lemon juice
- 1/4 oz Honey syrup
- one Egg white
- Rocks, iced, Orange twist

An ounce and a half of bourbon, three-quarters elderflower, half an ounce each of dry vermouth and lemon, a quarter of honey, egg white. The foam carries the flower; dry vermouth keeps it lean. Shaken, rocks with ice, orange twist. Bourbon under elderflower.

A drink called Little Honey does not appear in the pre-1970 manuals, nor under that name in Difford's, Punch, or Imbibe. The nearest parents are the Gold Rush, T.J. Siegal's bourbon, lemon, and honey sour at Milk & Honey around 2000, and the Bee's Knees, with St-Germain, launched by Robert Cooper in 2007, in the elderflower slot. This menu adds dry vermouth and egg white, pours an ounce and a half of bourbon, and serves it over ice with an orange twist.

- [Punch, How the Gold Rush Became a Modern Classic](https://punchdrink.com/articles/gold-rush-bourbon-cocktail-recipe-became-modern-classic/)
- [VinePair, 8 Things You Should Know About St-Germain Elderflower Liqueur](https://vinepair.com/articles/ntk-st-germain/)

#### Brown Derby

`2,1,h,c` · shaken · Bourbon · Sour family

- 2 oz Bourbon
- 1 oz Grapefruit juice
- 1/2 oz Honey syrup
- Coupe

Two ounces of bourbon, a full ounce of grapefruit, half an ounce of honey syrup. Grapefruit is a third of the glass, so pith and a low bitterness arrive before the corn does. Honey is heavier than sugar and sits under the juice rather than dissolving through it. Shaken, coupe, no ice.

The formula is older than the name. Judge Jr. printed it in Here's How in 1927 as Scotch, grapefruit, and honey, and Harry Craddock printed the same proportions as the De Rigueur Cocktail in the 1930 The Savoy Cocktail Book. George Buzza Jr. copied Craddock into Hollywood Cocktails in 1933 and renamed it the Brown Derby, after the hat-shaped restaurant on Wilshire. Dale DeGroff revived that version in The Craft of the Cocktail in 2002 and gave it to Billy Wilkerson's Vendome Club on Sunset around 1930; Robert F. Moss has since argued the record will not carry that: the Vendome opened in May 1933, and the Brown Derby Esquire prints in 1939 is a rum drink. This menu pours two ounces of bourbon, an ounce of grapefruit, and half an ounce of honey syrup, shaken, coupe.

- [Robert F. Moss, The Tale of Two Derbies (Brown Ones)](https://robertfmoss.com/features/The-Tale-of-Two-Derbies-Brown-Ones)
- [Punch, Brown Derby](https://punchdrink.com/recipes/brown-derby/)

### Rye

#### Scofflaw

`1,1,h,h,1,co` · shaken · Rye · Sour family

- 1 oz Rye
- 1 oz Dry vermouth
- 1/2 oz Grenadine
- 1/2 oz Lemon juice
- 1 dash Orange bitters
- Coupe, Orange twist

Equal ounces of rye and dry vermouth, so the wine is half the drink. Half an ounce of grenadine, half of lemon, one dash of orange bitters. Shaken, coupe, orange twist. The rye is spice, the grenadine pomegranate, the lemon a sour cut through the dry vermouth.

Delcevare King, a Massachusetts teetotaler, ran a 1924 contest for a word to shame drinkers who flouted Prohibition; Henry Irving Shaw and Kate L. Butler split the prize for "scofflaw." The Chicago Tribune reported a Scofflaw cocktail at Maxim's in Paris on 21 January 1924: three parts rye, two parts French vermouth, a dash of lemon and of grenadine. Harry MacElhone claimed Jock at Harry's New York Bar invented it days later, with orange bitters and equal Canadian Club and French vermouth. Difford's notes the Tribune piece on Maxim's predates MacElhone's claim. This menu is one to one rye to dry vermouth, half an ounce each of grenadine and lemon, one dash of orange bitters, shaken, coupe, orange.

- [Difford's Guide, Scofflaw](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/1755/scofflaw)

#### Harvest Sour

`1,1,Q,h,ccin` · shaken · Rye · Sour family

- 1 oz Rye
- 1 oz Apple brandy
- 3/4 oz Lemon juice
- 1/2 oz Simple syrup
- one Egg white
- Coupe, Grated cinnamon

Equal ounces of rye and apple brandy. Three-quarters of an ounce of lemon, half an ounce of simple, egg white. The foam is the texture; grated cinnamon on the coupe is the spice. Orchard, pepper, lemon, and a dry foam.

The Harvest Sour is Sam Ross at Attaboy in New York, printed by Punch and dated by Difford's to around 2017: one ounce rye, one ounce applejack, three-quarters lemon, three-quarters simple, egg white, apple slice and cinnamon. Ross's other split-base drinks, the Paper Plane among them, are the parent method. A drink of this name does not appear in the pre-1970 manuals. This menu keeps the equal rye and apple brandy, the lemon, the egg white, and the cinnamon. It pours half an ounce of simple rather than three-quarters, and it skips the apple slice.

- [Punch, Harvest Sour](https://punchdrink.com/recipes/harvest-sour/)
- [Difford's Guide, Harvest Sour](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/23034/harvest-sour)

#### Final Ward

`Q,Q,Q,Q,c` · shaken · Rye · Daisy family

- 3/4 oz Rye
- 3/4 oz Chartreuse
- 3/4 oz Maraschino liqueur
- 3/4 oz Lemon juice
- Coupe

Equal three-quarters of rye, green Chartreuse, maraschino, and lemon. The Last Word on whiskey: herbal, cherry, and lemon against rye pepper. Shaken, coupe.

Phil Ward built the Final Ward at Death & Co in New York in 2007, a Last Word with rye in place of gin and lemon in place of lime. Robert Simonson treats it as a modern classic. Equal parts, shaken, coupe, no garnish. This menu keeps Ward's pour.

- [Punch, Final Ward](https://punchdrink.com/recipes/final-ward/)
- [Difford's Guide, Final Ward](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/2478/final-ward)

#### Blinker

`2,1,h,c` · shaken · Rye · Sour family

- 2 oz Rye
- 1 oz Grapefruit juice
- 1/2 oz Grenadine
- Coupe

Two ounces of rye, an ounce of grapefruit, half an ounce of grenadine. The grapefruit is sour and bitter where lemon would be only sour, and the grenadine's pomegranate sits under it as the sugar. Rye spice on top, a pink colour. Shaken, coupe. Drier than it looks.

Patrick Gavin Duffy prints it in 1934 in The Official Mixer's Manual as a long drink: three parts grapefruit juice to two of rye and one of grenadine. David Embury, in 1948, called it not particularly good but not too bad. Ted Haigh recut it in Vintage Spirits and Forgotten Cocktails in 2004 as a short sour, two of rye to one of grapefruit with a teaspoon of raspberry syrup, and that is the shape the revival kept; PDT printed it in 2011. This menu pours two ounces of rye, an ounce of grapefruit, and half an ounce of grenadine, shaken, coupe.

- [Difford's Guide, Blinker](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/243/blinker)
- [Punch, A Forgotten Rye Whiskey Cocktail Makes a Comeback](https://punchdrink.com/articles/blinker-cocktail-rye-whiskey/)

### Scotch

#### Mickie Walker

`1h,h,h,h,cc` · shaken · Scotch · Sour family

- 1 1/2 oz Scotch
- 1/2 oz Sweet vermouth
- 1/2 oz Grenadine
- 1/2 oz Lemon juice
- Coupe, Cherry

An ounce and a half of scotch, then a half ounce each of sweet vermouth, grenadine, and lemon. The lemon and pomegranate are real pours, not dashes, so the drink is shaken and pink. Coupe, cherry. Scotch, grape, and a sour pomegranate cut.

Harry Craddock prints the Mickie Walker Cocktail in The Savoy Cocktail Book in 1930: one dash grenadine, one dash lemon juice, a quarter Italian vermouth, three-quarters Scotch whisky, shaken. The spelling is Craddock's; the name tracks Edward Patrick "Mickey" Walker, the New Jersey boxer who took the welterweight title in 1922 and the middleweight in 1926. The 1937 UKBG Approved Cocktails repeats Craddock's dashes. This menu keeps the name Mickie Walker and the four ingredients, yet it pours a half ounce each of vermouth, grenadine, and lemon against an ounce and a half of scotch.

- [The Savoy Cocktail Book (1930), p. 104](https://euvs-vintage-cocktail-books.cld.bz/1930-The-Savoy-Cocktail-Book/104/)

### Light Rum

#### Daiquiri

`2,Q,h,c` · shaken · Light Rum · Sour family

- 2 oz Light rum
- 3/4 oz Lime juice
- 1/2 oz Simple syrup
- Coupe

Two ounces of light rum, three-quarters lime, half an ounce of simple. Lime leads; the sugar is only there to keep the rum from going thin. Shaken hard and strained into a coupe, no ice in the glass, no blender. Cane and pith, cold.

Jennings Stockton Cox, an American mining engineer at the Daiquiri iron mines near Santiago de Cuba, mixed Bacardi, lime, and sugar around 1898. Francesco Domenico Pagliuchi wrote in 1948 that he was there and suggested the name; Basil Woon's 1928 When It's Cocktail Time in Cuba records Cox naming it at Santiago's Venus bar. The first recipe-book printing is Jacques Straub's 1914 Drinks, misspelt Daiguiri. Constantino Ribalaigua Vert later numbered several Daiquiris at El Floridita in Havana; the frozen drink is his, not this one. This menu is two ounces of light rum, three-quarters lime, and half an ounce of simple, shaken, coupe.

- [Difford's Guide, Daiquiri history](https://www.diffordsguide.com/g/1083/daiquiri-cocktail/story)
- [Difford's Guide, Daiquiri (Difford's recipe)](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/611/daiquiri-diffords-recipe)

#### Honeysuckle

`2,Q,Q,c` · shaken · Light Rum · Sour family

- 2 oz Light rum
- 3/4 oz Lime juice
- 3/4 oz Honey syrup
- Coupe

Two ounces of light rum, three-quarters lime, three-quarters honey syrup. Equal lime and honey, so the sour sits on beeswax rather than cane. Honey is thicker than simple; the rum tastes rounder than the Daiquiri beside it, and a little floral. Coupe.

David Embury, in The Fine Art of Mixing Drinks (1948), writes that a Bee's Knees with white Cuban rum in place of gin is a Honeysuckle, and with Jamaica rum a Honey Bee. He also notes that the Honeysuckle is sometimes called the Airmail; later writers treat the Airmail as the honey Daiquiri lengthened with Champagne. Esquire's 1949 Handbook for Hosts prints a Honey Bee of honey, Bacardi, and lemon. This menu keeps Embury's rum and honey, uses lime rather than lemon, and pours them equal at three-quarters of an ounce against two ounces of light rum.

- [Difford's Guide, Honeysuckle Daiquiri](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/970/honeysuckle-daiquiri)
- [Difford's Guide, Honey Bee](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/962/honey-bee)

#### Santiago

`2,Q,h,c` · shaken · Light Rum · Sour family

- 2 oz Light rum
- 3/4 oz Lime juice
- 1/2 oz Grenadine
- Coupe

Two ounces of light rum, three-quarters lime, half an ounce of grenadine. Same bones as the Daiquiri, pomegranate in the sugar slot. Pink, tart, a little berry where the other is only cane. Shaken, coupe.

Harry Craddock prints the Santiago Cocktail in the 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book: two dashes of grenadine, two dashes of lemon juice, one glass of Bacardi. Santiago de Cuba is the city nearest the Daiquiri mines, and the name tracks that. Difford's notes that with lime instead of lemon the same idea is a Bacardi Cocktail. This menu is a grenadine Daiquiri, not Craddock's dashes: two ounces of light rum, three-quarters lime, half an ounce of grenadine.

- [Difford's Guide, Santiago Daiquiri](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/1746/santiago-daiquiri)
- [The Savoy Cocktail Book (1930), p. 141](https://euvs-vintage-cocktail-books.cld.bz/1930-The-Savoy-Cocktail-Book/141/)

#### Stan Lee

`1h,Q,Q,h,1,c` · shaken · Light Rum · Sour family

- 1 1/2 oz Light rum
- 3/4 oz Gin
- 3/4 oz Lime juice
- 1/2 oz Grenadine
- 1 dash Angostura bitters
- Coupe

An ounce and a half of light rum and three-quarters gin, so the rum leads and the gin is botanicals underneath. Three-quarters lime, half an ounce of grenadine, one dash of Angostura. Pink, bark through the pomegranate. Shaken, coupe.

A drink called Stan Lee does not appear in the pre-1970 manuals, nor under that name in Difford's, Punch, or Imbibe. The nearest parent is Harry Craddock's Stanley Cocktail in the 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book: equal gin and rum, a sixth each of lemon juice and grenadine. This menu keeps the split base and the grenadine, swaps lime for lemon, leads with an ounce and a half of rum against three-quarters gin, and adds a dash of Angostura.

- [Difford's Guide, Stanley Cocktail](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/1867/stanley-cocktail)

#### Lani-Honi

`1q,1q,Q,R` · shaken · Light Rum · Daisy family

- 1 1/4 oz Light rum
- 1 1/4 oz Bénédictine
- 3/4 oz Lemon juice
- Rocks, iced

Equal ounces and a quarter of light rum and Benedictine, three-quarters lemon. The liqueur is honey and spice, the lemon a sour cut, the rum a cane floor. Rocks glass with ice: it sits and dilutes. Herbal punch, not a coupe sour.

Jeff Berry and Annene Kaye print the Lani-Honi in Beachbum Berry's Grog Log. It was served aboard the Matson Line's SS Mariposa on its 42-day South Seas cruise in 1962: an ounce and a half of Benedictine, an ounce of light Puerto Rican rum, half an ounce of lemon, shaken and strained into a wine goblet of crushed ice. The original is a liqueur drink with rum riding second. This menu equalizes rum and Benedictine at an ounce and a quarter each, raises the lemon to three-quarters, and pours it over ice in a rocks glass.

- [Kindred Cocktails, Lani-Honi](https://kindredcocktails.com/cocktail/lani-honi)
- [Summit Sips, Lani-Honi](https://summitsips.com/2023/12/lani-honi/)

#### The Rum Drink

`2,Q,h,1b,c` · shaken · Light Rum · Sour family

- 2 oz Light rum
- 3/4 oz Lime juice
- 1/2 oz Simple syrup
- 1 barspoon Campari
- Coupe

The Daiquiri's two ounces of light rum and three-quarters lime, with only a half ounce of simple, then a barspoon of Campari. The Campari is a bitter orange film, not a pour. Pink at the rim, dry at the back. Coupe.

John Lermayer mixed The Rum Drink at Sweet Liberty in Miami Beach; Eater printed it in March 2016: two ounces of white rum, three-quarters lime, three-quarters simple, one spoon of Campari, shaken, coupe. Kevin Armstrong's Dry Daiquiri, at London's Match Bar in 2005, is an earlier Campari Daiquiri, with passion fruit syrup in the mix. This menu keeps Lermayer's name, rum, lime, and barspoon of Campari, and cuts the simple to half an ounce.

- [Eater, The Rum Drink (Sweet Liberty)](https://www.eater.com/2016/3/21/11272946/rum-cocktail-campari-sweet-liberty)
- [Punch, How the Dry Daiquiri Became a Modern Classic](https://punchdrink.com/articles/dry-daiquiri-cocktail-trend-london/)

#### King's Jubilee

`1h,h,h,cc` · shaken · Light Rum · Daisy family

- 1 1/2 oz Light rum
- 1/2 oz Maraschino liqueur
- 1/2 oz Lemon juice
- Coupe, Cherry

An ounce and a half of light rum, half an ounce of maraschino, half an ounce of lemon. Cherry stone and almond against the lemon, rum underneath. Coupe, cherry. Maraschino is half the sour; it is not a dash.

Harry Craddock invented the King's Jubilee in 1935 for the Silver Jubilee of King George V, while head bartender at the American Bar in the Savoy. William James Tarling prints it in the 1937 Cafe Royal Cocktail Book, Coronation Edition, as Craddock's: half Daiquiri rum, a quarter Luxardo maraschino (dry), a quarter lemon juice. The United Kingdom Bartenders' Guild Approved Cocktails of the same year carries the same formula. This menu is an ounce and a half of light rum and half an ounce each of maraschino and lemon, coupe, cherry.

- [Difford's Guide, King's Jubilee](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/2880/kings-jubilee)
- [Cafe Royal Cocktail Book (1937), p. 108](https://euvs-vintage-cocktail-books.cld.bz/1937-Cafe-Royal-Cocktail-Book-Coronation-Edition/108/)

#### Twelve Mile Limit

`1,h,h,h,h,c` · shaken · Light Rum · Sour family

- 1 oz Light rum
- 1/2 oz Rye
- 1/2 oz Cognac
- 1/2 oz Grenadine
- 1/2 oz Lemon juice
- Coupe

One ounce of light rum, then half ounces of rye, cognac, grenadine, and lemon. Three spirits, rum first. The grenadine is pomegranate, the lemon the sour, the rye and cognac spice and grape under the cane. Shaken, coupe.

Ted Haigh, in Vintage Spirits and Forgotten Cocktails, credits the Twelve Mile Limit to Tommy Millard, a war correspondent, and the name to the Prohibition coastal limit: three miles, then twelve, the distance you had to sail to drink. Imbibe reprints Haigh's pour. The Three Mile Limit is the rum, brandy, lemon, and grenadine parent; this one adds rye. This menu is one ounce of light rum and half an ounce each of rye, cognac, grenadine, and lemon, shaken, coupe.

- [Imbibe, Twelve Mile Limit Cocktail](https://imbibemagazine.com/recipe/twelve-mile-limit-cocktail/)
- [Saveur, Twelve Mile Limit Cocktail](https://www.saveur.com/article/recipes/classic-12-mile-limit-cocktail/)

#### Elderflower Daiquiri

`2,Q,1,c` · shaken · Light Rum · Daisy family

- 2 oz Light rum
- 3/4 oz Elderflower liqueur
- 1 oz Lime juice
- Coupe

Two ounces of light rum, three-quarters elderflower liqueur, a full ounce of lime. No simple: the liqueur is the sugar. Lime is a third of the drink, so it reads tart, then floral. Coupe.

The parent is the Daiquiri, rum, lime, and sugar, in print from Jacques Straub's 1914 Drinks. An Elderflower Daiquiri cannot predate Robert Cooper's St-Germain, launched in 2007; the Seattle Times, citing Cooper's New York Times obituary, notes the liqueur was ubiquitous in bars by 2008. This menu puts three-quarters of an ounce of elderflower in the sugar slot and a full ounce of lime against two ounces of light rum. No simple.

- [Difford's Guide, Daiquiri history](https://www.diffordsguide.com/g/1083/daiquiri-cocktail/story)
- [The Seattle Times, St-Germain](https://www.seattletimes.com/pacific-nw-magazine/st-germain-liqueur-tastes-old-world-but-is-a-modern-take-on-elderflower/)

#### Hemingway Daiquiri

`2,h,h,Q,c` · shaken · Light Rum · Daisy family

- 2 oz Light rum
- 1/2 oz Maraschino liqueur
- 1/2 oz Grapefruit juice
- 3/4 oz Lime juice
- Coupe

Two ounces of light rum, half an ounce of maraschino, half of grapefruit, three-quarters of lime. The maraschino is all the sugar there is, so it runs dry, with cherry pit sitting under the citrus. Grapefruit puts pith and a slow bitterness on top of the lime's acid. Shaken hard and strained into a coupe.

Constantino Ribalaigua Vert, head bartender at El Floridita in Havana, mixed this for Ernest Hemingway in the early 1930s, after Hemingway tried the house frozen Daiquiri and asked for it without sugar and with double the rum. Hemingway had haemochromatosis, an inherited condition he shared with his father, which is the usual explanation offered for the aversion to sugar. The first version was rum and lime and nothing else. Antonio Meilan, Ribalaigua's successor as head bartender, added the maraschino and the grapefruit later, and the name moved from Daiquiri Like Papa to Papa Doble to Hemingway Special. This menu pours two ounces of light rum, half an ounce of maraschino, half of grapefruit, and three-quarters of lime, shaken, coupe.

- [Difford's Guide, Hemingway Special Daiquiri (Papa Doble)](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/954/hemingway-special-daiquiri-papa-doble)

### Cachaça

#### Caipirinha

`2,3b,1h,R` · shaken · Cachaça · Sour family

- 2 oz Cachaça
- 3 barspoons Sugar
- 1 1/2 oz Lime juice
- Rocks, iced

Two ounces of cachaça, three barspoons of sugar, an ounce and a half of lime, muddled and dumped with the ice. The lime is juice and hull. Grassy cane, pith, and sugar. Rocks with ice. It sits.

The Caipirinha is Brazil's national cocktail: cachaça, lime, and sugar, muddled, ice dumped in. The name is a diminutive of caipira, a person from the countryside. It was a countryside drink before it was a bar drink; the twentieth century brought it to the cities and then to the IBA list. This menu pours two ounces of cachaça, a tablespoon of sugar, and an ounce and a half of lime, shaken and dumped, no strain.

- [Difford's Guide, Caipirinha](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/334/caipirinha)
- [The Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails, The Caipirinha](https://www.spiritsanddistilling.com/dictionary/acref-9780199311132-e-275)

#### Pey-Lé

`1h,1,Q,h,h,c` · shaken · Cachaça · Sour family

- 1 1/2 oz Cachaça
- 1 oz Honey syrup
- 3/4 oz Lemon juice
- 1/2 oz Grapefruit juice
- 1/2 oz Peychaud's bitters
- Coupe

An ounce and a half of cachaça, a full ounce of honey syrup, three-quarters lemon, half an ounce of grapefruit. Half an ounce of Peychaud's is a pour, not a dash, so anise and cherry run through the sour. Shaken, coupe. Cane, honey, and a lot of bitters.

Brett Adams and Jacob Grier print Pey-Lé in Raising the Bar (2022): an ounce and a half of cachaça, an ounce of honey syrup, three-quarters lemon, half an ounce of grapefruit, and half an ounce of Peychaud's, shaken, coupe. The name is the bitters. A drink of this name does not appear in the pre-1970 manuals. This menu keeps that pour, including the half ounce of Peychaud's.

- [Willamette Week, Raising the Bar](https://www.wweek.com/drink/2023/03/29/a-new-book-by-two-local-mixologists-tells-you-how-to-stock-your-bar-cart-one-bottle-at-a-time/)

### Tequila

#### Margarita

`2,Q,Q,cS` · shaken · Tequila · Daisy family

- 2 oz Tequila
- 3/4 oz Orange liqueur
- 3/4 oz Lime juice
- Coupe, Salt rim

Two ounces of tequila against three-quarters each of orange liqueur and lime. The tequila is the drink; the orange and lime are equal and small, peel and acid around agave. Shaken, coupe, salt rim. Short, no ice in the glass.

The origin is a pile of claims. William J. Tarling prints the same three ingredients as the Picador in the 1937 Cafe Royal Cocktail Book in London. Charlie Connolly's 1939 Cotton Club booklet has a Tequila Sour with Cointreau, lime, and a salt rim. Under the name Margarita it surfaces in a 1953 Santa Rosa Press Democrat item from Ensenada. Claimants include Danny Negrete at Tehuacan in 1936, Johnny Durlesser at the Tail o' the Cock in Los Angeles, Pancho Morales in Juarez in 1942, Danny Herrera at Rancho La Gloria, and Margaret Sames in Acapulco in 1948. This menu pours two ounces of tequila, three-quarters orange liqueur, three-quarters lime, shaken, in a coupe with salt.

- [The Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails, The Margarita](https://www.spiritsanddistilling.com/dictionary/acref-9780199311132-e-360)
- [Difford's Guide, History of the Margarita cocktail](https://www.diffordsguide.com/g/1138/margarita-cocktail/origins-and-history)

#### Mexican Firing Squad

`2,Q,Q,2,cc` · shaken · Tequila · Sour family

- 2 oz Tequila
- 3/4 oz Grenadine
- 3/4 oz Lime juice
- 2 dashes Angostura bitters
- Coupe, Cherry

Two ounces of tequila, three-quarters grenadine, three-quarters lime. Equal pomegranate and lime, a pink tequila sour. Two dashes of Angostura pull clove through the fruit. Shaken, coupe, cherry. Short.

Charles H. Baker records the Mexican Firing Squad Special in The Gentleman's Companion, Volume II (1939), as a drink he found at La Cucaracha Bar in Mexico City in 1937: two jiggers tequila, juice of two small limes, one and a half to two teaspoons of grenadine, two dashes of Angostura, in a tall collins packed with cracked ice, garnished with orange, pineapple, and cherry. Period menus from the bar do not list it; it may have been off-menu. This menu keeps the tequila, grenadine, lime, and Angostura, equalizes the grenadine and lime at three-quarters, and pours it short in a coupe with a cherry.

- [Difford's Guide, Mexican Firing Squad Special](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/4945/mexican-firing-squad-special)

#### Vermouth-arita

`1h,1,h,h,Rc` · shaken · Tequila · Daisy family

- 1 1/2 oz Tequila
- 1 oz Sweet vermouth
- 1/2 oz Orange liqueur
- 1/2 oz Lime juice
- Rocks, iced, Cherry

An ounce and a half of tequila against a full ounce of sweet vermouth, so the wine is a second base. Half an ounce of orange liqueur and half of lime are the Margarita's other two, cut down. Shaken, rocks, ice, cherry. A tequila Manhattan that took a lime.

A drink called Vermouth-arita does not appear in the pre-1970 manuals, nor under that name in Difford's, Punch, or Imbibe. The parent is the Margarita: tequila, orange liqueur, and lime, a formula in print by 1937 as William J. Tarling's Picador and under this name by 1953. This menu keeps the tequila and the shake, puts a full ounce of sweet vermouth in the glass, cuts the orange liqueur and lime to half an ounce each, and pours it over ice with a cherry.

- [Difford's Guide, History of the Margarita cocktail](https://www.diffordsguide.com/g/1138/margarita-cocktail/origins-and-history)

#### Stingless Bee

`2,Q,h,h,c3` · shaken · Tequila · Sour family

- 2 oz Tequila
- 3/4 oz Honey syrup
- 1/2 oz Lime juice
- 1/2 oz Lemon juice
- one Egg white
- 3 dashes Peychaud's bitters (on top)
- Coupe, 3 dashes of bitters

Two ounces of tequila, three-quarters honey syrup, half lime, half lemon. The citrus is split, so neither fruit wins; the honey is waxier than sugar. Egg white gives it a foam cap. Three dashes of Peychaud's are dropped on the foam, cherry-anise on the white. Coupe.

The Bee's Knees is a gin sour with honey, first printed in Paris around 1929. Frank Meier's Bar de Ritz recipe appears in Cocktails de Paris that year; a Brooklyn Standard Union article of 22 April 1929 credits Mrs. J.J. Brown of Denver and Paris, later called Molly Brown. Both claims stay in print. A drink called Stingless Bee does not appear in the pre-1970 manuals, nor under that name in Difford's, Punch, or Imbibe. This menu swaps gin for tequila, splits the citrus between lime and lemon, shakes egg white, and drops three dashes of Peychaud's on the foam.

- [Difford's Guide, Bee's Knees](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/2144/bees-knees)

### Mezcal

#### Mezcal Margarita

`2,Q,Q,rS` · shaken · Mezcal · Daisy family

- 2 oz Mezcal
- 3/4 oz Orange liqueur
- 3/4 oz Lime juice
- Rocks, Salt rim

Two ounces of mezcal against three-quarters each of orange liqueur and lime. The mezcal is the drink; the orange and lime are equal and small, peel and acid around smoke. Shaken, rocks, no ice, salt rim. Short, same pour as the Margarita, different bottle.

The Margarita's three ingredients take mezcal as readily as tequila. Difford's and later books print a Mezcal Margarita as the same sour with the agave swapped. This menu keeps the house Margarita's two ounces of spirit and three-quarters each of orange liqueur and lime, and it pours it in a salt-rimmed rocks glass with no ice, as the recipe that landed here specified.

- [The Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails, The Margarita](https://www.spiritsanddistilling.com/dictionary/acref-9780199311132-e-360)
- [Difford's Guide, History of the Margarita cocktail](https://www.diffordsguide.com/g/1138/margarita-cocktail/origins-and-history)

#### Mezcal Sour

`2,Q,h,Rl` · shaken · Mezcal · Sour family

- 2 oz Mezcal
- 3/4 oz Lime juice
- 1/2 oz Honey syrup
- one Egg white
- Rocks, iced, Lemon twist

Two ounces of mezcal, three-quarters of lime, a half ounce of honey syrup, egg white. The foam carries the smoke up first, then the lime arrives, and the honey sits under all of it. Shaken, rocks with ice, lemon twist. The house sour ratio with mezcal in the whiskey's place.

The sour is the older shape: spirit, citrus, and sugar, printed by Jerry Thomas in 1862, with egg white a European habit that reached American bars later. Mezcal came to it late. Artisanal mezcal barely existed in the United States until Ron Cooper founded Del Maguey in 1995 and began importing single-village bottlings, and the sour built on it belongs to the revival that followed rather than to any one bar or year; Difford's dates its own spec to March 2025, and most others are undated house pours. This menu uses the same ratio as the Whiskey Sour and the Gin Sour, with honey syrup for the sugar and a lemon twist over the ice.

- [Difford's Guide, Mezcal Sour](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/33255/mezcal-sour)
- [Difford's Guide, Del Maguey Single Village Mezcal](https://www.diffordsguide.com/producers/1451/del-maguey-single-village-mezcal)

### Vodka

#### Lemon Drop

`2,Q,1,1b,cs` · shaken · Vodka · Daisy family

- 2 oz Vodka
- 3/4 oz Orange liqueur
- 1 oz Lemon juice
- 1 barspoon Simple syrup
- Coupe, Sugar rim

Two ounces of vodka, three-quarters orange liqueur, a full ounce of lemon, one barspoon of simple. The lemon is louder than the orange liqueur; a barspoon of sugar barely covers an ounce of juice. Shaken, coupe, sugar rim. Candy, then pith.

Norman Hobday, who ran Henry Africa's in San Francisco, the fern bar that opened in 1969, built the Lemon Drop in the 1970s as a vodka sour in a sugar-rimmed cocktail glass. Martin Cate, in The Oxford Companion, files it with the Harvey Wallbanger and the wine spritzer. Later bars reduced it to a chilled vodka shot with a sugared lemon wedge. This menu keeps the glass and the sugar rim, with two ounces of vodka, three-quarters orange liqueur, a full ounce of lemon, and a barspoon of simple.

- [The Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails, The Lemon Drop](https://www.spiritsanddistilling.com/dictionary/acref-9780199311132-e-354)

#### Katinka

`1h,Q,h,c` · shaken · Vodka · Daisy family

- 1 1/2 oz Vodka
- 3/4 oz Apricot liqueur
- 1/2 oz Lime juice
- Coupe

An ounce and a half of vodka, three-quarters apricot liqueur, half an ounce of lime. Stone fruit and lime; the apricot sweetens the sour by itself. Shaken, coupe. Short, tart apricot.

David Embury prints a Katinka in The Fine Art of Mixing Drinks (1948): vodka, apricot liqueur, and lime. Haus Alpenz reprints that spec as two ounces of vodka and half an ounce each of apricot and lime. This menu is leaner on the vodka and heavier on the apricot: an ounce and a half, three-quarters, and half a lime, shaken, coupe.

- [Haus Alpenz, Katinka (Embury)](https://alpenz.com/recipe-G2mUOQsZth.html)

#### Queen Bee

`Q,Q,Q,q,1,cl` · shaken · Vodka · Sparkling family

- 3/4 oz Vodka
- 3/4 oz Elderflower liqueur
- 3/4 oz Lemon juice
- 1/4 oz Honey syrup
- 1 oz Champagne
- Coupe, Lemon twist

Three-quarters each of vodka, elderflower, and lemon, a quarter of honey, an ounce of Champagne. The Champagne is the volume. Shaken, then the wine, coupe, lemon twist. Flower, honey, bubbles, a small drink that foams from the fizz.

Charles H. Baker prints a Queen Bee in 1951 The South American Gentleman's Companion on apple brandy, lemon, honey, and curaçao; that is not this drink. A vodka, elderflower, lemon, honey, and Champagne Queen Bee does not appear in the pre-1970 manuals. St-Germain, the elderflower liqueur this recipe calls for, launched in 2007. This menu pours three-quarters each of vodka, elderflower, and lemon, a quarter of honey syrup, and an ounce of Champagne, coupe, lemon twist.

- [Punch, Bring Back the Queen Bee](https://punchdrink.com/articles/bring-back-charles-baker-queen-bee-cocktail-recipe/)
- [VinePair, 8 Things You Should Know About St-Germain Elderflower Liqueur](https://vinepair.com/articles/ntk-st-germain/)

#### Kamikaze

`1,1,1,cL` · shaken · Vodka · Daisy family

- 1 oz Vodka
- 1 oz Orange liqueur
- 1 oz Lime juice
- Coupe, Lime twist

An ounce each of vodka, orange liqueur, and lime. A third of the glass is lime juice, so it lands sour first and orange second, and the vodka is there to carry both. Three ounces in a coupe rather than the shot glass it usually arrives in, which gives it room to read as a drink. Lime twist.

Two accounts, a decade apart. Peter Miller, writing in Ski in October 1979, put the drink out of Florida in the early to mid 1970s and moving from there to New York, and printed the earliest known recipe: an ounce and a half of pre-chilled vodka, a dash of lime, and one drop of Cointreau, served with no ice because everything in it was already frozen.
