John Mariani, in Motorboating and Sailing for January 1989, credited Tony Lauriano at Les Pyrenees in New York in 1972, who called it the Jesus Christ Superstar until customers found the name strange. Montebello Brands was bottling an Original Kamikaze Cocktail by 1975. This menu pours an ounce each of vodka, orange liqueur, and lime, shaken, coupe, lime twist.

- [Vintage American Cocktails, Kamikaze](https://vintageamericancocktails.com/kamikaze/)

#### Vodka Gimlet

`2,Q,h,c` · shaken · Vodka · Sour family

- 2 oz Vodka
- 3/4 oz Lime juice
- 1/2 oz Simple syrup
- Coupe

Two ounces of vodka to three-quarters of lime and a half ounce of simple, the Gimlet's pour exactly. The lime is the flavor and the vodka is the cold and the length behind it. Shaken, coupe. Tart, thinly sweetened, short.

The Gimlet was gin and Rose's lime cordial, a navy drink that Harry MacElhone printed under the name in 1922 and that Raymond Chandler set loose in fiction, half gin and half Rose's, in The Long Goodbye in 1953. Vodka took the gin's slot as vodka took the American well; Difford's dates the substitution to the 1990s and the early 2000s and notes that gin has since taken the drink back. This menu pours the Gimlet's spec with the bottle changed: two ounces of vodka, three-quarters of fresh lime, a half ounce of simple, coupe.

- [Difford's Guide, Gimlet cocktail](https://www.diffordsguide.com/encyclopedia/445/cocktails/gimlet-cocktail)
- [The Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails, A Gimlet](https://www.spiritsanddistilling.com/dictionary/acref-9780199311132-e-324)

### Gin

#### Gimlet

`2,Q,h,c` · shaken · Gin · Sour family

- 2 oz Gin
- 3/4 oz Lime juice
- 1/2 oz Simple syrup
- Coupe

Two ounces of gin against three-quarters of lime, so the lime is loud, then a half ounce of simple. Shaken, coupe. The lime is fresh and tart; the syrup is a thin coat of sugar, enough to take the edge. Juniper under citrus.

Lauchlan Rose of Edinburgh patented an alcohol-free lime cordial in 1867, the same year the Merchant Shipping Act required British ships to carry lime juice against scurvy. Officers mixing gin with Rose's is the navy story; a gimlet is also a barrel tap. The first named print is Harry MacElhone's 1922 Harry's ABC of Mixing Cocktails: equal parts Plymouth gin and Rose's, "a very popular beverage in the Navy." Rear-Admiral Sir Thomas Desmond Gimlette is sometimes credited; his Times obituary does not mention the drink. This menu pours two ounces of gin, three-quarters of fresh lime, and a half ounce of simple, coupe.

- [The Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails, A Gimlet](https://www.spiritsanddistilling.com/dictionary/acref-9780199311132-e-324)
- [Difford's Guide, Gimlet (Difford's recipe)](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/831/gimlet-diffords-recipe)

#### French 75

`1h,1,h,3,Rl` · shaken · Gin · Sparkling family

- 1 1/2 oz Gin
- 1 oz Lemon juice
- 1/2 oz Simple syrup
- 3 oz Champagne
- Rocks, iced, Lemon twist

An ounce and a half of gin against a full ounce of lemon, so the citrus is a real pour, then a half ounce of simple and three ounces of Champagne. Shaken, then the wine. Rocks with ice and a lemon twist, not a flute. The lemon stays loud over the bubbles; the cube melts into it.

The name is the French 75-millimetre field gun of the First World War. The first drink so called, reported by O. O. McIntyre in the Washington Herald in 1915, is gin, applejack, grenadine, and lemon; Robert Vermeire, in 1922, credits Henry Tépé of Henry's Bar in Paris. The gin, lemon, sugar, and Champagne formula first prints in Judge Jr's 1927 Here's How, in a tall glass: if you use club soda, you have a Tom Collins. Harry Craddock repeats it in the 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book, poured over cracked ice. The flute is later. This menu keeps the gin and the ice, yet it pours a full ounce of lemon and three of Champagne into a rocks glass with a lemon twist.

- [The Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails, The French 75](https://www.spiritsanddistilling.com/dictionary/acref-9780199311132-e-317)
- [Difford's Guide, French 75 cocktail history](https://www.diffordsguide.com/encyclopedia/1267/cocktails/french-75-cocktail-history)

#### Bennett

`1h,Q,h,2,c` · shaken · Gin · Sour family

- 1 1/2 oz Gin
- 3/4 oz Lime juice
- 1/2 oz Simple syrup
- 2 dashes Angostura bitters
- Coupe

An ounce and a half of gin against three-quarters of lime, a half ounce of simple, two dashes of Angostura. The bitters are bark and clove under the lime. Shaken, coupe. Lime, juniper, and a bitter finish. A Gimlet with spice, not honey.

Robert Vermeire prints the Bennett in 1922 Cocktails: How to Mix Them: two-sixths of a gill of Old Tom, one-sixth fresh lime, two dashes of Angostura, no sugar. "This cocktail, which is very popular in Chili, is called after the well-known and popular landowner and millionaire of that country." Nakata Seizo repeats it in Japan in 1926; Jimmy of Ciro's London does the same in 1930. The Chilean namesake is not further identified. This menu adds a half ounce of simple, pours an ounce and a half of gin and three-quarters of lime, two dashes of Angostura, coupe.

- [Difford's Guide, Bennett Cocktail](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/3655/bennett-cocktail)

#### Gin Sour

`2,Q,h,Rl` · shaken · Gin · Sour family

- 2 oz Gin
- 3/4 oz Lemon juice
- 1/2 oz Simple syrup
- one Egg white
- Rocks, iced, Lemon twist

Two ounces of gin, three-quarters of lemon, a half ounce of simple, and egg white. The white is foam and a silk coat; the lemon is tart underneath. Shaken, rocks with ice, lemon twist. It sits: gin, citrus, and a head that lasts while the cube melts.

Jerry Thomas prints the Gin Sour in 1862 How to Mix Drinks as the Gin Fix without the fruit: sugar, water, lemon, gin, in a small bar glass. A sour is a punch for one. The first record of the name is an 1856 list at Mart Ackermann's Saloon in Toronto. Egg white is later; Eddie Clark's 1947 King Cocktail and the 1955 UKBG guide treat it as optional, not original. This menu pours two ounces of gin, three-quarters of lemon, a half ounce of simple, and egg white, over ice with a lemon twist.

- [Difford's Guide, History of sour cocktails](https://www.diffordsguide.com/g/1133/sour-cocktails/history)
- [Jerry Thomas, Bar-Tender's Guide (1862), p. 59](https://euvs-vintage-cocktail-books.cld.bz/1862-Bar-Tender-s-Guide-price-1-50-by-Jerry-Thomas/59/)

#### Bee's Knees

`2,Q,Q,c` · shaken · Gin · Sour family

- 2 oz Gin
- 3/4 oz Lemon juice
- 3/4 oz Honey syrup
- Coupe

Two ounces of gin, three-quarters of lemon, three-quarters of honey syrup, so the honey is a full partner to the citrus. Shaken, coupe. The honey is floral and thick where simple would be thin; the lemon keeps it tart. Gin, pith, and a coat of honey.

The Bee's Knees first prints in 1929, twice. Cocktails de Paris credits Frank Meier, head bartender at the Hotel Ritz in Paris from 1921; Meier reprints it in his 1936 The Artistry of Mixing Drinks. A Brooklyn Standard Union piece of 23 April 1929, cited by Jared Brown and Anistatia Miller, ascribes the drink to Mrs. J.J. Brown of Denver and Paris, Margaret Brown of the Titanic. David Embury, in 1948, calls the equal-parts gin, lemon, and honey a pernicious Prohibition recipe meant to cover vile gin, and dries it out. Both claims stay in print. This menu pours two ounces of gin and three-quarters each of lemon and honey syrup, coupe.

- [The Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails, Bee's Knees](https://www.spiritsanddistilling.com/dictionary/acref-9780199311132-e-248)
- [Epicurious, Bee's Knees](https://www.epicurious.com/recipes/food/views/bees-knees)

#### Pegu Club

`1Q,Q,h,1,1,c` · shaken · Gin · Daisy family

- 1 3/4 oz Gin
- 3/4 oz Orange liqueur
- 1/2 oz Lime juice
- 1 dash Angostura bitters
- 1 dash Orange bitters
- Coupe

One and three-quarters ounces of gin against three-quarters of orange liqueur and only a half ounce of lime, so the lime is a squeeze under the peel. One dash of Angostura and one of orange bitters sit on the orange, bark and pith over a small lime. Shaken, coupe. Gin, candied orange, and a thin lime line.

The Pegu Club was the house cocktail of the British officers' club of the same name, just outside Rangoon, Burma, now Yangon. Who mixed the first one is unknown. Harry MacElhone prints it in the 1920s: gin, orange curacao, lime, and a dash each of Angostura and orange bitters. Harry Craddock reprints it in the 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book as a drink that has travelled, and is asked for, round the world. Craddock's lime is a teaspoon of Rose's; Jimmy, late of Ciro's, equalizes the curacao and the lime that same year. This menu pours one and three-quarters gin, three-quarters orange liqueur, half an ounce of lime, and one dash of each bitters.

- [The Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails, The Pegu Club Cocktail](https://www.spiritsanddistilling.com/dictionary/acref-9780199311132-e-380)
- [Difford's Guide, Pegu Club Cocktail](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/2728/pegu-club-cocktail-diffords-recipe)
- [The Savoy Cocktail Book (1930), Pegu Club Cocktail](https://savoycocktaildatabase.com/cocktails/pegu-club-cocktail)

#### White Lady

`1h,Q,Q,1b,c` · shaken · Gin · Daisy family

- 1 1/2 oz Gin
- 3/4 oz Orange liqueur
- 3/4 oz Lemon juice
- 1 barspoon Simple syrup
- one Egg white
- Coupe

An ounce and a half of gin, three-quarters each of orange liqueur and lemon, a barspoon of simple, and egg white. The white is foam and a silk coat over lemon pith and candied peel. The barspoon of simple is a thin sweetness against equal orange and lemon. Shaken, coupe.

Two drinks share the name. Harry MacElhone prints a White Lady in 1922 in Harry's ABC of Mixing Cocktails as brandy, creme de menthe, and Cointreau. The gin, lemon, and Cointreau version prints in Harry Craddock's 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book at half gin and a quarter each of Cointreau and lemon, with no egg. MacElhone later claimed a 1929 gin revision at Harry's New York Bar in Paris; Victor Cabrin at London's Grosvenor House also claimed 1929. Egg white is later, New York in the late 1930s. This menu is gin, orange liqueur, lemon, a barspoon of simple, and egg white.

- [The Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails, White Lady](https://www.spiritsanddistilling.com/dictionary/acref-9780199311132-e-446)
- [Difford's Guide, White Lady](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/2091/white-lady-cocktail)
- [The Savoy Cocktail Book (1930), White Lady Cocktail](https://savoycocktaildatabase.com/cocktails/white-lady-cocktail)

#### Fine and Dandy

`1h,Q,Q,1b,2,c` · shaken · Gin · Daisy family

- 1 1/2 oz Gin
- 3/4 oz Orange liqueur
- 3/4 oz Lemon juice
- 1 barspoon Simple syrup
- 2 dashes Angostura bitters
- Coupe

An ounce and a half of gin, three-quarters orange liqueur, three-quarters lemon, a barspoon of simple. Two dashes of Angostura pull bark and clove through the orange. Shaken, coupe. Peel, pith, and a little clove on the gin.

The Fine and Dandy prints in Harry Craddock's 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book: a quarter lemon, a quarter Cointreau, half Plymouth gin, and one dash of Angostura, shaken. It is a White Lady with bitters and without egg, under another name. Craddock does not claim it. This menu keeps the two-to-one gin against equal orange liqueur and lemon, adds a barspoon of simple, and doubles the bitters to two dashes.

- [Difford's Guide, Fine and Dandy](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/746/fine-and-dandy)
- [The Savoy Cocktail Book (1930), Fine and Dandy Cocktail](https://savoycocktaildatabase.com/cocktails/fine-and-dandy)

#### Jasmine

`1h,Q,q,q,cl` · shaken · Gin · Daisy family

- 1 1/2 oz Gin
- 3/4 oz Lemon juice
- 1/4 oz Campari
- 1/4 oz Orange liqueur
- Coupe, Lemon twist

An ounce and a half of gin against three-quarters of lemon; a quarter each of Campari and orange liqueur. The Campari is bitter orange in a sour, so the drink reads pink and like grapefruit. Shaken, coupe, lemon twist. Gin, pith, and a thin bitter film.

Paul Harrington mixed the first Jasmine in 1993 at Townhouse Bar and Grill in Emeryville, California, for Matt Jasmin, a classmate who asked for something Harrington had never made. Harrington riffed on a Pegu Club he knew from Trader Vic's: Campari in place of the two bitters, lemon in place of lime, and a lemon twist. He misspelled Jasmin's name and the drink kept the extra e. It prints in Cocktail: The Drinks Bible for the 21st Century, which Harrington wrote with Laura Moorhead in 1998. This menu is Harrington's pour: an ounce and a half of gin, three-quarters lemon, a quarter each of Campari and orange liqueur, coupe, lemon twist.

- [The Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails, The Jasmine](https://www.spiritsanddistilling.com/dictionary/acref-9780199311132-e-347)
- [VinePair, The Jasmine](https://vinepair.com/cocktail-recipe/the-jasmine/)

#### Rendezvous

`1h,h,h,c` · shaken · Gin · Daisy family

- 1 1/2 oz Gin
- 1/2 oz Maraschino liqueur
- 1/2 oz Lime juice
- Coupe

An ounce and a half of gin, half an ounce of maraschino, half an ounce of lime. The cherry liqueur is almond and pit as much as fruit, and it does all the sweetening. Equal maraschino and lime, so neither wins. Shaken, coupe. Gin, cherry stone, and a tart lime line.

Diane Lapis and Anne Peck-Davis print a Rendezvous Cocktail in Cocktails Across America (2018), dated 1938 and tied to the Muehlebach Hotel in Kansas City: one ounce of gin, half an ounce of maraschino, half an ounce of lime. The hotel opened in 1915. A different modern drink of the same name is gin, Campari, and kirsch; that is not this pour. This menu scales the 1938 hotel drink to an ounce and a half of gin against half an ounce each of maraschino and lime, shaken, coupe.

- [Diane Lapis and Anne Peck-Davis, Cocktails Across America (2018)](https://archive.org/details/cocktailsacrossa0000lapi)

#### Pendennis Club

`2,1,Q,2,cLw` · shaken · Gin · Daisy family

- 2 oz Gin
- 1 oz Apricot liqueur
- 3/4 oz Lime juice
- 2 dashes Peychaud's bitters
- Coupe, Lime wheel

Two ounces of gin against a full ounce of apricot liqueur, so the stone fruit is a third of the drink. Three-quarters lime is tart against the apricot; two dashes of Peychaud's pull cherry and anise through it. Shaken, coupe, lemon twist and a wheel. Pink, lime, and apricot.

The Pendennis Club in Louisville, founded in 1881, gives the drink its name. Two recipes print under it. William T. Boothby's 1908 World's Drinks lists gin, apricot brandy, and French vermouth, no lime. Charles H. Baker's 1939 Gentleman's Companion calls it The Pendennis Club's Famous Special: gin, dry apricot brandy, lime or lemon, two dashes of Peychaud's, strained over a split kumquat. The club later lost the running story of who mixed it. This menu is Baker's sour: two ounces of gin, one of apricot, three-quarters lime, two dashes of Peychaud's, shaken, with a lemon twist and a wheel and no kumquat.

- [Difford's Guide, Pendennis Club Special](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/1504/pendennis-club-special)
- [Toby Cecchini, The Secret Signature Cocktail of Louisville, Saveur](https://www.saveur.com/puzzling-pendennis-club-cocktail/)

#### Hat Tip

`1h,Q,q,h,1b,c` · shaken · Gin · Daisy family

- 1 1/2 oz Gin
- 3/4 oz Elderflower liqueur
- 1/4 oz Campari
- 1/2 oz Lemon juice
- 1 barspoon Simple syrup
- Coupe

An ounce and a half of gin, three-quarters elderflower, a quarter of Campari, half an ounce of lemon, a barspoon of simple. The elderflower is the sweet; Campari is a bitter pink film. Shaken, coupe. Floral gin, lemon pith, and a thin bitter edge.

No first printing or named bartender turned up for the Hat Tip. Elderflower liqueur in this form dates to St-Germain, launched in 2007, so the combination is recent. This menu shakes an ounce and a half of gin with three-quarters elderflower, a quarter of Campari, half an ounce of lemon, and a barspoon of simple, in a coupe.

#### Olivette

`1,1,h,cO` · shaken · Gin · Martini family

- 1 oz Gin
- 1 oz Dry vermouth
- 1/2 oz Elderflower liqueur
- Coupe, Olive

Equal ounces of gin and dry vermouth, a fifty-fifty Martini, with a half ounce of elderflower as the sweet. No juice, no bitters. Shaken, so it clouds a little. Coupe, olive. Floral gin, dry wine, and a brine finish.

Harry Craddock's 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book prints an Olivette Cocktail of Plymouth gin, absinthe, orange bitters, and syrup, with an olive; that is not this drink. This menu's Olivette is gin, dry vermouth, and elderflower, the formula St-Germain publishes as a house cocktail: equal gin and Noilly Prat, half an ounce of the liqueur, green olive. St-Germain itself dates to 2007. Dante in New York bottles a related Olivette Martini with both vodka and gin. This menu shakes the St-Germain pour and keeps the olive.

- [St-Germain, Olivette](https://www.stgermainliqueur.com/us/en/cocktails/olivette/)
- [The Savoy Cocktail Book (1930), Olivette Cocktail](https://savoycocktaildatabase.com/cocktails/olivette-cocktail)

#### Southside

`2,Q,Q,cm` · shaken · Gin · Sour family

- 2 oz Gin
- 3/4 oz Lime juice
- 3/4 oz Simple syrup
- one Mint
- Coupe, Mint

Two ounces of gin, three-quarters of lime, three-quarters of simple, mint shaken in with them. Lime and sugar are matched at three-quarters each, so it runs sweeter than a Gimlet, and the mint oil sits over the juniper rather than under it. Double strained into a coupe with no soda, mint on top.

The drink comes off the Mint Julep at Snedecor's Tavern on Long Island in the 1890s, a place that later became the South Side Sportsmen's Club, where wealthy Manhattanites went to hunt and fish. Hugo Ensslin printed a South Side Fizz in the 1917 second edition of Recipes for Mixed Drinks, the whole instruction being that it is made the same as a Gin Fizz, adding fresh mint leaves. New York's Twenty-One Club claimed it as a Prohibition house drink and poured it until the room closed in 2020. The other story, that it belongs to Chicago's South Side and its bootleggers, is bar lore. This menu leaves the soda out: two ounces of gin, three-quarters of lime, three-quarters of simple, and mint, shaken, coupe.

- [Difford's Guide, South Side Fizz](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/2584/south-side-fizz)
- [Punch, Southside](https://punchdrink.com/recipes/southside/)

#### Alexander

`1,1,1,c` · shaken · Gin · Fancy family

- 1 oz Gin
- 1 oz Crème de cacao
- 1 oz Cream
- Coupe

Equal ounces of gin, crème de cacao, and cream. The gin is the drink the Brandy Alexander forgot. Shaken, coupe. Juniper, cocoa, and cream.

Hugo R. Ensslin prints the Alexander in Recipes for Mixed Drinks (1916): equal gin, crème de cacao, and sweet cream. The brandy version crowded it out. This menu is Ensslin's original, one ounce each, shaken, coupe.

- [Difford's Guide, Alexander](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/48/alexander)

#### Campari Alexander

`1,1,1,c` · shaken · Gin · Fancy family

- 1 oz Campari
- 1 oz Crème de cacao
- 1 oz Cream
- Coupe

Equal ounces of Campari, crème de cacao, and cream. No base spirit. Bitter orange and chocolate under cream. Shaken, coupe. Pink, cocoa, and a bitter finish.

Brett Adams and Jacob Grier print the Campari Alexander in Raising the Bar (2022): equal Campari, crème de cacao, and cream, shaken, coupe. It is Ensslin's Alexander with Campari in the gin slot. A drink of this name does not appear in the pre-1970 manuals. This menu keeps the equal ounces.

- [Willamette Week, Raising the Bar](https://www.wweek.com/drink/2023/03/29/a-new-book-by-two-local-mixologists-tells-you-how-to-stock-your-bar-cart-one-bottle-at-a-time/)

#### Last Word

`Q,Q,Q,Q,cc` · shaken · Gin · Daisy family

- 3/4 oz Gin
- 3/4 oz Chartreuse
- 3/4 oz Maraschino liqueur
- 3/4 oz Lime juice
- Coupe, Cherry

Equal three-quarters of gin, green Chartreuse, maraschino, and lime. Each is a quarter of the drink. Herbal, cherry, and lime around the gin. Shaken, coupe, cherry.

The Last Word is credited to the Detroit Athletic Club around 1915, and to Frank Fogarty, a vaudeville comedian, who took it to New York. Ted Saucier prints it in Bottoms Up (1951). It nearly vanished, then Murray Stenson put it on the list at Seattle's Zig Zag Café in 2003, and the equal-parts formula spread. This menu keeps three-quarters each of gin, Chartreuse, maraschino, and lime, coupe, cherry.

- [Punch, Last Word](https://punchdrink.com/recipes/last-word/)
- [Difford's Guide, Last Word](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/1158/last-word)

#### Barbary Coast

`Q,Q,Q,Q,c` · shaken · Gin · Fancy family

- 3/4 oz Gin
- 3/4 oz Scotch
- 3/4 oz Crème de cacao
- 3/4 oz Cream
- Coupe

Three-quarters each of gin, Scotch, white crème de cacao, and cream, so the two spirits are half the glass and the cream is a quarter of it. Shaken, coupe. Chocolate and smoke over a thin cream body, with juniper coming up behind the whisky.

The Barbary Coast is a Prohibition-era drink with no known author. Harry Craddock prints it in The Savoy Cocktail Book in 1930 as equal parts gin, Scotch, crème de cacao, and cream, and Crosby Gaige runs the same drink in his 1945 Cocktail Guide and Ladies' Companion under the name Death and Mr. Morgenthau. The name is San Francisco's: the nine blocks around Pacific Street that worked as a red-light district for sailors from the 1850s until the city shut it down. This menu pours three-quarters of each, shaken, coupe.

- [Difford's Guide, Barbary Coast](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/170/barbary-coast)
- [cocktail virgin, Barbary Coast](https://cocktailvirgin.blogspot.com/2021/01/barbary-coast.html)

#### Gin Fizz

`2,1,h,t,h` · shaken · Gin · Highball family

- 2 oz Gin
- 1 oz Lemon juice
- 1/2 oz Simple syrup
- top with Soda water
- Highball

The Collins pour, shaken hard first and served tall with no ice in the glass: two ounces of gin, an ounce of lemon, half an ounce of simple, then soda. The shake beats air into the lemon, so there is a foam head over a short cold body. Drink it while the fizz is still on it.

Jerry Thomas prints the Gin Fizz in the 1876 edition of his Bar-tenders Guide, as the Whiskey Fizz with gin in the whiskey's place: shake the spirit, lemon, and sugar with ice, strain, and top with seltzer. The Fizz is the Sour served long and strained off its ice; the Collins is built in the glass. Henry Charles Ramos built the famous variant at the Imperial Cabinet Saloon in New Orleans in 1888, with cream, egg white, and orange flower water, and held the formula until Prohibition closed him in 1919. This menu pours two ounces of gin, an ounce of lemon, and half an ounce of simple, shaken, then soda in a tall glass with no ice.

- [Difford's Guide, Gin Fizz](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/840/gin-fizz)
- [Difford's Guide, History of gin cocktails](https://www.diffordsguide.com/encyclopedia/1068/cocktails/history-of-gin-cocktails)

### Vermouth

#### Queen Elizabeth

`1h,Q,Q,c` · shaken · Vermouth · Daisy family

- 1 1/2 oz Dry vermouth
- 3/4 oz Bénédictine
- 3/4 oz Lime juice
- Coupe

An ounce and a half of dry vermouth, three-quarters of Bénédictine, three-quarters of lime. No base spirit. The liqueur is honey and herbs; the lime matches it, so the drink is tart as well as sweet. Shaken, coupe. Vermouth and Bénédictine, then pith.

Queen Elizabeth is a crowded name. The version here is the vermouth one: dry vermouth, Bénédictine, and lime, with no gin and no brandy. David Wondrich found the formula in a Bénédictine advertisement in the February 1935 Esquire, billed as the prize-winning recipe in a nationwide cocktail contest. Difford's Guide credits Herbert L. Quick, head bartender at the Benjamin Franklin Hotel in Philadelphia in 1934, who named it for his wife, not the monarch. Other Queen Elizabeths in the manuals are gin drinks, or brandy and sweet vermouth. This menu pours an ounce and a half of dry vermouth and three-quarters each of Bénédictine and lime.

- [Esquire, Queen Elizabeth (David Wondrich)](https://www.esquire.com/food-drink/drinks/recipes/a3687/queen-elizabeth-drink-recipe/)
- [Difford's Guide, Queen Elizabeth Wine](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/14241/queen-elizabeth-wine)

#### Dry Vermouth Sour

`2,Q,h,c` · shaken · Vermouth · Sour family

- 2 oz Dry vermouth
- 3/4 oz Lemon juice
- 1/2 oz Simple syrup
- one Egg white
- Coupe

Two ounces of dry vermouth, three-quarters lemon, half an ounce of simple, egg white. The foam is the texture; the vermouth is the spirit, so the sour is grape and lemon under a dry foam. Shaken, coupe. A short sour with a dry cap.

A drink called Dry Vermouth Sour does not appear under that name in the pre-1970 manuals, nor in Difford's, Punch, or Imbibe. The parent is the sour itself: spirit, citrus, and sugar, printed by Jerry Thomas in 1862, with egg white common in American sours by the 1940s. Vermouth as a base is older still; J. Haney's 1869 Steward and Barkeeper's Manual already has a Vermuth Cocktail, and Harry Johnson's 1882 manual dresses vermouth with gum, bitters, and maraschino. This menu puts two ounces of dry vermouth through the sour template: three-quarters lemon, half an ounce of simple, egg white, coupe.

- [The Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails, The sour](https://www.spiritsanddistilling.com/dictionary/acref-9780199311132-e-422)
- [Difford's Guide, Vermouth Cocktail](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/5639/vermouth-cocktail)

#### Sherry Cobbler

`3,2b,Hom` · shaken · Vermouth · Vermouth family

- 3 oz Sherry
- 2 barspoons Sugar
- Highball, iced, Orange twist, Mint

Three ounces of amontillado and two barspoons of sugar, shaken until the sugar is gone, then poured over a highball packed with ice. Nutty, dry sherry with just enough sugar to taste like fruit, and very cold. The orange goes in over the top and the mint sits under your nose. Low proof and made for a hot afternoon.

David Wondrich found the earliest Cobbler in the 1838 diary of Katherine Jane Ellice, who met it travelling in the United States. Dickens has Martin Chuzzlewit drink one through a straw in 1844, and it was the drink that carried the American bar abroad through the second half of the century. Jerry Thomas prints it in 1862: two wine glasses of sherry, a tablespoonful of sugar, two or three slices of orange, shaken, served on shaved ice with berries on top. This menu pours three ounces of sherry and two barspoons of sugar, shaken, over ice in a highball, orange and mint.

- [Difford's Guide, Sherry Cobbler](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/2895/sherry-cobbler)
- [Difford's Guide, Cobblers](https://www.diffordsguide.com/encyclopedia/1227/cocktails/cobblers)

## Built

Made in the glass it is served in. Ice, spirit, then the mixer on top; one lift with a barspoon.

### Aged Rum

#### Dark and Stormy

`2,h,t,HLw` · built · Aged Rum · Highball family

- 2 oz Aged rum
- 1/2 oz Lime juice
- top with Ginger beer
- Highball, iced, Lime wheel

Two ounces of aged rum, half an ounce of lime, and ginger beer over ice. Molasses against ginger heat, with lime cutting across both. Rounder and darker than the same build in vodka, and a lime wheel on the rim.

Bermuda's national drink, and nobody knows who first poured it. The story is British sailors on shore leave after the First World War. Gosling Brothers, a Bermuda merchant house since James Gosling landed at St George's in 1806 and renamed when Ambrose joined, sells both the Black Seal rum and a ginger beer, and was among the first to trademark a cocktail, in the late 1970s. That registration is why the trademarked spelling names Gosling's rum specifically, and why a generic pour goes under a plainer name. This menu pours two ounces of aged rum, half an ounce of lime, and ginger beer over ice, with a lime wheel.

- [Difford's Guide, Dark N Stormy (Difford's recipe)](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/619/dark-n-stormy-diffords-recipe)
- [Difford's Guide, Trademarking cocktails](https://www.diffordsguide.com/encyclopedia/1150/cocktails/trademarking-cocktails)

### Cognac

#### Champagne Cocktail

`b,3,h,t,hl` · built · Cognac · Sparkling family

- 1 barspoon Sugar
- 3 dashes Angostura bitters
- 1/2 oz Cognac
- top with Champagne
- Highball, Lemon twist

A barspoon of sugar soaked with three dashes of Angostura, half an ounce of cognac, then Champagne poured on top. The sugar is there for the bead as much as the sweetness; it dissolves slowly and keeps a stream of bubbles rising off it. Bitters give it clove and bark, the cognac gives it weight, and the wine stays dry under a lemon twist.

Robert Tomes describes one in Panama in 1855, made with Mumm, bitters, sugar, and ice. Jerry Thomas prints it in the first cocktail book in 1862 with no brandy in it at all. The cognac arrives later. Difford's traces it to W. J. Tarling's 1937 Cafe Royal Cocktail Book, which allows a dash of brandy as required. David Wondrich makes the point that the sugar cube earns its place on the bubbles it keeps sending up. This menu pours a barspoon of sugar, three dashes of Angostura, half an ounce of cognac, and Champagne, with a lemon twist.

- [Difford's Guide, Champagne Cocktail](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/393/champagne-cocktail)

### Bourbon

#### Whiskey Highball

`2,t,Hl` · built · Bourbon · Highball family

- 2 oz Bourbon
- top with Soda water
- Highball, iced, Lemon twist

Two ounces of bourbon and soda over ice, with a lemon twist. Water and gas open the whiskey out, so corn and barrel come forward and the vanilla rides up on the bubbles. The twist puts oil on the surface, so the first sip is citrus over sweet grain.

The word turns up in the 1890s. A character asks for a high ball of whiskey in Ha Du Souchet's 1894 play My Friend From India, and Chris Lawlor's 1895 The Mixicologist prints High Ball as ice, seltzer, and brandy or whiskey; Harry Johnson's 1900 Bartenders Manual settles it as one word. Gary Regan offered a different etymology in The Joy of Mixology (2003): a highball was a railroad signal, the ball on a float in a steam engine's water tank showing there was water enough to go. This menu pours two ounces of bourbon over ice, tops with soda, and twists lemon over it.

- [Difford's Guide, Highball history](https://www.diffordsguide.com/g/1086/highballs/story)
- [Difford's Guide, Highball (generic name)](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/2179/highball-generic-name)

#### Mint Julep

`2,q,Rm` · built · Bourbon · Old-Fashioned family

- 2 oz Bourbon
- 1/4 oz Simple syrup
- one Mint
- Rocks, iced, Mint

Two ounces of bourbon and a quarter ounce of simple over ice, with mint muddled into the glass. A quarter of syrup against a full pour of whiskey is a light hand, so the drink is bourbon and mint oil, cold. It frosts the glass while it sits and it keeps diluting as it goes.

The word comes through the Arabic julab, rosewater, and the drink through Persia and Europe, where mint took the place of rose petals. John Davis, in Travels in the United States (1803), defines a julep as a dram of spirituous liquor that has mint steeped in it, taken by Virginians of a morning. Captain Frederick Marryat carried it back to Britain in 1839 and called it one of the most delightful and insinuating potations that ever was invented. Brandy and rum gave way to whiskey by 1900, and Churchill Downs made it the official drink of the Kentucky Derby in 1938. This menu pours two ounces of bourbon, a quarter ounce of simple, and muddled mint over ice in a rocks glass rather than a silver cup.

- [Difford's Guide, Mint Julep](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/1330/mint-julep)
- [Difford's Guide, Julep cocktails](https://www.diffordsguide.com/encyclopedia/1562/cocktails/julep-cocktails)

#### Kentucky Mule

`2,h,t,HLw` · built · Bourbon · Highball family

- 2 oz Bourbon
- 1/2 oz Lime juice
- top with Ginger beer
- Highball, iced, Lime wheel

Two ounces of bourbon, half an ounce of lime, and ginger beer over ice. Ginger sits on the corn sweetness and the whiskey still reads through the heat. Lime keeps it from going syrupy.

The Mule became a template the moment the Moscow Mule sold vodka: spirit, lime, ginger beer, ice. The bourbon version is the Kentucky Mule, which Difford's also files as the Bourbon Mule. It is the older Buck pattern, spirit with citrus and ginger, under a newer name, and no bartender or date is attached to it. This menu pours two ounces of bourbon, half an ounce of lime, and ginger beer over ice, with a lime wheel.

- [Difford's Guide, Bourbon Mule](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/13404/bourbon-mule)

#### Seelbach

`1,h,7,7,t,ho` · built · Bourbon · Sparkling family

- 1 oz Bourbon
- 1/2 oz Orange liqueur
- 7 dashes Angostura bitters
- 7 dashes Peychaud's bitters
- top with Champagne
- Highball, Orange twist

An ounce of bourbon, half an ounce of orange liqueur, then seven dashes each of Angostura and Peychaud's, which is enough bitters to colour the glass and to run the drink. Champagne on top, an orange twist over that. Spiced orange over whiskey, dry at the finish.

Adam Seger created this at the Seelbach Hilton in Louisville in 1995, then invented a history for it: he said he had found it on the hotel's pre-Prohibition menus and dated it to about 1917. The Louisville Courier-Journal reported the rediscovery, Gary and Mardee Regan printed it in New Classic Cocktails in 1997, and Ted Haigh repeated it in Vintage Spirits and Forgotten Cocktails in 2009, by which point it was taken as fact. Seger confessed to Gary Regan, and Robert Simonson published the debunking in The New York Times in October 2016. The drink is real; only its age was made up. This menu pours an ounce of bourbon, half an ounce of orange liqueur, seven dashes each of Angostura and Peychaud's, and Champagne, with an orange twist.

- [Difford's Guide, Seelbach](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/1807/seelbach)

### Scotch

#### Scotch and Soda

`2,t,H` · built · Scotch · Highball family

- 2 oz Scotch
- top with Soda water
- Highball, iced

Two ounces of Scotch and soda to the top of an iced glass. Whisky, water, and gas, so what you taste is the bottle you bought, pulled open: smoke and cereal where the neat pour was tight. Long and cold, and it stays that way.

Patrick Gavin Duffy claimed in his 1934 The Official Mixer's Guide that he brought the highball to America in 1895, at his cafe by the Lyceum Theatre in New York, after an English actor asked for Scotch and soda and he laid in a stock of Usher's. He said the Broadway Scotch craze followed. The New York Times printed his letter making the claim in 1927 without checking it, and Difford's still files it as a claim. This menu pours two ounces of Scotch over ice and tops with soda, no garnish.

- [Difford's Guide, Highball history](https://www.diffordsguide.com/g/1086/highballs/story)
- [Difford's Guide, Scotch Whisky Highball](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/4794/scotch-whisky-highball)

### Light Rum

#### Mojito

`2,Q,h,t,Hm` · built · Light Rum · Highball family

- 2 oz Light rum
- 3/4 oz Lime juice
- 1/2 oz Simple syrup
- one Mint
- top with Soda water
- Highball, iced, Mint

Two ounces of light rum, three-quarters of lime, half an ounce of simple, mint muddled into the glass, then soda over ice. Bruised mint gives oil; shredded mint gives green. Cane, lime, and cold air. A sprig on top, slapped once to wake it up.

The ancestor is the Draque, cane spirit with lime, sugar, and mint, which Cubans were taking daily as medicine by the 1830s and which legend ties to Francis Drake in 1586. When Bacardi's rum replaced the rough aguardiente the drink got the new name. Printed recipes turn up as Mojo Criollo in 1927 and Mojo de Ron in 1929, and the name Mojito appears on the souvenir menu of Sloppy Joe's Bar in Havana for the 1931-32 season, alongside a gin version. La Bodeguita del Medio hangs a note signed by Hemingway claiming his Mojito; Difford's doubts it, since nothing Hemingway published mentions either the drink or the bar. This menu pours two ounces of light rum, three-quarters lime, half an ounce of simple, muddled mint, and soda over ice.

- [Difford's Guide, Mojito cocktail history](https://www.diffordsguide.com/g/1228/mojito-cocktail/mojito-cocktail-history)

### Tequila

#### Paloma

`2,1,h,h,t,HS` · built · Tequila · Highball family

- 2 oz Tequila
- 1 oz Grapefruit juice
- 1/2 oz Lime juice
- 1/2 oz Simple syrup
- top with Soda water
- Highball, iced, Salt rim

Two ounces of tequila, a full ounce of grapefruit, half an ounce each of lime and simple, then soda over ice. Building the grapefruit half out of juice, syrup, and plain soda leaves the agave in front; a grapefruit soda would sit over it. Salt on the rim pulls the bitter edge off the grapefruit.

The paper trail starts with a 1950 brochure for Squirt, an American grapefruit soda, suggesting the mix with tequila. Squirt launched in Mexico in 1955 and advertised hard there in the early 1970s, and who first adapted it to Mexican taste is unknown. It was a Jalisco drink through the 1970s and 1980s, associated with the bars on the Parian square in Tlaquepaque, reached Southern California by the late 1990s, and spread across the United States in the early 2000s. Paloma is Spanish for dove. This menu builds the soda half from an ounce of fresh grapefruit, half an ounce of lime, half an ounce of simple, and plain soda water, over ice with a salt rim.

- [The Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails, The Paloma](https://www.spiritsanddistilling.com/dictionary/acref-9780199311132-e-379)
- [Difford's Guide, Paloma](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/1456/paloma)

### Mezcal

#### Mezcal Mule

`2,h,t,HLw` · built · Mezcal · Highball family

- 2 oz Mezcal
- 1/2 oz Lime juice
- top with Ginger beer
- Highball, iced, Lime wheel

Two ounces of mezcal, half an ounce of lime, and ginger beer over ice. Smoke and ginger are both loud and they hold each other up; the lime keeps the middle clean. Agave all the way down, under a lime wheel.

The Mule template took a Mexican spirit early. Difford's files the tequila version as the Mexican Mule, also called El Burro, and the mezcal version is the same build with the smoked agave in the spirit slot. Nothing is on record about who poured the first one. It dates from the 2000s, when mezcal reached American back bars. This menu pours two ounces of mezcal, half an ounce of lime, and ginger beer over ice, with a lime wheel.

- [Difford's Guide, Mexican Mule](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/1306/mexican-mule)

### Vodka

#### Moscow Mule

`2,h,t,HLw` · built · Vodka · Highball family

- 2 oz Vodka
- 1/2 oz Lime juice
- top with Ginger beer
- Highball, iced, Lime wheel

Two ounces of vodka, half an ounce of lime, and ginger beer over ice. Ginger and lime carry it, with the vodka as weight underneath, so the drink gets sharper the hotter the ginger beer is. Lime wheel.

The usual story puts it at the Cock 'n Bull in Los Angeles in 1941, where John G. Martin of Heublein was trying to sell Smirnoff and the owner Jack Morgan was trying to sell his ginger beer. The bar's head bartender, Charles Wesley Price, said he made the first one and served it to Broderick Crawford and Rod Cameron. A competing account has Martin and Morgan working it out in New York first, and the Oxford Companion calls the whole thing possibly apocryphal. The copper mug was a marketing decision, and Martin went bar to bar with an instant camera photographing bartenders holding one. This menu pours two ounces of vodka, half an ounce of lime, and ginger beer over ice in a highball, with a lime wheel.

- [The Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails, The Moscow Mule](https://www.spiritsanddistilling.com/dictionary/acref-9780199311132-e-371)
- [Difford's Guide, Moscow Mule](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/1366/moscow-mule)

#### Vodka Soda

`2,t,HLw` · built · Vodka · Highball family

- 2 oz Vodka
- top with Soda water
- Highball, iced, Lime wheel

Two ounces of vodka and soda over ice. It drinks like cold water with weight in it and a mineral edge off the bubbles. The bottle you poured is all the flavour there is, and a lime wheel is all the seasoning.

Nobody invented this one. It is the highball template with vodka in the spirit slot, and it arrived with vodka's rise in American bars after the Second World War. Difford's puts the ratio with the widest appeal at two and a half parts soda to one of vodka, and notes that a couple of dashes of grapefruit bitters round off the edge. This menu pours two ounces of vodka and soda over ice, with a lime wheel.

- [Difford's Guide, Vodka Soda](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/4280/vodka-soda)

#### Vodka & Tonic

`2,t,HLw` · built · Vodka · Highball family

- 2 oz Vodka
- top with Tonic water
- Highball, iced, Lime wheel

Two ounces of vodka, then tonic to the top of an iced highball. With no juniper in the way the drink is the tonic itself: quinine bitter, a little sweet, cold and long. The lime wheel is a squeeze of oil and acid on the way in, and it is most of what you smell.

Vodka came up in America in the 1940s and 1950s on the back of the Moscow Mule and Smirnoff's advertising, and tonic was the obvious second mixer once gin had shown the way. In Britain it overtook the Gin and Tonic in the 1980s, helped along by television: Arthur Daley in Minder ordered a large V.A.T. often enough that the initials stuck. Difford's pours it long over ice with a lime wedge. This menu pours two ounces of vodka and tops with tonic over ice, lime wheel.

- [Difford's Guide, Vodka & Tonic (VAT)](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/10383/vodka-and-tonic-vat)

#### Salty Dog

`2,4,RS` · built · Vodka · Highball family

- 2 oz Vodka
- 4 oz Grapefruit juice
- Rocks, iced, Salt rim

Two ounces of vodka and four of fresh grapefruit juice, built over ice in a rocks glass with a salt rim. Grapefruit is bitter and sour at once, and the salt on the rim takes the bitter edge down so the fruit reads sweeter than it is. Cold, tart, and salty at the lip. Without the rim it is a Greyhound.

The Greyhound, gin and grapefruit juice, is in Harry Craddock's 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book. The salt rim arrives in the 1950s and is usually credited to the entertainer George Jessel, who is said to have added it to soften the grapefruit; the drink first prints under this name in the 1962 revised edition of Ted Saucier's Bottoms Up. Gin was the original spirit and vodka took over as it took over everything else in that decade. This menu pours two ounces of vodka and four of grapefruit over ice, salt rim.

- [Difford's Guide, Salty Dog](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/1735/salty-dog)

### Gin

#### Gin & Tonic

`2,t,HLw` · built · Gin · Highball family

- 2 oz Gin
- top with Tonic water
- Highball, iced, Lime wheel

Two ounces of gin, then tonic to the top of an iced highball. Quinine is bitter and the tonic is sweet, and carrying both at once is what rounds the juniper off. The lime wheel is oil and a squeeze on the way in. Cold and long, with the bitterness arriving last.

Quinine went into carbonated water as a malaria tonic in the 1850s, and Schweppes put out its own in 1870 under the name Indian Tonic Water. British India is where gin met it: the Raj was drinking a great deal of gin already, and the quinine dose went down easier sweetened and mixed. Difford's puts the drink in the second half of the nineteenth century and says the first pour is lost. This menu pours two ounces of gin and tops with tonic over ice, with a lime wheel.

- [Difford's Guide, Gin and Tonic](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/835/gin-and-tonic)

#### Gin Rickey

`2,h,t,HL` · built · Gin · Highball family

- 2 oz Gin
- 1/2 oz Lime juice
- top with Soda water
- Highball, iced, Lime twist

Two ounces of gin, half an ounce of lime, and soda over ice. Lime and bubbles are the only things standing next to the gin, so it lands sharp and the juniper is bare. Long and dry, lime twist on top.

The Rickey is a Washington drink. Joseph Kyle Rickey, a Missouri lobbyist, was drinking whiskey with carbonated water at Shoomaker's bar in the late 1880s, and the bartender George Williamson is credited by some with adding the squeezed half lime. Rickey said he introduced the drink rather than invented it, and put the idea down to Enno Sander, a Prussian physician who argued carbonated water made the more refreshing mixer. The name was circulating by 1889, and by the mid-1890s gin had displaced the bourbon. The city council made it the official cocktail of the District of Columbia in 2011. This menu pours two ounces of gin, half an ounce of lime, and soda over ice, with a lime twist.

- [The Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails, The Rickey](https://www.spiritsanddistilling.com/dictionary/acref-9780199311132-e-400)
- [Difford's Guide, Gin Rickey](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/1676/gin-rickey)

#### Tom Collins

`2,1,h,t,Hlc` · built · Gin · Highball family

- 2 oz Gin
- 1 oz Lemon juice
- 1/2 oz Simple syrup
- top with Soda water
- Highball, iced, Lemon twist, Cherry

Two ounces of gin against a full ounce of lemon, half an ounce of simple, and soda to the top over ice. A gin sour stretched long, and that much lemon stays loud through the dilution, with the syrup a thin coat under it. Lemon twist and a cherry on top.

The drink is named for John Collins, head waiter at Limmer's Hotel on Conduit Street in London, whose gin punch was famous by 1814 and who got his own limerick out of it. The split is in the gin: Harry Johnson's 1882 Bartenders' Manual prints a Tom Collins on Old Tom, the sweetened style, and a John Collins on Holland gin. There is also the Great Tom Collins Hoax of 1874, a New York joke in which a man was sent across town to confront a Tom Collins who had been insulting him; whether the joke named the drink or the drink named the joke has never been settled. This menu pours two ounces of gin, an ounce of lemon, half an ounce of simple, and soda over ice, with a lemon twist and a cherry.

- [Difford's Guide, Tom Collins](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/1972/tom-collins)
- [Difford's Guide, Collins cocktails](https://www.diffordsguide.com/encyclopedia/490/cocktails/collins-cocktails)

#### Elderflower Collins

`1h,Q,Q,t,Hl` · built · Gin · Highball family

- 1 1/2 oz Gin
- 3/4 oz Elderflower liqueur
- 3/4 oz Lemon juice
- top with Soda water
- Highball, iced, Lemon twist

An ounce and a half of gin, three-quarters of elderflower liqueur, three-quarters of lemon, and soda over ice. The elderflower is the sugar in this Collins, so the sweetness arrives floral, and the lemon keeps it tart underneath. Long and light, lemon twist.

A Collins is gin, lemon, sugar, and soda, and the modern habit is to move the sugar into a liqueur. St-Germain, the first elderflower liqueur, arrived in 2007, made from flowers picked in the Haute-Savoie and macerated within 48 hours, and the Elderflower Collins followed the bottle onto back bars. Difford's prints a version that adds a touch of maraschino beside the elderflower. No creator and no date are attached to it. This menu pours an ounce and a half of gin, three-quarters of elderflower, three-quarters of lemon, and soda over ice, with a lemon twist.

- [Difford's Guide, Elderflower Collins](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/704/elderflower-collins)
- [Difford's Guide, St Germain Elderflower Liqueur](https://www.diffordsguide.com/beer-wine-spirits/182/st-germain-elderflower-liqueur)

### Vermouth

#### Americano

`1h,1h,t,Ho` · built · Vermouth · Highball family

- 1 1/2 oz Campari
- 1 1/2 oz Sweet vermouth
- top with Soda water
- Highball, iced, Orange twist

An ounce and a half each of Campari and sweet vermouth, then soda over ice. Equal pours, so bitter orange and grape sit level, and the soda stretches both into something you can drink for an hour. Low proof, and it stays bitter to the end. An orange twist goes over the top.

Gaspare Campari put his bitter together with Turin vermouth at the Caffe Campari on Milan's Piazza del Duomo in the 1860s and called it the Milano-Torino, after where the two bottles came from. Adding soda made it the Americano, American-style, though the name first belonged to a category: Italian producers sold vermouth with bitters already in it as vermouth americano, and Ferruccio Mazzon's 1920 Il Barista prints two different Americanos. It is the first drink Bond orders in Casino Royale. This menu pours an ounce and a half each of Campari and sweet vermouth over ice, tops with soda, and twists orange over it.

- [Difford's Guide, Americano](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/61/americano)
- [Difford's Guide, Milano Torino](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/3495/milano-torino-mi-to-cocktail)

#### Negroni Sbagliato

`1,1,t,Ro` · built · Vermouth · Sparkling family

- 1 oz Campari
- 1 oz Sweet vermouth
- top with Champagne
- Rocks, iced, Orange twist

An ounce each of Campari and sweet vermouth with sparkling wine on top, over ice. Two thirds of a Negroni with the bubbles doing the gin's lifting: bitter orange and grape, lighter and lower in proof, fizzing at the edge under an orange twist.

Sbagliato means bungled. Mirko Stocchetto, at Bar Basso in Milan, reached for the spumante instead of the gin while building a Negroni and kept the result; Difford's dates the mistake to the late 1980s. Bar Basso has served it ever since, in spumante rather than prosecco, in the oversized stemmed chalices Stocchetto designed in the 1980s and licensed to WMF. He died on 10 November 2016 and his family still runs the bar. This menu pours an ounce each of Campari and sweet vermouth, tops with Champagne, and serves it over ice with an orange twist.

- [Difford's Guide, Negroni Sbagliato](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/2515/negroni-sbagliato)

#### Campari & Tonic

`1h,t,Ho` · built · Vermouth · Highball family

- 1 1/2 oz Campari
- top with Tonic water
- Highball, iced, Orange twist

An ounce and a half of Campari, then tonic to the top of an iced highball. Two bitters meet, gentian and orange peel from the Campari and quinine from the tonic, and the tonic's sugar carries both. Red, dry, and cold. The orange twist sits on the Campari's own orange.

Gaspare Campari made his bitter in Novara in 1860 and the family sold it in Milan from the 1860s on, where it went into soda for the Campari Soda and into vermouth for the Americano. Cutting a bitter liqueur with tonic instead of soda is the Italian aperitivo habit that Punch describes alongside Spain's fortified wines and tonic: the quinine adds a second bitterness and the sugar rounds the first. This menu pours an ounce and a half of Campari and tops with tonic over ice, orange twist.

- [Punch, Pour Some Tonic On It](https://punchdrink.com/articles/beyond-the-gin-and-tonic-cocktail-recipes/)
- [Difford's Guide, 20 best Campari cocktails](https://www.diffordsguide.com/encyclopedia/2343/cocktails/20-best-campari-cocktails)

#### Vermouth & Tonic

`2,t,Ho` · built · Vermouth · Highball family

- 2 oz Sweet vermouth
- top with Tonic water
- Highball, iced, Orange twist

Two ounces of sweet vermouth, then tonic to the top of an iced highball. Wormwood, vanilla, and dried orange from the vermouth over quinine, with the wine's sugar and the tonic's meeting in the middle. Low proof and long; an orange twist on top.

Spain drinks vermouth as its own occasion, la hora del vermut, poured from the tap in bars across Madrid and Barcelona from the late nineteenth century on and served over ice with a slice of orange, an olive, and a splash of soda or tonic. Punch lists tonic with vermouth beside sherry and white port as the Iberian answer to the Gin and Tonic, fortified wine in the spirit's place. This menu pours two ounces of sweet vermouth and tops with tonic over ice, orange twist.

- [Punch, 10 Classic Spanish Cocktail Recipes](https://punchdrink.com/articles/classic-spanish-cocktail-recipes-spain/)
- [Punch, Pour Some Tonic On It](https://punchdrink.com/articles/beyond-the-gin-and-tonic-cocktail-recipes/)

#### Sherry & Tonic

`2,t,Hl` · built · Vermouth · Highball family

- 2 oz Sherry
- top with Tonic water
- Highball, iced, Lemon twist

Two ounces of amontillado, then tonic to the top of an iced highball. The sherry is nutty and bone dry, the tonic is bitter and a little sweet, and together they make a long drink with almost no sugar in it. The lemon twist brightens the nut. It drinks like a cold aperitif from Jerez.

In Andalusia sherry has always been a long drink as well as a wine: fino goes into lemon soda for the Rebujito at the ferias, and fino or amontillado goes into tonic at the bar. Punch groups it with vermouth and white port as the fortified wines Spain and Portugal take with tonic. Amontillado, a fino aged on past its flor, is the bottle this shelf carries, and its nuttiness stands up to the quinine better than a fino would. This menu pours two ounces of sherry and tops with tonic over ice, lemon twist.

- [Difford's Guide, Sherry cocktails](https://www.diffordsguide.com/g/1277/sherry-cocktails)
- [Punch, Pour Some Tonic On It](https://punchdrink.com/articles/beyond-the-gin-and-tonic-cocktail-recipes/)

### Absinthe

#### Death in the Afternoon

`1h,t,h` · built · Absinthe · Sparkling family

- 1 1/2 oz Absinthe
- top with Champagne
- Highball

An ounce and a half of absinthe with Champagne poured onto it. The wine goes cloudy as the anise louches, and that milkiness is the trick of it. Anise, wormwood, and fennel over dry bubbles, in a tall glass with no ice. It drinks easier than its proof.

Hemingway contributed it to So Red the Nose, or Breath in the Afternoon, a 1935 collection of cocktails by authors, and named it after his 1932 book on bullfighting. His own instruction: pour one jigger of absinthe into a Champagne glass, add iced Champagne until it attains the proper opalescent milkiness, and drink three to five of these slowly. He credited the recipe to himself and three officers of HMS Danae, after seven hours in the water trying to get Captain Bra Saunders' fishing boat off a bank. This menu pours an ounce and a half of absinthe and tops with Champagne.

- [Difford's Guide, Death In The Afternoon](https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/623/death-in-the-afternoon)
